en: (ṇoḥ - 1633ka) (Ṭīkā on the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā) (Extent: 83 folios)
(From Āgeḥ – Saṃvat 1950) (Subject:
Tantra) Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. The Heart of the Illustrious Śrīkośa, Part Five...

The fruit of the wish-fulfilling creepers consists of a lion-throne, radiant with five jewels; it resides within the treasury of the four lineages, bringing joy to the fourfold assembly, and is offered at the abode of the Supreme Brahman, which is eternally blissful.
For the sake of attaining [this state], the illustrious Goddess said: "O Great God, O you who are beautiful with the bliss of grace! I desire to know in truth that abode consisting of Brahman;
how, O Lord, is it accompanied by Śrī, and how does it hold the treasury of Śrī in its heart?"

How is it served by the five lion-thrones? How is it of the nature of the wish-fulfilling creeper? How is it of the nature of jewels, O God? How is it of the nature of a sanctuary? How is it to be served as the primordial source? How is it of the nature of the eternal?

The venerable Lord said: This reality, which is the self of all, is the supreme goddess Tripurā; she is served by the four Lakṣmīs, who are the bestowers of the nectar of her own form—namely, Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī.

Likewise, Triśakti and Sarvasāmrājyalakṣmī are proclaimed as the five [deities]. The seed-syllable (bīja) consisting of the Bindu and Nāda, which is the letter 'va' from the Vāruṇa [group] situated upon the letter 'ra' from the Vahni [group] and joined with a long eye (ī), is declared to be the Lakṣmī-mantra.
O beloved, for this [mantra], the seer is Bhṛgu, the meter is Nivṛt, and the presiding deity is Śrī;
the seed-syllable is *śat*, the power (*śakti*) is *ya*, and the peg (*kīlaka*) is said to be the letter *ra*.
O beautiful one, with the second, fourth, sixth, and seventh [syllables], [one attains] Indra.

O beautiful one, having worshipped the Vidyā along with the digit of the moon (the *nandakalā*), the practitioner of mantra should constantly perform the six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in this sequence: first the heart, then the head, then the crest, then the armor, then the eye, and finally the weapon, using the syllables *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *huṃ*.
One should install [the mantras] along with *vauṣaṭ*, *astra* (*phaṭ*), and *ca-phaṭ*. One should draw an eight-petaled diagram and draw a square enclosure outside it.
Having placed a flower in the center, one should worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*). Vibhū...
One should worship Tīrth (the sacred ford), Kānti (splendor), Sṛṣṭi (creation), Kīrti (fame), Saṃtati (progeny), Vyuṣṭi (prosperity), Utkṛṣṭi (excellence), Ṛddhi (abundance),
and Vasu in the various directions; O Dear One, having worshipped the Lion-throne in the center, which consists of all powers, one should meditate.
Then [he beheld] that beautiful Śrī, saluted by all the gods, shining with the luster of refined gold, adorned with divine jewels,
being sprinkled with nectars and the liquid flow of pearls and gems, and radiant with a brilliant white light.

The wise man should repeatedly meditate upon Padmākṣmī in the heart of Padmanābha— she who is beloved by the pair of bees, whose crown is set with a multitude of jewels, and whose limbs are radiant with pure silk garments. Thus.
Having meditated, one should always worship the Goddess, who holds a pair of lotuses, who is rich in the splendor of granting boons and dispelling fear, four-armed, and three-eyed;
one should display the mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), in their proper sequence. Uccāṃ.

One should turn the *añjali* downward; this becomes the *āvāhanī* (invocation) mudrā. However, when it is reversed, it becomes the *sthāpanī* (establishment) mudrā. When both fists have the thumbs pointing upward, that is the *sannidhāpanī* (presence) mudrā. The *aṃ* [is used].

By pressing the thumb and fist together, that is the "confinement" (saṃnirodhinī) mudrā; by rotating [the hands] with the two index fingers, it becomes the "totalization" (sakalīkaraṇa). Having formed the añjali as for the arghya offering, it becomes the "transformation into the supreme" (paramīkaraṇa); then, having turned [them] around...

One should place the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and little finger of the right hand against those of the left hand respectively; this is the *Amṛtīkaraṇa* mudrā, O Goddess, which has the form of a cow (*dhenu*). This is the general [mudrā] for these.

O Dear One, having shown [the deity] the *drāstu* [mudrā], one should worship perfectly with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. The worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjana*) is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, Vāyu, and in the center; and [the goddesses] Lākā and Vimalā [are worshipped].
One should worship Kamalācanālikā, Vibhīṣikālikā, Śāṅkarī, and Sumālikā in front, proceeding in order by way of circumambulation; [and likewise] Indrāgnī.

One should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) known as Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Anila, Kuvera, and Īśāna in the sequence beginning with the Earth; one should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu as the world-protectors of the upper and lower directions respectively; [and perform] one hundred thousand recitations of the Sun-mantra.

One should recite the mantra and, according to that same proportion, perform fire oblations (*homa*) with lotuses mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). Thereby, one becomes a practitioner who has completed the preliminary course (*puraścaraṇa*).
Thus, when the mantra is fully perfected, it bestows universal sovereignty. [Thus ends the Śrīda...]
In the Kṣīrāmūrtisaṃhitā, the first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Single-Syllable Lakṣmī," Lord Īśvara said: "O Maheśānī,
I shall declare the supreme *Lakṣmīhṛdaya*, the power of which..."
Great calamities flee at the mere knowledge [of this].

Having first uttered the syllable "Hari," which is one's own self, [one should recite] the "Śrī-enclosure" (śrīpuṭa), or else "Kamala," "Brahmā," and likewise "Bhānu"; [the mantra] should be placed in the middle of the "Lāpa."
One should place that ground in the station of Rudra; the pair of *prasīda* [mantras] with the seed-syllables enclosed as before, ending with the heart of Mahālakṣmī,
consists of twenty-eight syllables, and Dakṣa Prajāpati is also [included].
The sage and the meter are likewise Gāyatrī; Lakṣmī is proclaimed as the deity. The second and third [syllables] are the seed and the power respectively, and O Goddess, the Praṇava is the bolt.
Then, the practitioner, being composed, should assign the limbs [of the deity] as before;
he should hold a pair of golden lotuses with eight petals at their tips,
along with a garland of fire and a shining mirror.
The third [form] has four arms, with shimmering jeweled anklets, radiant with a crown, enriched with necklaces, armlets, and long pendants, adorned with tinkling bells and jeweled earrings,
seated upon a lotus throne, and surrounded by female messengers.

Having thus meditated upon that Great Divine Lady, whose body and garments are always white, one should worship the Goddess as before at the eastern entrance; first worshipping her limbs as previously described, O Supreme Sovereign.
One should worship Bhāratī, Pārvatī, Caṇḍī, and Śacī in the cardinal directions;
and for the sake of attaining all perfections (siddhis), one should worship these—Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Viśvarūpadhṛk—in the intermediate directions. Following this...
One should worship Rāga, Viṣamvāda, Vijaya, Vallabha, Mada, Harṣa, Bala, and Tejasvin, beginning from the east; having worshipped Indra and the others as well,
the wise one should again worship the Goddess and perform three hundred thousand recitations.
The practitioner, desiring prosperity, must regularly offer oblations with lotuses according to one-tenth of the mantra's count;
for him, great elephants and horses will be born in his home, adorned with gold, jewels, ornaments, and the like.

"From that, one shall become a practitioner [thus ends the second chapter, the procedure for the worship of Mahālakṣmī, in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā]. The Lord said: I shall now describe the worship of the Three Powers."

One should write the seed-syllable of Śrī, the supreme seed-syllable, and the seed-syllable of Kāma, which bestows all accomplishments upon men. O Goddess, this triple power (triśakti) is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. Its seer is Brahmā, its meter is Gāyatrī...

O Dear One, one should recite the mantra mentioned in the *Dīpikā* two times over the limbs of the deity consisting of the three powers (*triśakti*). O Dear One, I shall now describe the yantra for the benefit of practitioners:
having first drawn a hexagon, [one should place] in the center...

The wise one should draw [the diagram] with repetition; he should worship that [deity] in each of the six corners of the hexagon. Outside, he should decorate it with eight petals adorned with long and short vowels, and he should draw a square mandala adorned with four gates.
Having invoked the Goddess into the center [of that], one should meditate upon her, the bestower of all prosperity,
seated upon an excellent jewel-throne situated within a great forest of Kalpa-trees, inside a pavilion with jeweled walls shimmering like fresh gold.

Richly adorned with the splendor of various seats, colored by jeweled anklets, her head radiant with shimmering gems, decorated with jeweled earrings, and graced with diverse ornaments fashioned from endless jewels; she who is... [da]...
She has six arms, holding a pair of lotuses, a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows;
she has a moon-like face and is surrounded by female messengers who hold beautiful chowries and carry gems, mirrors, and fine vessels in their hands. Her... [I worship] her.
With hands holding boxes of ornaments and vessels of refined gold,
one should worship [the deity] in the previously mentioned maṇḍala, which shines like molten gold;
having propitiated [her] with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should then worship the limbs and the surrounding deities (aṅgāvaraṇa) as before.

Then one should worship the retinue of the Supreme Lord: Lakṣmī and Hari, Girijā and Śiva, and Rati and Aṅgaja, in due order, beginning from the front corner. Then, on both sides of the hexagon, one should worship Śaṃ...
The two worthy ones, Kha and Padmanidhi, are in the center; on the eight petals are the Mothers:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh.
One should first worship the great goddess Hālakṣmī; then, having worshipped Indra and the others who have assumed the forms of amorous women—
intoxicated by their youth and beauty, and intent on the propitiation of the Goddess— [one should proceed].

O Goddess, the wise practitioner of mantras, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule; O Mistress of the Gods, he should then perform a fire sacrifice with *kiṃśuka* flowers using a tenth part of that number.
By this procedure, O Beloved, the practitioner of mantras becomes one who has completed the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
[Thus ends the third chapter, the ritual for the worship of Lakṣmī of the Three Powers, in the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā. The Lord said:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the deity who bestows universal sovereignty.
O Dear One, by the propitiation of this Vaiṣṇavī Vidyā, Viṣṇu himself became the Lord of Lakṣmī; Candra became Śaṃkara; and Agni became the Lord of the Earth adorned with long eyes.
This [Vidyā] is joined with the Mistress of the Mountain (Umā). O Śrī, this is the Vaiṣṇavī.
One should perform the *jasaṃpuṭa* (encasement with *ja-sa*), which bestows universal sovereignty. Hari is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī meter in the *chaṃdas* style is prescribed for it.
The deity is Mohinī Lakṣmī, the bestower of great imperial power. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *kū*.
The syllable *ṬAṂ* is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śakti; having pierced it with the six vowels, one should assign the six limbs.
[One should meditate on her] resembling the flower of the *atasī*, adorned with all kinds of jewels, and holding a conch...

The wise one, having meditated upon her as eight-armed— holding a lotus, a noose, a discus, a bow, and arrows in her hands, while with two hands she wields a sword and is graced by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness— should recite the mantra one hundred and twenty thousand times, and its tenth part...
O beloved, for the sake of attaining the empire of Tuḥuṇe with the Śenapadmas, listen to the extraction of the yantras according to the rules by one who has conquered the senses:
one should draw a triangle, an eight-spoked yantra, and the orb of the earth upon that [base].
One should draw this yantra, richly adorned with four beautiful gates;
having invoked the Goddess into it, one should worship her with ritual offerings (upacāras) as before, O Supreme Lady, and perform the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅga).
O Goddess, one should worship Yajñī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī in sequence from the foremost portion, and likewise Brahmī and the others individually with their respective vowels;
on the eight petals on the ground, one should worship them with a single utterance.
One should write "namo" to the eighteen great koṭis of yoginīs with this mantra;
thereafter, one should worship Indra and the other [deities],
and then again worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) and the yoginīs.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sāmrājyavidyā," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. The Lord said:
Now, O Pārvatī, hear the fourfold group of the Śrī-kośa vidyās, by the mere knowledge of which there is no further rebirth. The Śrī-vidyā is the supreme light, the supreme, partless deity. A...
The *japā-mātṛkā* is proclaimed to consist of five sheaths (*pañcakośa*).
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should write the words *māyā* and *ahaṃsa*; then *so'haṃ* is the head (*śiras*) of the deity. This is declared to be the *vasuvarṇā*.
The Praṇava is to be known as the digit of consciousness (citkalā), whose form is pervaded by Māyā;
the word "Haṃsa," O Mistress of Gods, is the direct embodiment of the Self.
Within it, the triad of dots (bindus) consists of the nature of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Beloved, she who gives birth through the Bindu and Nāda is Vāmā, whose form is Brahman; she who protects the three worlds with the second [Bindu],
Bindunātha, is this Jyeṣṭhā, the primordial Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, characterized by the quality of Sattva.
Enveloped by darkness, she devours everything with the three parts and the *bindu*.
O Goddess, when the three *bindus* are produced from Aṃbikā, then Raudrī manifests herself;
this is the withdrawal known as Haṃsā, when she reveals the Self. At that time...
From the form of a mirror, it then becomes composed of light;
from the two syllables of the wife of Fire (Svāhā), O Dear One, this is the supreme light. Contemplating thus, the practitioner of mantra shall become manifest Brahman. The seer is Brahmā...

The meter of this mantra is said to be Gāyatrī; its deity is proclaimed to be the Supreme Light itself. The syllable Om (Praṇava) is the seed (bīja), the two [syllables] following it are the power (śakti), the remainder is the bolt (kīlaka), and Svāhā is the end.
The heart is *haṃ*, the shoulder is *haṃ*, the head is *haṃsaḥ*, and the crest (*śikhā*) becomes *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*).

The armor (*kavaca*) is formed with the seed-syllable *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), and the three eyes are formed with the entire mantra, O Goddess of Gods; by touching [these parts] with the mantra, one becomes auspicious through knowledge.
"By offering oblations of the syllables of the Mother-mantra (Mātṛkā) as sacrificial fuel with this mantra,
one shall attain the state of Nirvāṇa in an instant.
Thus ends the Ātma-aṣṭākṣara [mantra] in the Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā.
[The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Ritual Arrangement of the Supreme Light"] The Lord said:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme, partless Deity,
by the mere remembrance of whom the body becomes filled with the bliss of consciousness.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, you who consist of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā through your grace;
this supreme Niṣkala Goddess is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, clad in white garments,
adorned with white garlands and unguents, and bearing the Jñāna-mudrā.

It is served by the assembly of the lords of yogis; the seer (ṛṣi) is Brahmā, the meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī belonging to Manu, and the deity (devatā) is Brahmā himself. The seed-syllable (bīja) and the power (śakti) therein follow the sequence beginning with the letter *ma*.

O Goddess of the gods, having placed the four vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* in the middle of the pair of vowels [e and o], which bestow the fruit of liberation from the stake and grant the knowledge [of the mantra],
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

The practitioner of mantra should draw a water-device (toya-yatra) consisting of a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square adorned with four gates; this bestows knowledge. Then, having meditated upon it at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), he should invoke the Supreme Goddess there.
One should perform worship with perfumes, flowers,
and other pleasing offerings in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, Vāyu, and the center;
one should worship Brahmā, whose form is the syllable *ṛ*, in the east with the syllable *a*.
One should worship Hari with the Sāmaveda accompanied by the syllable *ukāra*.
One should worship the Goddess to the south, and then worship Śiva in the final corner;
O beloved, the form of the Yajurveda is said to be in the triangle at the time [of worship].

O Dear One, one should worship the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Knowledge-Self (Parama-jñānātman) in the four directions of the eight-petaled lotus, following the sequence starting from the East; likewise, one should worship the tetrad of Nivṛtti,
Pravṛtti, Vidyā, and Śānti in the intermediate directions.
The practitioner of mantra should worship Kṣu, and thereafter worship Brahmā and the others; then,
in those very eight petals of the lotus and in the square [mandala],
he should worship the world-protectors, Indra and the rest, in order starting from the east.
One should satisfy [the deity] with offerings of perfumes, flowers, food, and libations;
then the practitioner becomes the embodiment of knowledge, and liberation rests in his hand.
Thus ends the section on the Praṇava in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Motionless Deity," the Lord said: O sinless Goddess, I shall describe to you the worship of Ajapā,
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes the Supreme Brahman itself.
O Goddess, if a person daily recites the *Śikha-haṃsa* mantra without knowing the supreme lords [of the mantras],
being bound by delusion, liberation does not arise for him; however, O Goddess,
when it is known through the grace of the venerable Guru, it is then recited.
Through the state of exhalation and inhalation, the bondage of that [individual soul] comes to an end.
In both exhalation and inhalation, there are the two syllables "Haṃ" and "Saṃ"; therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa), known as Haṃsa, abides in the form of the Self (ātman).
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* are considered one *nāḍikā*;
sixty *nāḍikās* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*).
O Goddess, the number of recitations for the mind is twenty-one thousand six hundred.

One should daily recite the supreme mantra consisting of bliss within the vital breath (prāṇa). Its commencement is birth, and its conclusion is death. O Lord of Gods, for the practitioner, there is no recitation without the breath; indeed, the breath itself is the recitation.
Then, O Goddess, the *peya* (the drink) was proclaimed as the cutter of the bonds of worldly existence;
it is obtained through the grace of the venerable Guru, O dear one, and not otherwise.
O Maheśānī, one should offer this recitation (*japa*) every day to Gaṇeśa.

O Maheśvarī, [one should offer oblations] to Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara; likewise, in the same sequence, to the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme soul (paramātman)— six hundred, six thousand,
and again six thousand [times].
Furthermore, one should offer one thousand stainless [lotuses] and another thousand to the Guru in due order;
one should meditate on these as being peaceful and beginning with the letter 'Va' within this golden-colored support (ādhāra). Melted...
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon the letters from *va* to *la*, which are golden-hued, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
and those from *ba* to *kṣa*, which possess the brilliance of a mass of lightning, in the Maṇipūraka located within the water.
O Dear One, one should contemplate the letters from *u* to *pha*, which possess the luster of great sapphires;
and one should contemplate the letters from *ka* to *ṅa*, which are of a golden hue and have the brilliance of the center of a great fire,
as struck by the fourth vowel (*ū*).
One should place the vowels of smoke-colored purity upon the red-colored [syllables];
in the Ājñā [cakra], which has the luster of lightning, one should contemplate the white *haṃ* and *kṣa*;
and within the thousand-petaled lotus, shining with the brilliance of camphor, [one should contemplate] the *nāda*.

Know it to be of the nature of Brahman in the *brahmarandhra*, O Supreme Goddess. Having offered the recitation (*japa*) consisting of what occurs day and night, O Beloved, to those [deities] stationed within these seven wheels (*cakras*), O Supreme Goddess—
O wise one, perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Haṃsa-Parameśānī:
the seer is Haṃsa, the meter is said to be the manifest Gāyatrī, the deity is the Supreme Self, and "Haṃsaḥ" is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*). It is that.
Śakti is the kīlaka, "I" (Ahaṃ) is the Praṇava, and indeed Tattva is likewise; O Supreme Goddess, Nāda is the station and the color is white; U is the accent—thus is the mantra proclaimed. Mo.
O Pārvatī, know that the application [of mantras] for the sake of protection should be performed in this manner;

thereafter, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) for the purification of the body. O Goddess, [one should worship] Sūrya, Soma, and likewise Nirañjana thereafter. Nirā...
One should sequentially place the syllables ending in *bhāsa*, followed by the dative case and *svāhā*;
then, having placed those ending in *kavaca*, one should contemplate the word *ananta*.
Then, having uttered the four syllables *tanu-sūkṣma*, one should utter *devī pracodayāt*.
The invocation is preceded by unmanifest syllables (*avyaktapada*) and ends with *svāhā*;
the self of awakening (*prabodhātman*) is recited with the fourth [case-ending], ending with the fire-mantra (*agnimantra*) and the *astramantra*.
Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the rules, the mantra-practitioner, being perfectly composed, [should proceed].
O Goddess, having filled the interior of that jar with the root mantra, one should perform the withdrawal by means of the right [nostril];
the holding of the nostril is performed with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
Prāṇāyāma should be understood as being performed without the index and middle fingers;
O Goddess,
the two eyelashes of this Haṃsa are Agni and Soma, and the head is the Tāraka.
The three *bindus* are proclaimed as the crest, the eyes, and the mouth; the sound (*nāda*) is the pair of the states of Śiva and Śakti, the two sides of the fire of time (*kālāgni*).
This is indeed the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*), all-pervading and luminous.
Resembling ten million suns, self-luminous, this *haṃsa*— which takes the form of transmigratory existence— shines forth here and reveals discernment (*viveka*).
This *gāyatrī* known as *ajapā* is difficult to find within the three worlds.
For one who constantly recites the *Jaya* mantra, rebirth no longer exists; there, for twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths],
the vital air (*vāyu*) moves throughout day and night— that *Jaya* bestows liberation.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Mātṛkā," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. The Lord said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the Mātṛkā, the mother of the world.
The deity who constitutes the constituent letters from *a* to *kṣa* is the deity of this mantra;
Brahmā is said to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is its meter (*chandas*). The Mātṛkā-deities are its seed-syllables (*bīja*) here on earth, and they are its powers (*śakti*).
The vowels, O Supreme Goddess, are born from the Unmanifest; the Kīlaka is the Unmanifest. The indescribable consonants indeed become unmanifest through Śakti.
Without Śakti, O Śivā, there exists no name, no subtle state, and no abode.

The letters are of the nature of existence; by their power, they are not turned away from being. They are to be uttered as the manifesting essence of existence, facing toward manifestation, having abandoned the vowels *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, and situated within the six-faced vowel (*u*).
Following the sequence of the six groups of consonants, the seventh group should be joined with the *krodha* (the letter *ya*).
Having placed it at the end, O Goddess of Gods, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
One should properly place the vowels upon the petals of the lotus of the throat, which represents the *kalā*.

O Great Goddess, one should constantly place twelve [syllables] on the lotus with sun-like petals; O Īśvarī, one should place ten syllables in the Maṇipūra [cakra] which has ten petals, and likewise six [syllables] on the six petals in the middle of the liṅga.
Likewise, one should place the four letters upon the fourteen-petaled foundation;
in the two-petaled space between the eyebrows, one should contemplate *ha* and *kṣa*, and then place the Mātṛkā [letters].
Likewise, in the Brahma-aperture, surrounding the wheel, and in the two eyes and the ears...
One should place [the syllables] in the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the two faces— thus sixteen locations;
one should then sequentially place them in the joints of the feet along with the knees, and in the pair of sides.
Then one should place [the letters] upon the two buttocks, the navel, and the abdomen.
The bodily constituents (dhātus) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen;
and the vital breaths (prāṇas), the individual soul (jīva), and the supreme [self] are situated in the [respective] upper [parts], the assistance [of the body], and so forth.
One should assign [the mantras] beginning with *meṇade* to the goddesses of the lords of the gods, consisting of that very self;
one should assign them at the root of the heart, and likewise assign them to the other [parts]:
starting from the heart, to both armpits, to the two hands and feet, and likewise to the belly.
One should place the goddess in the form of the letters upon the two faces; by means of this method of letter-assignment (*varṇanyāsa*),
the practitioner, possessing the very nature of the letters,
should meditate in due order on her who is enriched by the forms of the letters and whose faces are the vowels.
She whose lotus-feet begin with the *ca*-group and end with the *ta*-group, whose beautiful sides are adorned with the *pa*-group,
who possesses a slender waist, and whose full, firm breasts are auspiciously marked with the limbs of the *ya*-group.
One should meditate upon her, whose garment is as white as the moon, who has bright eyes and a slender waist;
whose body is colored with white garlands, who is adorned with a rosary at her hips,
whose virtuous hands are depicted in a state of contemplation, and who bestows all boons.
Having meditated thus upon the Goddess, the wise man should perform the sacrifice; first,
he should draw a circle called the pericarp, containing the *haṃsa* mantra, the grace, and the creation, and outside of that, having drawn eight petals, he should place the vowels upon the filaments.

Then, O Supreme Goddess, by means of the division of pairs and pairs, one should place the eight groups of consonants beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'lakṣa' upon the eight petals; thereafter, one should draw a square that bestows success, inscribing it within the cardinal directions.
Having likewise drawn four *ṭha*-letters ending in a line on the exterior,
and having inscribed the *vāruṇa* [mantra], the wise one should invoke the Goddess,
after first performing worship at the pedestal (*pīṭha*) preceded by the nine *śaktis*.
One should worship Medhā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Vidyā, Dhīr, Dhṛti, Smṛti, and Buddhi, as well as Vidyeshvarī, in the directions starting from the east and in the center;
thereafter, having invoked [the deity], one should present the services (upacāras) such as perfumes and so forth.
O Goddess, one should perform the worship of the limbs in the directions of Agni (southeast), Īśa (northeast), Sūrya (southwest), Vāyu (northwest), and the center;
having joined each with the pair of vowels ending in *namaḥ*,
one should worship separately in eight ways, individually upon the filaments.

In the same manner, one should separately offer salutations to each group beginning with 'ka' and so forth; this is the eightfold worship of the groups (vargapūjā). Thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the Goddess by approaching her with the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī, and then with the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One who observes restricted diet should perform the *puraścaraṇa* by offering one hundred thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Thus ends the section on the *Mātṛkā* [in the Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā].
The Eighth Chapter, named *Dhī*. The Lord said:
"O Maheśvarī, you have asked about the Vidyā to be recited while seated upon the lion-throne;
that which is recited by me through the face of Tatpuruṣa, listen to it, O beloved."
O lady of excellent vows, this knowledge, which has no equal and is difficult to find even in the three worlds,

should be performed together with the sound of the water-drops. Having uttered this speech-born [mantra], one should utter the entire seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) while assuming the *vāmana* posture.

The imperishable Bhṛgu, who brought forth the creation from his eyes and is endowed with grace—this three-syllabled Vidyā shall thus come to be. Then, one should place Dakṣiṇāmūrti as the Seer (Ṛṣi) upon the head; next, the Metre (Chandas).
The lineage (paṅkti) should be understood as follows: having placed the deity at the mouth, the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava is said to be in the heart, O Supreme Goddess;
the Śakti-seed is indeed Śakti herself, and the Kāma-seed is Kāla. This is the Vidyā.

O Maheśānī, bestower of the goals of human endeavor, one should place the *āyā* mantra from the feet up to the navel, and likewise the *madhyama-śakti-bīja* from the throat to the top of the head; [one should place it] starting from the left foot.

One should place these two mantras in the hands of Akṣapāṇi; by doing so in both [hands] joined together, there shall be this twofold placement (nyāsa). Thereafter, the wise one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, enclosed within those two, marked with the nine-yoni diagram.
O lotus-eyed one, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the two ears,

the lips, O Goddess, on the conch-like mouth, the two eyes, and the nose; O Goddess, one should place [the mantras] on the two shoulders, the heart, the two elbows, the two sides of the abdomen, the two knees, and the two feet.

O Dear One, one should place the pair of syllables in the secret parts and the genitals in sequence; one should also place the pair in the sides, the heart, and the throat. One should place the three seed-syllables in the nine locations in that very same order, repeating them for the limbs.
Having placed the five arrows, the wise one should perform the nyāsa; having written the syllable *da*, joined with the letter *va* and fire (*ra*) in two parts,
and adorned above with the two dots (*bindu*) and the infinite eye (*a*).
One should write the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), joined with Kālādi (A), Tādivādī (Ū), and Pṛthivī (L), enriched by a long *karṇa* (Ṛ) and a *bindu* (Ṃ), as an *ajāpāta* [mantra] in sequence;
one should then place it on the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and *mūlādhāra*.
Furthermore, one should place five seed-syllables (*bījas*) within these:

the seed-syllable consisting of *hrīṃ* and *klīṃ*, or else one should write the fourth as the *vāṇa*. Then, the fifth consists of *trīṃ*; these are proclaimed as the five arrows of desire (*pañcakāma*).
O Pārvatī, having thus disposed the body and restrained the vital breaths (prāṇas),
one should meditate upon the Goddess Maheśānī, who dwells in the midst of a Kadamba forest,
within a great jewel pavilion in the heart of a vast primordial forest (mahākalpavana). She is adorned with pearls...
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the shade of a palm tree,
she was radiant with a crown fashioned from priceless gems and shimmering earrings;
she was adorned with necklaces and exquisite gem-studded neck-chains, and resplendent with bracelets.

She is adorned with the beautiful ornaments of pearl necklaces and radiant pure silk garments; she is made lovely by charming ankle-bells, her lotus-feet are like red lotuses, her limbs are beautified by pure unguents,
and she is resplendent with the finest camphor.

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess— who holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, a rosary in her right, who is intent on granting boons, and who perfectly bestows the essence of Sarasvatī—
one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Alternatively, O Lord of the Gods, when this *nandaveda* occurs, then the Vidyās— which grant all aims and bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation—
attained through the grace of the venerable Guru, lead to the fulfillment of all desires and purposes.

O Śivā, one should meditate upon the Goddess of gods, who is the mistress of the gods, possessing the luster of a ruby, clad in red garments, adorned with red ornaments, having the nature of the half-syllable *ha*, and endowed with three *bindus*. Thus.
One should always perform meditation on the Kāmakalā; having prepared the oblation, one should offer it with *kiṃśuka* flowers soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*) for one-tenth of that amount.
Furthermore, one should perform libations (*tarpaṇa*) for one-tenth of that, numbering one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) or ten thousand (*ayuta*).
O beloved, one should perform libations again with water from the Gaṅgā according to the sequence of debts,
and likewise with water scented with camphor. Now,
O Maheśānī, I shall describe the yantra that bestows the accomplishment of all goals.

Having drawn the *dauśakti*, one should draw that same [line] around it, slightly expanded; then, having joined them together somewhat with fire according to the sequence of breaking the joints, it becomes the ninefold *yoni*.
One should write the syllable *hasauṃ* in the center and the one called Kāma in the eight yonis;
having drawn it surrounded by fire and adorned with eight petals,
O Supreme Goddess, one should join the vowels in pairs within the filaments.
Having written the letters of the Caṭāstapa mantra along with the *lakṣa* and the Supreme Goddess upon the eight petals, the practitioner should then draw an eight-pronged trident; thereafter,
he should inscribe the letters in their proper sequence at the tips of the petals.
Upon those tridents, one should draw the vowels from *ka* onwards in order starting from the east;
one should draw *ṅa*, *cha*, and *ja* in the south-eastern quarter; one should draw *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭha* in the southern direction;
one should draw *ḍa*, *ḍha*, and *ṇa* in the south-western quarter; and one should draw *tha*, *dha*, and *da* in the western direction.
One should draw an elephant in the northwestern direction (the region of Vāyu) and a bee in the northern direction; then,
one should draw a circle in the northeastern region (the place of Īśa), and subsequently,
one should draw another circle and within it the seed-syllable using the Mātṛkā letters, and then draw the mandala of the earth.
One should place a flower in the center of that which is enriched with the beauty of four gates;
then the practitioner of mantras should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha), which is pleasing to the Goddess.
Then [the mantras] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Cāmuṇḍā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and Icchā follow.
O Dear One, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kuñcikā, Viśvādevī, Viṣaghnikā, Dūtī, and likewise Ānandā should be worshipped on all sides;
and the mantrin should worship the lion-throne with the central seed-syllable.
One should draw the seat of the great corpse Sadāśiva upon a lotus;
O Goddess, one should worship the lion-throne ending with "Ṅe" and "Namaḥ," O Beloved;
[and one should draw] a pearl parasol and chowries shaped like the moonlight of the autumnal moon.
A pair of fly-whisks with beautiful moon-patterns cast upon their handles, a long necklace shining like a string of pearls, a golden mirror, a small seat,
a casket made of ornaments, and a box filled with moon-like jewels.

O Beloved, having meditated upon her holding in sequence a cup filled with camphor powder, a golden comb, and a vessel of saffron filled with beautiful flowers, one should then invoke the Goddess starting from the left.
Having worshipped [the deity] equally with ritual offerings, one should perform the libations;
O Goddess, one should place the limbs of dissolution and display the mudrās upon the body.
The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Svara (Sūrya), Vāyu, and the center.
Beginning from Meṇapura, Ratī, Prīti, and Manobhava are at the tips of the three corners, O Lord of Gods; outside of those are the deities of the arrows.
To the right of the principal deity are two each, on the left one, and one in front. Anaṅga...
Gānāṅgakusumā, likewise Anaṅgamekhalā, the goddess Anaṅgamadanā, Subhagā, Bhagā, Bhagasarpiṇī, O Goddess, and likewise Bhagamālinī, Purāra—

One should worship Bhya-devī by circumambulating from left to right; one should also worship her in the eight corners and on the beautiful petals outside of that: Asitāṅgī, Brāhmī, Ruṃ, and likewise Ruru-Māheśvarī, and Caṇḍa.
Ḍaṅkaumārikā, Krodhavaiṣṇavī, Unmattavārāhī, Kapālinī,
Māhendrī, Bhīṣaṇā, and thereafter Cāmuṇḍā, O Goddess. Saṃ...
O Goddess, one should worship Hārabhairava and Mahālakṣmī in sequence;
the Goddess [should be worshipped] with the vowels according to the distinction between even and odd [syllables], while the Bhairavas are [worshipped] as follows:
Kāmarūpa and, secondly, Devimalaya.
The seat of Kolagiri, the seat of Kulāntaka, and thereafter,
O Lord of Gods, Cauhāra; and thereafter Jālandhara, Kapālin, Ekapāda, and thereafter Bhīmarūpa.
One should first worship Cala and Hāṭaka; thereafter,
O Goddess, one should worship Indra and the others in the four corners in sequence, and then Vaṭuka and the rest— beginning with Vaṭuka.

O Dear One, one should worship the Yoginīs, the Kṣetrapālas, and Gaṇapati in the cardinal directions starting from the east; then the Vasus, the Rudras, and all the Bhūtas in the corners in the order of the sun; and thereafter, one should again worship the Goddess. Vanamālini.
"O you who are born from the spittle of the gods, rich in fragrance, the best of scents, the offering of incense belonging to Agni for all beings—please accept this.
Thus is the mantra for incense declared, with the three seed-syllables at its end. Well-spoken.
"Kāśī is the great lamp that dispels darkness from all sides;
this lamp, which is light both within and without, is now accepted. Likewise, O beloved, hear this mantra for the lamp, and perform the *ārārtika* ceremony."
O Goddess Tripura, in this maṇḍala which is the excellent seat of the six wheels and whose form is Brahman, accept this *ārārtika* for my spiritual success.
O Goddess, at the conclusion of the Vidyā, this mantra is proclaimed for the *ārārtika*: "Ā Rārtike... [etc.]
Having performed the japa according to one's capacity, one should perform the daily fire sacrifice (nityahoma).
One should offer five oblations with the root mantra and perform the six-limbed homa (ṣaḍaṅga-homa). This is the method for the daily fire sacrifice, which destroys all obstacles.

I shall explain the arrangement as it is for the removal of all obstacles: the knower of mantras should draw a triangle, a circle, and a square mandala in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners.
One should briefly place four mandalas there as vessels;
one should remember the sixfold body (ṣaṭkāyana), Mohya, Gānta, Gaṇapati, Ādyau, Savindu, and Pañca, and offer salutations to the Yoginīs.
"O beloved, at the conclusion, one should offer everything with the mantra: *mamaiva śaṃ cānayaḥ prānte tataḥ sarvopacārataḥ sa hitaṃ ca baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*.
Then, *kṣamaṃte kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*—these are the four mantras."
One should worship the maṇḍalas with forty-two *vaṃ* mantras. [The invocation is:
"Come, come, O Devī-putra, O Vaṭuka-nātha, O Kapila, O one radiant with matted locks, O three-eyed one, O Jvālā..."

"Destroy, destroy all obstacles from the very face [of the practitioner]; accept this offering (bali) together with all its accompaniments"—this mantra, ending with the two feet [namely, *svāhā*] and joined with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*), is declared for Vaṭuka. Ū..."
Whether it be within the expanded cosmic egg, or in the divine atmosphere, or in the sky, or on the surface of the earth, or indeed on the ground that is free from parts (niṣkala),
or in the netherworld (pātāla), or at the edge of the waters— one should draw the seat of the Lord.
One should write that they are situated at the end of the wind, at the end of space, or anywhere at all;
likewise, one should write them in the field (*kṣetra*), in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), and in the minor seats (*upapīṭha*) and so forth.
Then, having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings upon the prepared spot, one should write the syllable *pa*.
By whom are the goddesses always pleased?

One should always write the auspicious *valya* according to the prescribed rite; at the end, one should cause the Lord of the Gods (*Devendrā*) to drink it, having uttered the salutation to the Yoginīs and the beloved of Fire (*Agnivallabhā*).

At the end of all [mantras], the mantra of the Yoginīs consists of the *cakravaca*, the weapon (*astra*), fire (*agni*), and the beloved (*vallabhā*). O Dear One, hear now the mantra of the Kṣetrapāla;
one should differentiate the letter *kṣa* by means of the six long vowels.
At the end of the words "vacaṃsthāna," one should write "kṣetrapāla. One should write twice:
"O beloved of Agni, O Kṣetrapa, accept this offered oblation of incense, lamps, and so forth, and fulfill all desires. This is the mantra.
Having written *gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ* at the beginning, one should write *gaṇapāṃ* at the end;
then the word *vara*, doubled at the end; then the word *sarvajana*;
then *me vaśam ānaya* at the end; and then [the mantra] for all ritual services (*sarvopacāra*).
"O beloved one, take this offering, take it, svāhā"—this is the mantra for Gaṇeśa, O lady of beautiful hips; with these mantras, one should present the bali-offering.
For Vaṭuka, O beloved, [one should offer] with the thumb together with the index finger.
O Goddess, it is said that for Kṣetrapāla, [the mudrā] is formed with the left thumb and ring finger;
for Gaṇeśa, it is the index finger alone;
and for the Yoginīs, it is described as having the form of a jackal’s face.
One should join the index, middle, and ring fingers in the shape of a yoni; during the rite of offering the bali-oblation, the practitioner should sequentially display the mudrā.
Having offered praise and prostrated, one should again unite the Goddess with the Goddess within oneself.
"Having gratified the Guru and the Deity with the principles of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva, the practitioner of mantra, accompanied by bliss, shall accomplish all rites.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Śrī Tripurā. The Lord said:
Seated upon the great lion-throne, this Vidyā is Tripureśvarī;
this Vidyā, the Supreme Goddess, is the Mistress of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) and is worthy of worship.
O Dear One, she consists of Śiva, the Moon, Fire, the left eye, the Bindu, and the Nāda. ŚA.
The seed-syllable *kṭi* is proclaimed at the end of the two *kalās*; let the third be the *śrī*-seed-syllable (*śrīṃ*). This becomes the *vidyā* consisting of four syllables;
this is the *unmanī* *vidyā*, the presiding deity of the Eastern Tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*).
O beloved, by this very [Vidyā], the goddess was honored by the god;
seated upon the eastern lion-throne, she bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even today, this beautiful one is recited with her eastern face.
[In the *Tiśrīdakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Pūrvāvrata Siṃhāsana Vidyā," the Lord said:
"O Lord of Devas, from my southern face [arose] Lalitā Tripurā."

One should now mutter the seed-syllable of Śakti, whose eyes are as red as Rākāmeśvarī; the Vāgbhava syllable is as before, and the Kāmarāja is likewise; the final syllable is conjoined with Śiva—this is the Supreme Goddess Tripurā. This indeed...

The entire procedure, including the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship, of the Goddess Litādevī, the Increaser of Great Good Fortune, belongs to Tripureśī; it must not be otherwise. I shall now describe her meditation (*dhyāna*) for the sake of the accomplishment of practitioners. [She is] rising...
Resplendent with the luster of a thousand suns, blazing with a crown of rubies,
adorned with jeweled earrings, strings of pearls, necklaces, and armlets; beautiful with jeweled anklets, wearing red garments and unguents.
One should meditate upon her, holding a goad, a lotus stalk, and a rosary, beautiful in every limb, for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Lalitā. The Lord said:
The seed-syllable of Kāma alone is called the seed-syllable of Kāmeśī. Kāma is the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra; Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas);
Kāmeśvarī is its deity; and Vīṃ is the seed and Śakti for the practitioner.
The supreme seed-syllable of the Earth (LṂ), declared as the *kīlaka*, brings about great subjugation;
one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the six long vowels.
O Dear One, one should also assign the five previously mentioned arrows as before.
One should meditate upon her who resembles a hibiscus flower, bearing a bow and arrows,
beautiful with various ornaments, and enchanting the three worlds;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with *bandhūka* flowers.
O Goddess of gods, the recitation of the mantra (puraścaraṇa) should then be performed with one-tenth of that number.
Next, I shall describe the yantra capable of attracting the three worlds:
one should draw a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and then a square.
Having written the seed-syllable interspersed in the middle, marked with the names of the practitioner and the person to be accomplished,
and having written the Vidyā separately at the tips of the three corners and on the eight petals and the tips of the petals, one should write it eight times within the square.
This Trailokyamohana Yantra is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds. Having placed a flower in the center, one should then perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha).
[The powers are] Mohitī, Kṣobhiṇī, Vaśinī, and Staṃbhinī.
One should worship Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, and likewise Ahlādinī, followed by Klinnā and Kledinī, in the directions and in the center;
thereafter, O Dear One, one should invoke the Goddess onto the lion-throne.
Having propitiated her with ritual services, one should display the secret mudrā;
O Supreme Goddess, the worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, followed by the worship of the letters of Tripureśī.
O beloved, one should likewise worship Ādānānaṅgarūpā, Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgamanmathā, and Anaṅgakusumā; and fifthly, one should worship Anaṅgakusumāturā. Anaṅ...
One should worship Gaśiśirā, Anaṅgamekhalā,
and Anaṅgadīpikā in sequence upon the eight petals;
Indra and the other guardians should also be worshipped, and then one should again propitiate Śivā.
[Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of Kāmeśvarī," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā. The Lord said:
I shall now describe Raktanetrā, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
Having drawn Tripureśī, adorned with the moon of Vāgbhava,
adorned with Jīva and Agni, and likewise at the end of the Kāma-bīja; she is Raktane-trā, Mahāvidyā, and the Goddess Tripureśvarī, who is Lalitā.
First, one should meditate upon this Lalitā-kumārikā;
she is mature in her youth, with full and elevated firm breasts, broad hips, a slender waist,
and beautiful eyes that are slightly reddish at the corners— this is the alternative form for worship.
Everything beginning with "Sā" belongs to Tripureśī Vasundharī. Thus ends the ritual procedure for Raktane-trā.
This is the eleventh chapter, the ritual for the Southern Lion Throne, in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.

Lord Īśvara said: O Mahādevī, I shall now describe the deities of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya. After [the syllable] Aim, one should then write "Muktā," followed by "Klinne," and then the Kāma-bīja (the seed-syllable of desire), and then "Madadrave" and "Kule."
O Dear One, this seat of Lkā-Tripureśī consists of the letters of fire (Ra), moon (Sa), and sun (Ha);
she is the deity of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya. This Vidyā of the Bhoginīs is renowned throughout the three worlds, O Goddess; by means of this Vidyā...

"The three gods have been honored; all [practices] such as meditation and worship are declared to be like those for a child. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Śrī Bhoginī-vidyā. The Lord said: "O Goddess, regarding the western face..."
Even now, this quartet of Vidyās is being recited;
listen there to Sañjīvanī, who is the embodiment of nectar and bliss, seated upon the great lion-throne, and who is adorned with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
O Dear One, one should draw Kha and Śivacandra, consecrated respectively with the Anusvāra and Visarga; then one should write Saṃjīvana (Jūṃ) and Jīvaṃ,
and the Prāṇagranthi, followed by the word Kuru and Bhṛgu.

The mantra consists of twenty syllables, beginning with *sargīva* and followed by *ktijā*. Śukra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (*chandas*), and Saṃjīvanī is its deity (*devatā*). The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the last one; the third and the group of four [are also specified].
Likewise, one should place the second pentad and the fourth dyad;
then the wise man should inscribe a six-cornered mandala on birch bark with milk and duly arrange the six limbs. [He should worship] her who has the luster of camphor and wears a necklace...
One should meditate upon another supreme goddess adorned with ornaments of pearls, holding the *jñānamudrā* and a rosary (*akṣamālā*). Having thus meditated,
one should invoke her into the center and worship her with ritual offerings (*upacāra*), beginning by worshipping her limbs (*aṅga*).
And one should worship in the six corners: Saṃjīvanī, then Buddhi, then Pūrvasaṃjīvanī, likewise Ahaṃkāramayī,
and Saṃjīvinī, O beloved, as well as Sarvasaṃjīvinī.

O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the Śaktis, Vīras, and Janas in sequence with mantras ending in *namaḥ*. For the sake of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; one should offer oblations of *ūrdhvā* grass ten times that number.
"Endowed with sweetness"—thus [ends the general section].
O Pārvatī, hear now the specific worship; having first performed the worship in this manner, hear the other enclosure (āvaraṇa). [One should meditate upon] Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, and Udāna.
One should worship Mānaka in the southeast corner, Vitata in the northeast,
Sukhira in the second corner [the southwest], and Vaikharīśa in the third corner;
these are known as Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Space.
One should worship sound, touch, form, taste, and smell in the fourth [triangle];
will, knowledge, action, and supreme *māyā* in the fifth;
and *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, and *satyaḥ* in the sixth triangle, in due order. One should worship them there.
At the end of every [mantra], one should utter the word "Saṃjīvinī" three times;
likewise, there is the worship of Saṃjīvanī and Mṛtyusaṃjīvinī.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Saṃjīvinī. The Lord said:
O Dear One, one should establish the lineage of Mṛtyuñjaya-Parāparā;
O Goddess, one should cast the speech of the dualistic disputant into the mire of words,
and one should write "klinne" and "kledini" a thousand times.

One should utter the seed-mantra *Tāra* (Oṃ), followed by the pair *Mahākṣobhaṃkuru*, then *Śivacaṃdrakalānalāt* (from the fire of the digit of the moon of Śiva), then the left eye (*I*), the bindu (*M*), and the nāda (*Aṃ*).

Then one should speak the pair *Mokṣaṃkuru*, then *Haṃsaḥ*, and finally the thunderbolt-sound (*H*) with the visarga (*Ḥ*). Thus, the mantra is: **Oṃ Mahākṣobhaṃkuru Śivacaṃdrakalānalāt Im Aṃ Mokṣaṃkuru Haṃsaḥ HḤ**.
This is the goddess Saṃjīvinī; the sage is Asitapriya;
the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is Bhairavī.
The first peak-syllable (kūṭa) is the seed (bīja), while the middle peak-syllable is the pin (kīlaka). The other...
The power residing in the *kuṭa* (the seed-syllable) is the direct destroyer of death.
One should place [the mantras] in the heart, the head, and the crest-lock in sequence using the nine, the eight, and the eight syllables;
having uttered them in this order, one should again place the final triad.
Then, having drawn a triangle, one should draw a hexagon;
outside, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and a square.
On the eight petals is the Kāmapīṭha, and in the hexagon is the Jālapīṭha.
Having meditated upon Oḍḍiyāna as a triangle with three divisions of the Vidyā, one should invoke the Goddess who dwells in the midst of the Kadamba forest,
holding a book in her left hand and a rosary in her right.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess as a maiden white as a jasmine flower;
having gratified her with all ritual offerings, one should worship the performance of the six limbs.
Then, by means of three portions of the Vidyā, one should worship Vasanta, Madana, and Candra within the triangle.
The practitioner should worship [the deities] by circumambulating from the front; at the end of the words "Brahmā," "Viśveśa," and "Śava," one should worship the triad of Saṃjīvinīs.
Thus, the wise one should worship the hexad of Saṃjīvinīs within the triangle.
One should worship the word *saṃjīvinī* at the end of *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*, as well as at the end of *japa* and near the end of *vidyā*, within the six corners; however,
at the end of the eight [petals], one should place the word *saṃjīvinī* for the Mothers.
By this method, the wise one should worship upon the eight-petaled lotus;
having assigned the world-protectors at the end [of the petals], and the word "Saṃjīvinī," O Goddess of Gods, he should worship in this sequence within the square.
O Maheśānī, by reciting "Make the *tāra* seed-syllable, the *śakti* seed-syllable, and the *śrī* seed-syllable the first," one becomes a bestower of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Furthermore, O Dear One, one should worship the Goddess again with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The method for the *ra* and *ca* vowels is as follows: "Outside [the previous], the *Saṃjīvinī*.
Thus ends the procedure for the *Bhairavī-saṃjīvinī*. The Lord said:
"The supreme *vāgbhava* is indeed the syllable consisting of the letters *ka*, *ra*, and *ma*."
Then, one should always draw the *mada-prānta* (the limit of intoxication) and *māyā*.
This [seed-syllable] is the color of the tip of a thunderbolt (*vajra*). Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra;
its meter (*chandas*) is Virāṭ, and Vajreśī is proclaimed as the deity (*devatā*).
One should then duly assign the limbs of the Goddess by means of the sequence of the five, five, four, seed-syllable, power-syllable (*śakti*), and the third [syllable] as the pin (*kīlaka*).
Having omitted the first and last seed-syllables, one should likewise omit the pair and the single form.
O Goddess, one should install the six limbs by placing them two by two.
Having fashioned a beautiful enclosure adorned with eight pericarp petals,
one should worship the great lion-throne in its center with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
One should draw the Vidyā there, enriched by the beauty of sun-leaves;
then, having constructed a square, one should place a flower in the center and,
having meditated upon her, invoke the Goddess who dwells in the midst of a grove of kadamba trees.
I saw her adorned with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
overflowing with the pride of great youth, embellished with three eyes,
and seated upon a great mechanical device shining within the ocean of blood.

One should meditate upon the Goddess, who holds a pomegranate, a sword, a noose, and likewise a goad, as well as a bundle of arrows, wearing red garlands and unguents, and laden with jewels; one should worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras). Having taken...
Having worshipped Vaṃgāni, one should worship [the goddesses] on the solar petals:
Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Nandā, Kṣobhiṇī, Madanāturā, Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, Klinnā, and Madanāvatī.
One should worship Khecarī, Indrāviṇī, and Vegavatī in sequence;
having worshipped them with the seed-syllable of Kāma, hear now another tradition:
one should draw a solar disc upon the ground as an eight-petaled lotus.

Having worshipped the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) there with oblations, and having again honored the Goddess, one who is pure should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed color. Then,
one should offer ten million oblations at the base of the lotus feet with flowers resembling red saffron.

The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Tivajreśī. The Lord said: Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme Bhairavī Tripurā, who is seated in the five mudrās and adorned with a garland of severed heads. Ātā... [text continues]

She who shines with the luster of ten million suns, adorned with jewel ornaments, holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons— the manifest Mother of the World; [who is] preceded by *haṃsa*, the *vāgbhava* [bīja], the fire [seed-syllable], and the supreme digit of the moon.

The mantra of Bhairavī begins with Śiva and the seed-syllable of the power of Pureśī; know that its entire ritual procedure is exactly like that of Tripureśī. A vidyā equal to this is difficult to find even within the three worlds.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of Tripurābhairavī. The Lord said:
"O Goddess, these four [seeds] exist within the ocean of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya):
the seed-syllable of Vāk, the seed-syllable of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Śrī, and the fire of Ha-Sa-Pha."
Having conjoined it with the sound of Rudra and marked with the Bindu and Nāda—
*Ha Sauḥ*— the wise one should write the thirty-two-syllable Vidyā enclosed by these.
First, one should write "Namo Bhagavati," and then the fourth Praṇava.

Then, in due order, one should write the word for Kubjikā beginning with the letter *śva*; after that, the word consisting of *hrīm*, and following that, the word consisting of *rum*. Then one should write "Aghore," "Yaghore," and subsequently "Aghoramukhi."
Chīṃ, Chīṃ, Kiṇi-yuga, Vicce, Kuvjikā, Sāṃbhavī,
and the supreme Parā; O Mistress of the Gods, these four, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, are declared to be that which is known as the Great Lion Throne (Mahāsiṃhāsana).
By this Vidyā, Gaurī has always been perfectly honored.
[Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Siṃhāsana-Vidyā of the Western Tradition," in the Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Saṃhitā.]
The Lord said: O Goddess of gods, even now I am reciting this at the northern face.
Seated upon the great lion-throne are Bhairavī and Ḍāmarīśvarī;
indeed, within the *Kāmakūṭa* of the previously mentioned goddess Bhairavī is the supreme Śiva.
Then one should utter this: "O Mistress of the Great Lion Throne of Ignorance, Sovereign of the Northern Tradition, Bestower of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation,
you who are pleased by the Bandhūka flower and worshipped with Bandhūka flowers..."

She dwells upon her own manifestation as the one residing on the fifth severed head; she wears a crown of jewels with a shimmering crescent moon and a garland of heads; she has three eyes, is clad in red garments, possesses full, high, and firm breasts, and holds a book.

One should constantly meditate upon her as she holds, in sequence from left to right, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, honored by the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya). One should draw the Great Caṇḍa, who is the self of the end of passion (Madanāntaka), as the Lord of Yoga.
This Kālikā, joined with the syllables *rā-ṇ-y-a-k-ṣ-i-y-u-tā-vi-ye-yaṃ*, consists of nine syllables;
one should meditate upon the Great Mistress, the Northern Leader. O Goddess, by means of this vidyā, she shall be perfectly honored. [The ritual of] placement (*nyāsa*)...

O Vasundharī, O Tripureśī, you are the bestower of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) and great prosperity, the Great Goddess who destroys all great fears. [Thus ends the section on the Siṃhāsana in the Uttarāmnāya of the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.]
[The Thirteenth Chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Goddesses Īśvarī,
Ḍāmaraśvarī, and Bhairavī"] Īśvara said: O Supreme Goddess, for Bhairavī who is worshipped upon four lion-thrones, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] bestows universal sovereignty.

One should draw the middle [line] according to the southern tradition; one should draw all five Rudra-syllables. One should meditate upon Bhairavī as Consciousness, holding a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup, and wearing a garland of five red severed heads.
Having worshipped Kāmeśvarī seated upon the throne of the *preta* (the corpse-seat), she who rests upon the lion-throne of the East—thus concludes the ritual procedure for Caitanyabhairavī.
Īśvara said: O Śivā, the life-force (*jīva*) is threefold, like the three lines of the syllable *oṃ*. It is the delight in the subtle essence (*urakṣmā*).
O beautiful one, having combined that [syllable] according to the sequence of the lunar digits (kalā) of the sun and the moon, make it consist of the Bindu and Nāda;
it is the primordial pair, possessing truth and the power of emission (visarga). O beautiful one, meditate upon Bhairavī, the sovereign of the three worlds, who consists of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā).

The goddess Bhairavī is served by the Dakṣiṇāmnāya; the triangle, the hexagon, the eight-petaled lotus, and that which consists of the earth (the square)— this is the worship of Tripureśī, beginning with the Ṛṣis and so forth.
It is destroyed.
In the triangle, one should worship, in sequence, the goddesses Ratī, Prītī, and Manobhavā;
likewise, in the six corners, one should worship Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Rākinī, and Hākinī in order.
O Lord of Gods, on the eight petals, one should perform the worship of Anaṅga and the others,
as well as the Mothers together with Bhairava, the Bhairavas of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and Indra and the other guardians; these are considered the Dakṣiṇāmnāya— thus there are six.
The Ritual of Kūṭabhairavī. The Lord said: One should write the syllables of the six-peaked Bhairavī according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
Thus, when properly joined, this Bhairavī is the constant remover of fear. [The six-peaked...]
Even if one performs the worship and other rites of the Bhairavīya system according to the power of the Paścimāmnāya, O Sovereign Goddess,
such a Vidyā as this is difficult to find in the three worlds; thus [it is] Nityābhairavī.

Regarding the ritual of Ravi, the Lord said: O Īśvarī, O Mistress of the Asuras, having set aside the *ḍā* from the *Ḍāmaraiśvara-bhairavī*, one should utter the seed-syllable of Śakti (*hrīṃ*), which is pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. This is the Bhairavī named Bhayavidhvaṃsinī (the Destroyer of Fear).
Thus has been proclaimed in the *Uttarāmnāya-gambhīrāḍāmara* the procedure for the worship of Śīca, which destroys all fear.
The Lord said: At the end of *hasa-svā*, the seed-syllable of the Self (*ātma-bīja*) is *pha-re-m*. It should be joined together...

One who knows the secret mantras should draw the form of Bhairavī, the destroyer of fear; this vidyā, consisting of the middle and the supreme mantra, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. It is the goddess Aghorabhairavī, Śyāmā, and Muṇḍā.
Crowded with vultures, she dwells upon five skulls in the south and north; she holds a book, a rosary, a noose, a goad,
as well as a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru drum, and a skull-cup.

One should worship the Supreme Sovereign Goddess, who holds a *laṃśūla* and is like the six-peaked [mountain], according to the procedure for Ghorabhairavī. The Lord said: [One should worship] Śrīsampadbhairavī, who is equal to the four lion-thrones...
O Lord of Gods, one should worship her preceded by Bhairavī, with the names beginning with Kheṭā and the third [name], joined with the fire-seed (Ra) and the wind-seed (Ya);
this [mantra] named Saṃpatpradā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
She is capable of upholding the teaching of the sixty-four million yoginīs;
she possesses the luster of a thousand copper-colored suns, faces the lunar disc,
wears a crown of jewels sparkling with crescent moons, and has slender, well-proportioned limbs.
She wears quivering red garments and red ornaments;
she is mature with the intoxication of youth, possessing full, high, and firm breasts;
her body is adorned with a garland of blood-stained severed heads, yet she is beautifully decorated with excellent ornaments.

She holds a staff and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary and the gesture of granting boons in her right hands; thus should Tripureśī be worshipped, and not otherwise. [Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of Bhairavī," in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.]
The Lord said: Now, O Goddess, even through this lower face, the fivefold knowledge—which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds—is being recited.
Listen to the Vāgbhava joined with Śiva, and then the middle Vāgbhava.
O Maheśānī, at the end of *hakalāṃ*, one should write the three seed-syllables of Śiva;
the third is composed of the letter *ra*, the left eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*). O beloved, this is the single Vidyā, the first of grace and creation, dear to Suṃdarī. *Ha*.
The practitioner of mantra should join the vowels from the Sun (R) to the Fourth (Ū), ending with the letter *sa* along with the *visarga*,
which consists of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the second *Sundarī*, or it may be recited alone.

O Goddess, listen to the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] in the middle; it is *hasarā* and should be joined with the thousand-rayed Vāgbhava. O Dear One, listen to the triple *Hṛt*, the *Kalahṛllekhā-Śakti-kūṭa*, and the fourth.

This third four-syllabled Sundarī, O Lord of Gods, consists of the seeds of Śiva (ŚK), Kaṃ (KAṂ), and Śiva (ŚA) followed by the letter *ra* (repha), the grace (*anugraha*), and emission (*sarga*). She protects the pair of Śivas (the two Śivas) through the three seeds with the Supreme (Parā).

O Beloved, one should make this cruel [mantra] condensed into three parts; one should write the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbhava), the seed-syllable of Desire (Kāma), and the seed-syllable of Power (Śakti).
This fourth [syllable] is known as Sundarī, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Jīva, Śiva-yuga, Jīva, Kṣmā, Kṣa, and Śiva-nuta—this is the first; the middle consists of Ha-sa-yuk, Kṣmā, Kṣa, and Indu-mat; and the other is adorned with Ha-sa-lakṣa, Indu-hendu, and Ākāśa.
The Tripureśī-mantra is known as the fifth, Sundarī;
one should meditate upon the excellent pentad consisting of Saṃpatpradā and Bhairavī.
The worship, beginning with the ṛṣis and so forth, is to be understood as that of Tripureśī, and not otherwise.
[The Fifteenth Chapter, titled "The Worship of Sundarī," from the *Tiśrīdakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*] Īśvara said: Now,
O Mahēśānī, beloved of the Vidyā-kalpalatā, I shall explain that which is...

By mere knowledge of them, great calamities flee away. Śrīvidyā, Pārijātī, Kāmeśvarī, Pañcavāṇeśvarī, and the goddess Kumārī are proclaimed as the five [Kumāris]. They are the bestowers of prosperity, Bhairavī, and Vāmā.
One who knows the ritual mantras should write the seed-syllable *gbhavaṃ* (gbhaṃ), enclosed by the *Tāra* (Oṃ) and the supreme [syllable] (Hrīṃ), O Goddess.
This mantra, ending with the heart of Sarasvatī and consisting of eleven syllables (*rudrārṇa*), has been proclaimed.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer (*ṛṣi*) and Gāyatrī is its metre (*chanda*).

It is said that the goddess Pārijāteśvarī is proclaimed as the presiding deity (vāṇī-devatā); O Maheśānī, the second and third [syllables] are the seed (bīja) and the power (śakti), while the Tāraka is the pin (kīlaka), bestowing great Sarasvatī.

One should assign the limbs with the seed-syllables interspersed with the six long vowels: in the aperture of Brahma (the crown), between the eyebrows, in the sockets of the eyes, in the cavities of the ears,
in the pair of nostrils, on the tongue, and on the penis and anus, respectively.

One should meditate upon that Goddess of the gods, the bestower of Sarasvatī, who is endowed with the color of gold, mounted upon a swan, adorned with shimmering pearls, dressed in pure white garments, possessing a radiant smile, bearing the moon upon her crest, and decorated with diamonds and pearls.
Having thus meditated upon her as bearing the Vidyā, the lute, the Svadhā-vessel, and the rosary, one should, with a concentrated and serene mind, recite the mantra one million times;
and with a clear intellect, one should offer ten thousand oblations with white lotuses while uttering the syllable "Huṃ."
Alternatively, O Lord of the gods, one should offer oblations with the five nāgas;

one should draw this yantra according to the Mātṛkā-valli and likewise worship it upon the pedestal (pīṭha). Having invoked Sarasvatī there, one should worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras).
Having fully worshipped the deities of the forest (dāvaṅga), one should worship the retinue;
then, on both sides of the principal deity, one should worship the consecrated goddesses:
Prajñā, Medhā, Stuti, Śakti, Smṛti, and Vāgīśvarī.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Sumati, Svasṛ, and Itri upon the petals;

then, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the sisters at the tips of the petals. Furthermore, having worshipped Indra and the others in the circle of the ground, one should again worship the Goddess Pārijātā.

"The Vidyā of Teśvarī is difficult to obtain in the three worlds"—thus ends the ritual procedure for worshipping Pārijāteśvarī. The Lord said: "Furthermore, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the auspicious Pañcavāṇīśvarī."
With those same five arrows, the five-syllable Vidyā arises.
Madanaga is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas),
and Kāmeśvarī is its seed-syllables (bīja) and this Īśvarī is its deity.
One should worship the limbs with the five arrows, both individually and collectively, as before;
the wise one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five colors as previously described,
and having placed the five desires (*pañcakāma*), O Supreme Goddess, [he should proceed] as before.
She shines like the sun, adorned with various ornaments,
wearing saffron-colored garments and body-unguents shaped like bandhūka flowers,
her two arms resplendent with a sugarcane bow and flowery arrows.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind for one hundred thousand syllables.
O Dear One, one should perform a fire sacrifice with *bandhūka* flowers for a tenth part of that amount.
Kāmeśvarī should be worshipped, with special emphasis on the worship of the arrows. (Tri)

(The worship of Tripureśī-Śiva): "Having fully worshipped Tripureśī-Śiva, one should conquer this world"—thus is the ritual procedure for Janavidhi, the Mistress of the Five Arrows. Īśvara said: Now I shall describe the fivefold desires.
One should worship Pikā, the Mother of the Universe, with the five previously mentioned Kāmas;
thus one becomes a Kāmīśvarī. The Ṛṣi is named Sammohana, the metre is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is this primordial Kāma, whose seed-syllable is Śakti.

The practitioner should place the *tukīlaka* at the end with these [syllables], both individually and collectively; he should perform the limb-assignment (*aṅganyāsa*) as before and worship the two types of Kāmabāṇa-nyāsa. She is red, her body clad in red silk garments, and anointed with unguents.

She is adorned with ornaments and holds a noose, a goad, a bow, arrows, a book, a rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is the one who brings the three worlds under her control.
All other details, such as the worship and so forth, are the same as for the Five Arrows (Pañcabāṇa).
This specific procedure for the worship of Pañcakāmeśvarī is declared as being surrounded by the five Kāmeśvarīs. [The worship] of Īśvarī (0).
Now, O Maheśānī, we shall describe Kumārī, the Mother of the Universe.
The wise one, having abandoned the *vāgbhava* [syllable] of the Goddess Tripureśānī— who is the sovereign mistress capable of attracting the three worlds— should contract it;
when situated between the two *kāma* and *śakti* [syllables], this vidyā becomes two-syllabled.

O Dear One, the great compeller [of will] is preceded by the seed-syllables of Tripureśī, Ṛṣi, and so forth, and followed by the Śakti; with the *kīlaka* at the beginning and end and the mantra in between, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) twice and then install the five arrows.

Having placed the five objects of desire, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra. One should worship the Goddess in the center of the great *yantra* of Kāmeśvarī. Listen to the specific detail regarding that very point, O Pārvatī: [one should place them] in the positions of the five arrows.
Having worshipped the Cakās, one should then worship the triad beginning with Rati.
Then, O beloved, one should worship the eight Aṅgas along with the Bhairavas and the Mothers on the eight petals; and in front, one should worship the eight Pīṭhas, beginning with Indra.

O beautiful one, having worshipped the [deities] beginning with Dayā, one should worship the Goddess in the center. O Maheśānī, by remembering her while performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite, one may enchant this entire world. At dawn—
Having the luster of a thousand suns, adorned with excellent ornaments of rubies,
richly clad in shimmering jewel-embroidered silken garments, and decorated with various ornaments;
holding a sugarcane bow and arrows, as well as a book and a rosary of beads.

One should constantly meditate upon her who brings all kings under one's control. Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Kumārī. [Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Kalpalatā," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.]

[Chapter on the Pañcaratna] The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, I wish to hear that which has been indicated by the Great Vidyā of the Five Jewels but not yet revealed; please show me your grace. The Lord said: "I shall proclaim the perfected Vidyā."
O Beloved, she who grants success even through mere remembrance, who bestows all desires and eternally grants all sovereignty— Śrīvidyā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī,
Bhuvaneśvarī, and Vārāhī— are proclaimed as the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna).

The venerable couple of Kāma has been proclaimed as consisting of Śiva, Agni, Vāma, the eye, the bindu, nāda, and kalā; having thus stated [the mantra], one should write at the end of the heart-mantra "Bhagavatyai" the four-syllabled mantra of Māheśvarī, which completes it.
O Maheśānī, this mantra, beginning with *Tārā* (Om), followed by the four classes (*catuvarṇa*) and the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*,
Svāhā), is proclaimed to consist of twenty syllables; one should worship it at dawn alone,
for by the mere remembrance of it, great calamities flee away.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra of Brahmāsya is declared to be Uṣṇik;
O Dear One, the deity is the perfected vidyā Annapūrṇeśvarī; and the seed-syllables, the power, the pinning-stake, and the hṛllekhā and so forth are now described.

O Pārvatī, having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) by combining the syllable *hṛllekhā* with the six long vowels, one should perform the placement of the letters (*varṇanyāsa*) as follows:
in the *brahma-randhra*, the *repha*, the *sīmanta*, the forehead, the two eyebrows, and the nose.

O Goddess of the gods, one should then perform the placement of the feet (*pādanyāsa*) on the face, throat, heart, belly, navel, and the *liṅga*; then on the *ādhāra*, the two buttocks, the two thighs, the two knees, and likewise on the two feet.

O Goddess of Gods, the placement of the feet (*pada-nyāsa*) is declared for the openings [of the body]— namely, the heart, the belly, the navel, the *liṅga*, the two buttocks, the two thighs, and the two knees— and the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) is performed with the root mantra (*mūla*).

O Supreme Goddess, for the purification of the body, I shall now describe the yantra that bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation: a triangle, a sixteen-spoked wheel, then an eight-petalled lotus, and a square representing the earth, with the *tāra* (the syllable Om) in the center.
One should place the three seed-syllables in the three corners, applying them in a clockwise direction.
O Dear One, listen: beginning from the front petal, one should assign the letters of the *kalās* starting from the east;
as for the remaining letters of the *kalās*, they follow from the east onwards.

One should draw it in sequence; O Dear One, one should write the long vowels upon the petals of the eight-petaled [lotus]. Having worshipped this seat three times with the Praṇava, the wise one should invoke therein the Goddess Annadā along with the common mudrās.

One should sacrifice by properly worshipping with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then worship the limbs [of the deity] in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center. Having meditated upon the Goddess, the Siddhavidyā, who is a great ocean of milk...
Surrounded by gods, [he saw her] shining within a palace with walls of various brilliant colors like an island of jewels,
