seated upon a throne enriched by the splendor of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa),
radiant in wonderful garments with a luster like the rising sun.
I bow to the Supreme Goddess, who has the moon as her crest-jewel, who is intent on the gift of food, and who is adorned with gems;
she is languid under the weight of breasts shaped like golden jars,
and she possesses two arms that bring joy to the *tāṇḍava* dance of Rudra.

One should meditate on her, richly adorned with the splendor of teeth and the gesture of fearlessness, always intent upon the gift of food; furthermore, in her right hand, one should visualize a golden ladle,
a vessel filled with milk-rice and adorned with divine jewels and other ornaments.
O Maheśānī, having meditated upon this Supreme Goddess with the left hand,
O Dear One, one should worship Rudra— who is preeminent in the *ṭaṇḍava* dance— standing before her. With the second seed-syllable, however, one should worship Brahmā, and with the third, Hari.
With the seed-syllable *ṇaṃ tu ryavī*, one should then worship the leaf-cluster;
first [worship] *natasurāmokṣadāyinī*, then *bhayahāriṇī*, then *gati*, then *haṃsī*, then *varākṣī*, and after that, *tīrtharūpā*. Then, Mā...
The Goddess who bestows the river of gold, the destroyer of enemies, the annihilator of misfortune,
the giver of joy to those who meditate upon her,
whose form is pure, the remover of debt, the Sovereign, and the beautiful consort of Hara— [Salutations to Her]. (16)
Having worshipped the Goddess of the letters (Varṇadevī) according to the sequence of salutations to Śāntinapūrṇā, one should then worship [Her] upon the eight-petaled lotus; thereafter,
O Mistress of the Gods, one should worship [the deities] within the square enclosure by means of the eight Brahmīs.

Furthermore, one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by means of the world-protectors (lokapālas). One should perform the recitation (japa) according to the prescribed rule until the target number is reached, and then offer oblations (homa) with clarified butter and sesame seeds amounting to a tenth part of that; this will certainly grant success.

Thus has been told the Siddhavidyā that bestows the fruit of the three goals of life. [Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, named "The Hymn to Annapūrṇā," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. The Lord said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Mātaṅgī, the deity of jewels:

one should write the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbhava), the seed-syllable of desire (Kāmavīja), and the seed-syllable of emission (Sargavān), followed by Bhṛgu (the letter *R*) in the highest position;
then, joined with the grace (Anugraha), one should again write the first supreme syllable, Śrīvīja (the letter *Śrī*).
"Jaṃtārakaṃ caiva namo bhagavati," "mātangīśvari," at the end of "sarvāṃte manohari-janādike," "sarvarājavaśaṃ ca ante kuru," "sarvanukhāntakaṃ," and "rañjani."
Then one should utter the word "all women" (*sarva-strī-śabda*), followed by "subjugation" (*vaśam*) at the end of the word "men" (*puruṣān*).

Having spoken thus, all wicked beings are brought under control. Then, having written "like a deer" (*mṛgam iva vaśam*), one should utter the word "all worlds" (*sarva-loka-padam*), and thereafter [the word] "subjugation" (*vaśam*).

Having written the word "likhya," one should write the supreme Śrī-kāma-bīja and the Vāgbhava-bīja there; O Dear One, these seventy-three syllables constitute the body of Mātaṅgī; this [is] the entirety...

The queen of the *dyānas*, who bestows the accomplishment of the goal of liberation; the sage is Mataṅga, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is the formless Supreme Goddess Mātaṅgī; [the seed-syllables are] Kāmabīja and Vāgbhava.

O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllables (*vīja*), powers (*śakti*), and the pin (*kīlaka*) as the third; indeed, the six-limbed rite is performed by repeating the first three seed-syllables twice.
[One should meditate on the Goddess] whose right foot is placed upon a lotus, who is radiant...
One should meditate upon Mataṅginī, whose swaying earrings are praised by the gentle resonance of her lute, who is beautiful with the radiance of her rows of teeth,
auspicious, lovely in all her limbs, and adorned with a garland of kadamba flowers.
For the attainment of all goals, one should meditate upon the dark-limbed goddess who is intent on playing the lute and wears a conch-shell bangle. Now I shall describe the yantras:
the triangle, the pentagon, the eight-petaled lotus, and the sixteen-petaled lotus.
One should draw a maṇḍala with eight petals, four petals, and four corners, provided with four gates; having properly invoked the deities,
one should worship them with ritual offerings in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
Now I shall describe the worship of the limbs, or rather, O Maheśānī, the worship of the attendants.
One should worship Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, in the four directions starting from the eastern gate, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
O beloved, as before, in the intermediate directions and starting from the left side, proceeding clockwise, [worship] Vaṭuka, Gaṇarāja, Kṣetrapāla, and the Yoginīs; then,
on the tips of the four petals, [worship] Siddha and Mātaṅginī in succession.
One should worship Siddhalakṣmī, who consists of Mahālakṣmī, and Mātaṅginī;
one should worship the goddess Mahāmātaṅginī by circumambulating her.
O Great Goddess, on the eight petals, one should worship the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga.
Sitāṅga, Urur, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta-Bhairava, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas;
one should worship them, O Lord of Devas, beginning from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, and Śraddhā as the fifth; Vāgīśvarī, Kriyāśakti, Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi,
Mohinī, Pramathā, Svāsā, Cīcī, and Vindumālinī.
Rā, Ānandā, Nāga, and Buddhi—these sixteen have been proclaimed.
O Goddess of the Gods, beginning from the east, one should worship them in a clockwise direction. Then, O Goddess, on the sixteen-spoked [cakra], there are Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Rati.

One should worship the eight Mothers—Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi, as before—on the eight petals, O Lord of Gods. Likewise, on the five petals as before, one should worship Drāviṇī and Śoṣiṇī. Then... [staṃ]... [Note: The provided text fragment ends here].

O Lord of Gods, one should worship Bhinī, Mohinī, and Ākarṣakāriṇī within the triangle, as well as Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava in front, according to the previous method, proceeding clockwise with the mantra.
O beloved, having again worshipped the Goddess of the gods with all necessary offerings, three hundred thousand repetitions for the rites of the feet are prescribed; O Goddess,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a coral rosary using a tenth part of that number.
The practitioner, being pure, should perform the rite in a triangular sacrificial pit using *vaṃdhūka* flowers.
Thus, with his mantra thoroughly purified, he shall accomplish all rites;
one seeking a kingdom should use *mallikā*, *jātī*, *puṃnāga*, and the leaves of the *śrīphala*.
O lady of excellent vows, one who desires fortune [should worship] with white lotuses or beautiful pink lotuses; one who desires enjoyments, with blue water-lilies;
and one who desires to bring others under control, with *japā*, *bandhūka*, *vakula*, and filaments (*kiñjalka*).
One seeking a wife should offer oblations of madhūka flowers mixed with honey;
for attraction, one should use salt and sesame seeds combined with the three sweets (trimadhu);
one desiring rain should use *vañjula* wood; and one seeking wealth should use golden flowers (*hemapuṣpaka*).

One desiring subjugation [should offer] *ekavaṃka* flowers; one seeking wealth, rice grains with clarified butter; one desiring sovereignty, cooked food with clarified butter; for subjugation, saffron and *rocanā*;
for good fortune, fragrant substances; and for eloquence, *nandyāvarta* flowers.

One who desires prosperity should offer *karipuṣpa* flowers; for the sake of splendor (*tejas*), one should sacrifice with *pālāśa* wood; furthermore, by offering oblations with *kāpila* ghee, one becomes radiant through the act of sacrifice. A sacrifice performed with *unmatta* flowers becomes a means of causing madness.
One should offer oblations into the fire-pit of Yama, which is filled with a heap of *ṣa-vṛkṣa*, *nīpa*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *vibhītaka* wood,
and surrounded by owls, vultures, and crows, and anointed with *nimba* oil,
for the destruction of the enemy.
Facing east and being unclothed, yet not defiled by the impurity of having seen [a corpse], there shall be eradication (*uccāṭana*) when piercing in the portion of Vāyu;
for the Lord of the Rākṣasas, it shall likewise be in the division of Indra and Agni. For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should face the east.

The teacher has declared that the rite of immobilization (*staṃbhanam*) is in the west; the practitioner should accomplish all rites, such as those for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*) and others, in the north.
He should perform them with milk-rice, jaggery, sugar-candy, and even sugarcane juice.

The oblation (homa) performed with only breast milk brings about peace; likewise, milk-rice mixed with ghee quickly destroys insanity, while that same preparation smeared with black pepper and sesame oil becomes a remedy for cough and asthma.
The destruction of wind-disorders occurs through the fire-oblation (*homa*) of *nirguṇḍī* roots;
now hear [the method for] swift attraction. Perform the threefold form-visualization, and then, having performed the *jīvanyāsa*, [fashion the image] with clay from a potter's workshop.
Furthermore, having fashioned another doll from beeswax and salt,
one should place it made of clay and marked with saffron, having performed the ritual intention (saṃkalpa) for its name;
it should be seven finger-breadths in height, with a salted girdle at the lower part.
Afterwards, one should hang [the honey] produced from bees upon a tree above.

O Dear One, the wise man, beginning with the right foot and ending with the left foot, should grind salt with honey and offer it into the fire using a ladle (*lāvanyā*). O Beloved, this is performed over the left foot.
O Goddess, O Mahādevī, I know that for women this is a reversal;
after seven nights, afflicted by separation,
they become agitated and fall into the lap of the practitioner, devoid of fear or shame.
For the destruction of enemies, one should perform oblations with salt and neem oil;
for the purpose of paralyzing [an opponent], one should offer salt mixed with turmeric powder.
A wise person should perform sacrifice during the forenoon and the early part of the night for the sake of auspicious results.
At midday or at midnight, one should perform rites such as *uccāṭana* (expulsion) and so forth;
having assumed the form of Mātaṅgī, the wise practitioner should accomplish all activities. Thereafter, he should effect possession (*āveśana*) in the presence of young maidens.
The worship of the maiden (kanyāpūjā) must be performed, especially for the Yoginīs;

having worshipped each group of eight with sixty-four [offerings], the wise one who brings satisfaction through songs of lamentation should afterwards present the bali offering to Mātaṅgī, O fair-faced one.
At the end of the name, one should also write "Bhagavati";
then one should say "Mātangī" and likewise write "Caṇḍālī";
thereafter, having uttered "Sarvajana," one should write "Evaśaṃ vaśam."
Having written "ānaya" (bring) and ending with the two syllables *ṭhaḥ*, this is called the mantra;
by means of this, the offering of bali should be made for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*) in Mātaṅgī.
In the same manner, the practitioner of mantras should properly cast the bali-offering for Vaṭuka and the others.
One shall accomplish all rites through the grace of Mātaṅgī.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Jewel-like Worship of the Goddess Mātaṅgī," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. Īśvara.
He said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the temple that brings joy to the worlds;
by the mere knowledge of which great calamities flee away.
It is Śiva mounted upon Fire, adorned with a left eye."
The seer is Śakti, the son of Vasiṣṭha;

the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is the supreme consciousness (saṃvit) that expresses awakening; the seed-syllable is the fourth state of Śiva (śivatūrya), the power is Kīlaka, and the letter 'Ra' is declared to be the bolt.

The knower of mantras, having split the Vidyā by means of the syllables *a*, *na*, *ta*, *va*, *ma*, *ne*, *trā*, *bhyāṃ*, *vā*, *ma*, *śru*, *tyā*, *dha*, *re*, *ṇa*, *ca*, *anu*, *gra*, *ha*, *vi*, *sa*, *rgā*, *bhyāṃ*, bestows the four aims of human life through the Mistress of the World (*Bhuvaneśānī*).

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should place the mantras beginning with *Hṛllekhā*. Then, one should dissolve the Mātṛkā in reverse order from the letter *A* down to the end, grouping it by pairs of consonant classes (*varga*) in reverse sequence.

The placement of the *saṃhāramātṛkā* (the alphabet of dissolution), radiant with the essence of the bliss of Brahman, is performed according to the method of the regions of the body (*rūpadeśavidhi*) and by way of the path of the reverse-order vowels.
Having become thus, the practitioner of mantra should then place [the letters] upon the fingers along with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having arranged the *naraṅga* syllables with the splendor of the bliss of consciousness,
one should place the five supreme sovereign goddesses— Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, the fourth, Karālikā— in the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
One should place Mahokṣuṣmāṇ and then place the three Śaktis—
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī as the third— at the throat, the left breast, and the right breast respectively; thereafter, one should place the triad of deities.

O beloved, one should then perform the placement (nyāsa) of those known as Hara, Viṣṇu, and Śiva on the left side and likewise at the heart; thereafter, one should place the Mothers on the right side—
specifically on the forehead, the left part, the side, and the right side of the belly.
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the syllables *daṃ*, *saṃ*, at the belly, the sides, the hair-tuft, and the root [of the tongue].
With a body equipped with the noose (*pāśa*), goad (*aṅkuśa*), boon-granting (*vara*), and protection (*abhaya*) mudrās,
one should draw [the deity] upon a cloth using saffron and other excellent substances.

The best of teachers, a master of mantras, having fashioned [the diagram] out of materials such as colored powders, silver, or copper, should draw the circle of fire (vahni-maṇḍala) with lines toward the directions of Indra, the Rākṣasa, and Vāyu; then, in its center, he should inscribe the Śakti marked with the name of the person to be accomplished.
Having encircled it with the letter *ṭha*, one should write the other [letters] at the tips of the corners;
this binding at the three locations is said to bestow success. One should then encircle the tips of the lines of those three seed-syllables in a clockwise direction.

One should encircle the three spokes with the tip of the *māyā* [syllable]; this is declared to be the "bond of power" (*śaktibandha*), beautiful through its mutual resonance. Within the interior of the triangle, one should place the left eye (*va*) accompanied by the *bindu*.

On each individual corner and side, one should place the syllable *ha* and the syllable *ra*; furthermore, this [syllable] *bha* in the center, along with the fourth [vowel] accompanied by the *visarga*.
Having thus done so, one should then encircle [the diagram] externally with these syllables, having first drawn a circle on the outside.

Furthermore, the wise one should write the syllable *padmaṃ* in the center, and then the syllables *vi-ra-vya-va-sva-raṃ* in the positions of the filaments; moreover, he should write *ha-pa-ṇaṃ* and *ha-rā-ṇaṃ* on each petal,
and he should also write the fourth vowel, *ha-raṃ*, and the fourth [consonant], *ha-riḥ*.
One should draw the eyes upon the petals and at the tips of the petals;
this triple-layered yantra, when encased externally in gold, bestows desires, grants liberation, is beautiful, and sets all sovereign powers in motion. In this [yantra]—
One should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭha-śaktis) upon the throne for the attainment of all goals:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Maghorā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Having worshipped the pedestal all around and meditated upon Nandin situated at the base of the pedestal,
one should visualize [the deity] as having the form of Kuṇḍalinī, possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun,
with three eyes and four arms holding a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons (vara), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).

Having worshipped [the deity], the best of teachers should worship the Goddess with captivating offerings (upacāras) after she has been brought forth; he should display the mudrās for invocation and so forth,
and perform the worship of the limbs in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
The best of teachers should worship the limbs of enjoyment for the sake of attaining enjoyment:
from the letters *u*, *ū*, *o*, *au*, *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, and *va* arise the *ava* [group] and the earthen (*pārthiva*) elements;
from the letters *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *au*, *ph*, *ḍha*, and *a*, the *dha* [group] and the watery (*nīraja*) elements arise.
The practitioner, being composed in mind, should worship the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *saumya* (the vowels) in the directions starting from the east; thereafter,
for the sake of his own accomplishment, he should worship the group of five [consonants] in those same locations.
One should worship the triad beginning with Gāyatrī in the southeast, southwest, and northwest corners respectively; thereafter, one should worship the triad beginning with Brāhmī.
Following that, those [deities] should be worshipped in the directions of the southeast, west, and northeast.
The Mothers of the petals are to be worshipped, followed by the adoration of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas).
Thus concludes the extraction of the triguṇita yantra of Bhuvanīśvarī. Īśvara said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the ṣaḍguṇita yantra.
O beloved, by the mere knowledge of which one becomes a lord of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiśvara*):

having drawn a fire-diagram (*vahnimālā*) enclosed [by lines], one should place the Power (*śakti*) in the center; in the portion of that *śakti* consisting of the letter *repha* (ṛ), one should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In the fourth vowel-syllable of the *khet*, one should write [the name] under the subject (*sādhya*) so that it is touched by it, for the sake of all accomplishments;
having surrounded it with the letter *ṭa*, one should place the power (*śakti*) outside in five ways.
Outside of that, one should likewise write the Śrī-bīja and the Kāma-bīja five times in rows; thereafter follows the method for the hexagon,
wherein in each of the six corners of the hexagon, one should write the letter *va* with a dot (the nasal *m*) and a left eye (the vowel *i*).
Furthermore, one should inscribe the seed-syllable of Śakti within the junctions of the hexagon;
as before, the seed-syllable of Śakti should be made devoid of contact.
The wise one should write it in the intervals between the three upper corners.
Then, the preceptor should write the syllables *dhaka*, *syasavi*, *dūtī*, *namaḥ*, and *ūrṇā* one after another;

furthermore, he should write the *śakti*, *śrī*, *kāma*, and *vāyu* seeds in that very same place. Then, the knower of mantras should [place them] in the three lower corners and in the intervals between them.

Having written the syllables of the name to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the seed-syllable of Power (*śakti*), the glorious seed-syllable of Desire (*kāma*), and the wheels (*cakra*) along with the *visarga*, and having performed the *vidarbha* [interlacing]— the servant of the Guru, in all the corners and sides, [should write] with the syllables of Hari and Hara.

Then, draw a circle outside that; fashion it like the full moon. Within that circle, write the fifty letters in direct order (anuloma), and likewise, on the exterior of that circle, write the Mātṛkā letters in reverse order (viloma).
One should draw two pairs of lines from the center, extending to the corners and forming a square enclosure;
O Lord of Gods, this then becomes a well-proportioned hexagon. One should inscribe the seed-mantra of Nṛsiṃha in the center and in the cardinal directions.
O Protectress, know that the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha consists of the letter *kṣa*.

Adorned with the letter *ra*, the letter *kṣa*, the letter *pa*, the letter *va*, the letter *na*, the letter *rṣī*, and the vowel *anu* (u), and further pervaded by the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and the *kalā*, this, O Beloved, is the Cintāmaṇi.
Then the mantra-knower should draw [the lines] in the corners; thereafter,
having drawn tridents at the junctions of the corners with *praṇavas*, he should then draw a beautiful lotus expanded by the syllables of the zodiac signs and twelve plows.
This aforementioned yantra, which sets all sovereignty in motion,
should be worshipped there; having honored the sacred seat (pīṭha) and invoked [the deity] as before, one should offer pleasing services with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having displayed the mudrās for invocation (*āvāhana*) and the others, the worship should take place.

Then, one should perform the second stage of worship, the enclosure of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāvaraṇa*), in the six directions—the corners of the hexagon at Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛti, Vāyu, and the center—as well as in the cardinal directions. [Then] Brahmā...
One should worship Gāyatrī together with Brahmā, Sāvitrī with Viṣṇu,
Sarasvatī with Śiva, and Śrī with Dhanada; likewise, one should worship Rati with Madana and Puṣṭi with Gaṇapa.
One should worship, starting from the eastern corner of the hexagon and proceeding clockwise,
the goddesses Raktā, Anaṅgā, Kusumā, Tṛtīyā, Kusumetarā,
Nityā, Anaṅgā, Madanā, Ṣaṣṭhī, and Madanāturā.
Rīcā, Gaganā, Gaganaveginī,
Padmābhayapramathinī, and Śaśiśekharā—
one should worship these twelve in the vessels, starting from the east in due order.

Having worshipped the four petals, one should worship Brāhmī and the others in the cardinal directions; in the earth-pavilion (bhūgṛha), one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas). O Dear One, when this is performed sixfold, all the siddhis, beginning with Vāgīśvarī, arise for the practitioner.
"Furthermore, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with offerings such as food oblations (naivedya).
Thus ends the extraction of the sixfold Yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī in the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*. The Lord said: Now, [the following].
I shall now describe the *Rkaguṇita* Yantra, the most excellent of all;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes the sovereign lord of the worlds.
First, having drawn a hexagon, [one should then place] the deities at its junctions.
Having produced another hexagon within it, there shall be a twelve-cornered [figure];
having drawn the Śakti in its center according to the procedure previously stated,
one should surround the letter *ṭha* in its middle on the outside in reverse order.
Then, having written the mantras with the three *samyagvyāhṛtis* in the junctions of the hexagon,
one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī as manifested in twelve places;
O Dear One, one should perform the binding of the Śakti in twelve ways as before.
Alternating them one by one, make it beautiful and adorned;
on the twelve spokes, one should draw the syllable *drum* (Dru) accompanied by a bindu and the letter *tūrya* (Tū).
Above that, in the corners of the sun (the triangles), one should write this for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.

Then, the mantra-adept should draw tridents within the intervals between the seed-syllables at the junctions of the twelve-spoked [diagram]; furthermore, he should write the Gāyatrī on each of the flanks of every spoke. Tat-pa...
One should write the *vīteṇiya* of the Sun-giver (*daṃsavituḥ*) in reverse order:
"bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. This eight-syllable mantra of the Goddess is proclaimed as beginning with "mahya" and so forth; it consists of twenty-four syllables.
In the center, one should write the *Gāyatrī* known as the Mother of the Gods (*Devamātṛkā*) in pairs;
then, outside that, on the sides of the corners, one should write the syllables of the *Gāyatrī* in reverse order,
starting from the southeast facing forward, followed by the *Praṇava*.

One should write this six-syllable mantra of Agni: *rbhuvaḥ svaḥ agne jātavede hāli khya vaha sarva catuṣṭayaṃ karma sādhaya svāhā*. This Vidyā of Agni is difficult to obtain; one should then write it.

O Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing all purposes, one should then encircle the *mātṛkā* both in direct and reverse order. Outside of that, one should draw a mandala consisting of an earth-enclosure (*bhūpuṭa*) adorned with seed-syllables as described previously.

Having worshipped the pedestal as before, one should invoke the Goddess as before [upon] the lotus of thirty-two petals endowed with thirty-two filaments, which is multiplied by twelve (the sun) and is the abode of the Vedas and Agamas.
O Dear One, one should perform the worship of the retinue first and the worship of the interior last; one should worship the five *hṛllekhā* mantras along with their syllables as before,
and worship the six pairs beginning with Brahmā separately in twelve ways.
In the corners, beginning from the eastern corner, one should worship the Kalās:
Karālī, Vikarālī, Umā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Śacī, Tṛṣā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, and Dhṛti.
Faith (Śraddhā), Intelligence (Medhā), Fortitude (Dhṛti), and Splendor (Kānti) are proclaimed as the sixteen noble ones;
they are to be worshipped in order starting from the east, upon the tips of the petals and at the joints.
Likewise, Prosperity (Śrī), Modesty (Hrī), Nourishment (Puṣṭi), Offspring (Prajā), Śinīvālī, and Kuhū.
Rudravīryā, Prabhā, Ānandā, Śoṣaṇī, Śuddhidā, as well as Kālarātrī, Mahārātrī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī,
Vikṛti, Nandinī, and thereafter Muṇḍinī.
Indrakhaṇḍā, Śikhaṇḍinī, Niśumbhamathinī, and Mardinī;
likewise Mahiṣamardinī, and after her Indrāṇī;
furthermore, Rudrāṇī is celebrated as the one who possesses half of Śaṅkara’s body.
This is the circle of thirty-two Śaktis: Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Triśūlinī, Pālinī, Ambikā, and Hlādinī;
outside of that, O Dear One, are Piṅgalākṣī and Viśālākṣī.
Sabuddhi, Vṛddhi, Svadhā, Svāhā, and likewise Śraddhā; Nityā, Vasuṃdharā, Dhātrī, and she who is foremost in the three worlds;
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Tridiveśvarī.
Rūpā, Vararūpā, Tathā, Bahurūpikā, Skandamātā, Cyutaprīti, Vimalā, Amalā, Aruṇī,
Vāruṇī, Prakṛti, and Vikṛti.
Sṛṣṭisthiti, Saṃhṛti, Sandhyāmātā, Satī, Vardikā, Jārī, Paradevādimātṛkā,
Bhagavatī, Devakī, and Kamalāsanā.
O you who have one face and likewise seven faces, O Goddess praised by the preceptors;
O Mardinī, accompanied by Surasvarā and others; thereafter, O you with protruding lips, upward-pointing hair, many heads, and a belly like that of a wolf.
Vṛkodārī, likewise Rekhā, Rathā, Diśā, Śirirekhikā, Aparāgamā, Vegāpavanavegikā,
as well as Bhuvanapālā and Madanāturā.
Naṅgā, Anaṅgamadanā, Tathānaṅgā, Mekhalā,
Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, Bhayaṃkarī, Asurāṇā, Akṣobhyā, Satyavādinī, and Vasurūpā.
One should worship these Śaktis—Tarā, Suvṛttā, Parameśvarī, Varadā, and Vāgīśī—in a clockwise order; they bestow the fulfillment of all desires and aims. These are the sixty-four great Śaktis.

The worship has been described to you; thereafter, the wise one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) upon the ground-mandala. Having again honored the Goddess, he should offer the food offering (naivedya) and other gifts. Thus, O God, has it been fully explained to you.

Even the name is difficult to obtain. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worship and the Description of the Extraction of the Yantra of the Twelvefold Guṇitas of Bhuvaneśvarī," in the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*.

The Lord said: O Pārvatī, know that the syllable *paśu* consists of the circular mouth-vowel (*o*) joined with the bindu and the letter *da*; it is the goad (*aṅkuśa*) accompanied by the essence of fire (*ra*). The Vidyā resides in the middle of this.

O Dear One, when the lords of the Asuras have been worshipped and the five-colored [syllables] are encapsulated by the two *prakṣara* vowels, then that which is difficult to obtain on earth— the extraction of the *gargala* at the beginning— is declared; by the mere performance of which, one attains the three worlds.
O Goddess, the attraction of the world occurs through the tradition;
endowed with the grace of the venerable Guru, one should properly fashion a well-rounded, excellent composition according to the sūtra.
Then, having joined the two circles together so they form a hollow space,
one should likewise draw an eight-cornered figure for the Goddess that is pleasing to the mind; then,
from those corners toward the eight directions, the practitioner should draw lines.

O Goddess, from two *khā* [units] an extremely beautiful bolt (*argala*) is produced; however, one should construct eight such bolts using that same single measurement. At its tip, the wise man should fashion a circle like the orb of the moon, and then again a line.
O Goddess, having drawn forth the supreme prior arrangement and fashioned it for the lord of practitioners,
one should arrange two groups of eight squares in succession so that they become manifest; O Goddess, there are two sets of eight petals and the bolts.

O Great Lord, when the movements of the breath proceed correctly in this manner, the attraction of the three worlds shall indeed take place. The seed-syllable of Śakti, joined with my name as the object to be accomplished, is for the practitioner. Pā.
The best of practitioners should inscribe [the mantra] enclosed by the pair of great seed-syllables *ŚĀṂ* and *KUŚAṂ* within the central circle of the pericarp;
he should then inscribe the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in due order upon the eight corners.
O beloved, having inscribed the mantras ending with "ka va ca" in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu,
the wise one should worship the Eye in the center; he should draw the Astra mantra four times in the four directions and the corners of the square.
One should write [the letters] from *ttā* up to the corner of *vasu* (the eighth letter) within the eight directions;
indeed, O Maheśānī, this is according to the sequence of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
Having abandoned the fire-power (*vanhi-śakti*), adorn that [space] with the earth (*bhū*) there; that is the seed-syllable (*vīja*).

O beautiful one, O beloved, one should write the twelve vowels— excluding *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*— in that manner; first, one should write the initial triad facing east, and then [the others] from the north.
The wise one should first draw [the line] facing east; second, on the southern side;
third, in the western part;
and likewise, fourth, the bolt (argala) on the northern end in the west. Bhū.
Having drawn the seeds of the sun (the letter *ra*), one should place the wind (the letter *ya*) there;
the practitioner should first write three [seeds] on the eastern bolt of fire,
and likewise another triad on the western side.
O beloved, one should draw the banner of the bolt of the Maruts in the west;
O Lord of Gods, it is the achiever of all purposes even in the east. O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the deity of the bolt of Yama, Vāyu.
Having omitted the seed-syllables of the Sun, one should place Varuṇa there;
the first [syllable] in the east, the second in the south, and the third reaching the western end;
thereafter, the wise one should draw the bolt (argalā) from the west toward the north.
O Goddess, O beautiful one, in the fourth [position] from the east, according to the path of the Guru,
having removed the water [element], one should place the letter *ra* of the solar seed-syllables there;
one should write the first triad and the subsequent triad upon the throat of the Rakṣas.
O Goddess, one should first write the *śaivārgala* from the north according to the sequence of the mantras,
and subsequently from the south;
this should be inscribed within the eight auspicious squares known as the *kesuras*.
The knower of mantras should write this golden seed-syllable of the four— Pāśa, Śrī, Bhuvaneśānī, and Kāma— in reverse order;
the practitioner, having omitted the final Pāśa, should join it with the goad (Śṛṇi).
Outside of that, one should indeed draw [the letters] in sequence within the eight corners:
Kāminī, Antarajinī, and then Agravallabhā;
the other eight syllables of the aforementioned form are in the filaments (kesara), and Antaka is at the end.
Having inscribed the mantra of Caṇḍī— consisting of five syllables, beginning with *caṃdra-kātyāyini*, followed by *śakti-gauri*, *trike-rudra-dayite*, *yogīśvarīm*,
and ending with *kavacāstrāgnivallabhā*— in her true form; O Gaurī, [this is the worship of] Caṇḍī.

The goddess Tyāyanī is difficult to find in the three worlds; therefore, I shall now fully explain her external form as it is encircled: the syllable *Haṃsa*, the *Vāmanetra* (the short *i*), adorned above by a *bindu*, and again *Haṃ*.

One should draw this five-syllabled [mantra] step by step, with the seven-syllabled [mantra] placed within the interior of each pair of vowels; thus it becomes eightfold. Outside, one should draw a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus upon its petals.

One should surround the mantra of Karṇikā, the woman, and oneself with the eight *sukras* using a noose and *kuśa* grass; outside of that, one should encircle it in a circular form and write the enclosure of the *mātrikās* in the order of *anuloma*.
In the same way, O beloved, there is the counter-clockwise encirclement by the Mātṛkās;

all of this, O beloved, one should encircle with the great letter *Ṭha*. This is the great jar-argala yantra, which bestows the fruits of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Within this, one should perform the invocation...

O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Hyadevī with ritual services; from the beginning up to the feet, O Mistress of the Gods, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and limbs. Having meditated upon her whose form is bliss, and possessing a body perfected by mudrās, one should perform the worship of the retinue during the first [pūjā].
O most beloved one, listen to the *caraṇa* [mantra] and the five *hṛllekhās*; this is the second limb.
Then, O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should worship the Mothers in the eight corners as before, and subsequently on the petals of the lotus, starting from the east.

Furthermore, O beautiful one, one should worship the Kapālas outside of that, individually with pleasing offerings ending with betel, while performing recitation according to one's capacity and with regular discipline;
this is the daily [rite].
As for the method, listen to the procedure for *puraścaraṇa*:

one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) and perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, using fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), as well as sesame seeds; thus one should properly offer the oblations in brief.
Then the practitioner of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) shall become [successful]: one desiring subjugation (*vaśya*) should offer *jātī* flowers;

O Dear One, one desiring prosperity should offer lotuses; and one desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*) should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *khādira* wood, O Beloved. Even in the case of the single-syllable mantra (*ekākṣara*), O Lord of Gods, there is success here on earth.
O Dear One, this [universe] does not arise from the seed-syllable of the sky (vyoma-bīja) established on Kailāsa and other such places;

rather, it is produced from the seed-syllables of Brahman (brahma-bīja) consisting of the various letters and so forth. By means of that, O Beloved, this entire existence of the terrestrial sphere (bhū-maṇḍala) proceeds in the world.
By the fourth vowel, in the form of Śeṣa, she supports the great circle of the earth; therefore, she is the mistress even of Pātāla. Thus, O Great Goddess, she becomes the sovereign of the worlds.
The letter *ha* is the sky (*vyoman*); with the fourth vowel, it is born from air (*anila*).
When there is modification (*vikāra*) with the letter *ra*, she is directly of the nature of fire (*vahni*).
The seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) is to be known as the earth (*vasu*); therefore, the letter *ra* is the earth (*vasu*).
In this very way, there is equality between Maheśāni and Ananta; and from the moon, the bindu, and the nectar, the Goddess, flowing as liquid, becomes the three worlds,
creating them by means of the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
Thus she is called Tevamaheśānī and Bhuvaneśī.
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Extraction and Accomplishment of the Jūṭārgala Yantra," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.]
Īśvara said: O beloved, I shall now describe the fifth, Ratnavidyeśī; listen. By the mere remembrance of her, even the wind becomes still.
Having uttered the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, one should add the Bindu that bestows grace upon the throat.
Then one should utter the seed-syllable of the Earth (laṃ), adorned with the sound *bhiḥ*. After that, one should again write the first syllable followed by "namo bhagavati" at the end.
One should then write the pair "vārāhī" twice; this is the third [syllable] to be written. Vā.

O Dear One, following that, there is the pair "rāhamukhi," then "ca" and "dvandva" without a conjunction; then "andhe," "cāndhini," and the seven-syllable [seed] ending with "hṛt. Then "ruṃdhe," "ruṃdhini," then "hṛt," "jaṃbhe," "jaṃbhini," and then "hṛt. Furthermore, "mo... [is added].
"O Maheśāni,

having spoken thus, she who exists with the infinite letter 'A'— meaning she whose form is endless— struck all the wicked ones with the *stambha* (paralysis) that steals away consciousness and the *stambhinī* (paralyzing power) that seizes it."
*Naṃ taṃ nāṃ ca sarveṣāṃ sarva-vāgi iti*. The mind, the eye, and the movement of the mouth are proclaimed;

*jihvā-stambhaṃ kuru dvayam* (paralyze the tongue, O pair); quickly, *vaśyaṃ kuru dvandvam vāgbhavaṃ pārthivaṃ punaḥ ṭakāraḥ* (subjugate the couple; the seed-syllable of speech, the earthly one, and again the letter *ṭa*).
The four *rasas*, the four corners, the armor (*kavaca*), the weapon (*astra*), and the beloved of Agni (the letter *ra*)—
these indeed constitute the one hundred and fourteen syllables of the mantra. Furthermore, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is proclaimed to be performed with forty-four words.
The knower of mantras should place the three syllables on the face and the ten syllables on the feet;
he should place twenty syllables on the joints of the arms and legs, including the tips, and having also placed the remaining syllables, he should place one supreme syllable on both sides.
In this very manner, the wise practitioner should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters;
thereafter, for the purification of the body, he should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*).
Following that, he should place the pair of feet of Vārtālī at the heart.
O Goddess, the pair of *rāhi*s is declared to be the *Śiro-mantra* (head mantra);
then the pair of *vārāhamukhi*s, followed by the seven-syllable *Śikṣā*;
then the armor (*kavaca*) with seven syllables; one should then assign the eye (*netra*) in due order.

Then, O beloved, one should perform the placement of the seven-syllable mantra and the six limbs; for the sake of all accomplishments, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the entire mantra.
I shall now proclaim the extraction of the *yantra* by which the three worlds are enchanted, [on] copper.
On a Monday, one should write [the mantra] on a golden birch-bark leaf using yellow pigment (rocanā),
saffron, saffron-water, agallochum, sandalwood, and turmeric;
one should draw a beautiful three-cornered wheel.

One should draw a five-cornered, a six-cornered, an eight-petaled, a hundred-petaled, and a thousand-spoked lotus, as well as the ground and the celestial sphere (*gagana-bimba*). One should worship the lion-throne in the center of that which is richly adorned with fourfold radiance; [therein] Vāṇī.
Having worshipped all the Mothers with the pair of seed-syllables *bhūḥ* and *bhuvaḥ*,
one should contemplate this pedestal situated in the midst of a mountain of crystal; there the wise practitioner should invoke the Goddess and perform meditation.
[He saw] the Mother of the Universe, seated within the interior of a lotus resembling the dawn at twilight, possessing the brilliant luster of a great sapphire,
adorned with a garland of *kadaṃba* flowers and human skulls, and embellished with nine precious gems.
Adorned with the splendor of a crown fashioned from priceless jewels, wearing a silken garment and beautiful ornaments of coral and gems, she shines with a plow,
a mace, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

One should worship with offerings and mantras that goddess who has conquered the four arms, who has tawny eyes, a slender waist, and a face like a blue lotus; she possesses firm, excellent breasts and a face like a boar. Gaṃ.

One should properly perform seventy thousand recitations with incense, flowers, and other offerings to achieve the fulfillment of all desires and aims; for the sake of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one hundred and ten thousand oblations and praises should be performed with *bandhūka* flowers as the tenth part of that total.
One should offer oblations with pieces of turmeric mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), as well as with lac, *agaru*, and various kinds of ground fragrant substances;
O Lord of Devas, the practitioner (*mantrin*) attains success—of this there is no doubt. Śṛ...

Now, for the procedure of worship, having first invoked the Goddess for the sake of accomplishment and performed the worship of the limbs (aṅga) and the enclosures (āvṛti) in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu,
listen as I describe [the worship] within the triangle in the three corners of the central directions.
One should worship a triad in sequence in the left, left-upper, and right [corners]:
Jambhinī, Stambhinī, and Mohinī, for the sake of all accomplishments (siddhi). O Lord of Devas, one should worship those beginning with Rūndhinī within the Stambhinī [mandala].
In the five-cornered [maṇḍala] of Mahādevī, according to the sequence beginning with the city (pura) and so forth, outside of that at the location of Mātṛs, there shall be the worship of the Mātr̥s;
starting from the six-spoked [maṇḍala], one should worship in a clockwise direction.
One should worship the goddesses Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī in the six-cornered [mandala]; furthermore,
for the sake of accomplishing all aims, one should worship two goddesses on either side of the six-cornered [mandala].
One should worship the wrathful Laṅkāpālī holding [an object] on the left;
one should worship the goddess Staṃbhinī holding a pestle and a brick on the right;
and one should worship Caṇḍoccaṇḍā Maheśānī in front of the hexagonal enclosure.
O beloved, one should worship the son of Pañcamī, who holds a skull, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a trident, whose head is adorned with matted locks as dark as a blue lotus;
then, on the petals of the eight-petaled lotus, one should worship the group of six Vārtālīs. Śṛ...
One should indeed worship that noble one with the eight great verses; [the mantra] which goes to the peaks,
empties the entrails, and cuts through the wheel of the belly,
resembling a dark blue cloud, is capable of destroying hundreds of enemies.
It should be worshipped in sequence by the Rudras (eleven), the Suns (twelve), the Vasus (eight),
and the Sūkas (seven), each recited three times separately, situated upon thirty-three petals; on the remaining petal, one should join it with Stambhinī and Jambhinī.
One should worship that foremost Maheshani as the Great Lion;
having worshipped a thousand-petaled lotus,
one should draw the image of Vārāhī, O Great Goddess, with a thousand [petals] and the goad.

O Goddess, one should worship with this very mantra a thousand times; one should worship Bhūviṃva, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, Yoginī, and Gaṇapa. Again, one should worship the Goddess with incense, flowers, and other offerings of libation.

Rosaries made of *kṣamā*, *lāha*, *haridrā*, and the like are primarily used for the purpose of immobilization (*stambhana*); or else, one may use those made of crystal, lotus seeds, rudrākṣas, or *ari* seeds.
For the sake of performing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite the mantra that is identical in essence to that [deity].
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worship in the Fifth Sequence," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
The Lord said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual of libation (tarpaṇa) on this earth.
One should satisfy Śivā with sesame seeds, maireya wine, and bandhūka flowers— difficult to obtain—
after worshipping her as before in a beautiful vessel made of gold or other materials; by this rite, O Brahmin, one will certainly become beloved.
O Supreme Goddess, there is a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for this very *vidyā*; its specific nature, which cuts down all enemies, is described here:
the pit is one cubit in height and one cubit in width at the bottom.
A delightful sacrificial pit (hastakhāta) is prescribed here, and the fire-offering (homa) is described as follows:
for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana), it should be in the direction of Śiva (the north); for suppression (nigraha), it should be in the direction of Yama (the south).
O Maheśānī, one should worship the Bhairava-fire in this sacrificial pit.

O Supreme Goddess, one should worship worldly desires with the mantras to be described hereafter. O Goddess, one should write the Heart-mantra with Bhuvaneśvarī, and then write Bhuvaneśvarī herself as the Śikhā-mantra; O Beloved, these three seed-syllables [constitute it].
Having uttered Bhairava with the suffix -ktā (past passive participle) and written his name in the dative case,
one should perform the worship of the fire; then, one should offer an oblation into the fire, writing the three seed-syllables as before and the syllable *viṭha* for the fire of Bhairava.
Having offered one oblation with this [mantra] to Bhairava-agni, O lady with the beautiful face of a blue lotus, one should worship with blue lotuses or even with *tāpiccha* flowers;
for a rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), four hundred [oblations] are to be known as required in the fire-sacrifice.
O beautiful one, with the wood of *vadāru*, lac, and turmeric, one should perform a hundred and eight oblations for each at the three middle watches of the night,
using the *hariṇī* mudrā; this is the homa that has been taught therein.
O beloved, to the south of the sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*), at a distance of one cubit,
on a wide vessel made of gold, silver, clay, crystal, or iron,
[one should place] a black cloth covered with blue lotuses and *tāpiccha* flowers.
The best of mantra-knowers should worship him with water mixed with sesame seeds;
having uttered the Vāgbhava (AIM) and the syllable for the Earth (LĀM), and for the purpose of attraction (KARṢAṆA),
he should write this mantra ending with the word "HṚD" (the heart), preceded by the syllable "HA".
One should draw the goad, the wrathful goddess, and the mace upon the forehead;
having recited the mantra of the goddess twenty-seven times,
and having touched the jar while meditating on the fifth Supreme Goddess within the heart, that jar...
A wise person, accompanied by the syllables *ka* and *pha*, should sprinkle the enemy with water from a vessel containing the letter *ṭa*;
by this, he will certainly become submissive, like a shadow.
Now, O beloved, listen as I describe the procedure for the *tīrthagraha-homa* (the fire sacrifice for seizing the *tīrtha*). *kha*.

O beloved, the practitioner should mix these with the blood from his own limbs, along with parched grain, powdered sesame, and a ball of food; he should then unite it with the *piṇḍa* for the sake of the goal, using white perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

One should offer the *yoginī-piṇḍa*, beautiful with supreme bliss, using a leaf-hut, a mound of earth, or a clay vessel; it should be offered into the mouth of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with oblations of sesame seeds, parched grain, and particles of powder. Ayu... [text truncated]
O Goddess, if one recites that [mantra] for three fortnights while offerings are made,
there is no doubt that the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen of the enemy will fall into the mouths of the Yoginīs here, O Goddess. Now...
I shall now fully explain that which brings joy to practitioners:

one should employ the *praṇava* (oṃ) by enclosing it with the *praṇava* itself. One should enclose the name of the target (*sādhya*) between the two *au*s, the two *glau*s, and the letter *ṭha*. Eight...
Having offered oblations with vajras, one should place *glauṃ* and *krauṃ* in between;
then, within the fire-vajra, one should write the seed-syllable of the sun, followed by the earthly mandala.
Within that fire-vajra, one should draw the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and externally inscribe the vidyā-mantra.

O fair-faced one, having placed everything restrained by the four goads upon the Rudra-svara, one should worship it with yellow flowers; together with this, the Pañcamī-śakaṭa-yantro is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
The wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and cast it into a vessel at night;
having written [the mantra] on birch bark, the self-controlled one should place it in a hole during the night.
Knowing the mantras, the practitioner should worship the *preta* with dark-red flowers.
Having cast incense and fire [into the vessel], one should perform the sacrifice according to the teacher’s injunctions;
one should worship this in sequence using vessels of gold, silver, or copper.
One who desires bracelets should propitiate Śivā with turmeric-colored flowers.
Having placed it in a heap of grain in the evening,
one should then write this [mantra] on a shallow vessel belonging to a potter;
then, having worshipped it with flower-like substances as dark as collyrium, the guide [should proceed] along the path.
Then, one should swiftly uproot even a very firm enemy stationed at the peak [of power]; having extracted him from that vessel—

which has been split by substances such as *aśī* (lead) and possesses the luster of *bhinna-añjana*— and having worshipped him, one should cast him into the house of a blacksmith, or else [dispose of him] in water.
The enemy shall meet death from diseases born of mental distress.
At night, the best of knowers of mantras should write [the mantra] on a copper plate and so forth;
upon hearing the sound of that [plate] during battle, even those of great strength will flee.

O Dear One, having drawn [the deity] upon a smoky-colored wall and worshipped with smoky-colored offerings, the sight of those enemies shall perish; it cannot be otherwise. O Dear One, having drawn [the deity] within a slab of turmeric stone and worshipped, [the same result follows].
One should cast that yantra with yellow flowers into the lower wheel;
O Supreme Goddess, the speech of disputants is quickly paralyzed.
Then, having inscribed [the name] on lead, one should worship it with *śamī* flowers, O Dear One.
By placing [the object] beneath a stone and so forth, the practitioner shall become victorious in legal disputes;
one should worship with white flowers in a vessel made entirely of iron,
and the mantra-practitioner should write [the name] upon the *pañcasāra* (five-essence) leaf.

One who performs all rites should worship with flowers of five colors; then, having worshipped with beautiful blossoms, the wise one should draw a pair of eyes upon a dark, cloud-like surface and consecrate it on a cremation ground.
By this, there shall be swift attraction even of young women; one should place the wheel, colored with lac, inside a vessel made of lead or within the interior of a tree,
so that the targets indeed enter from the outermost parts of the tips.

O Goddess, one should place the wheel within the womb of the Nakṣatra-tree; whatever is performed for the target (sādhya) becomes manifest. When thrown into water, it bestows defects; when thrown into fire, it causes burning and bestows disease.
O beloved, [the mantra] cast into ashes brings benefit; when directed toward the earth, it bestows food;
when cast into a water-jar, it grants sons;
when cast in the eastern direction, it shall bring fear to enemies; and in the southeast...

In the south-eastern quarter, it brings about enmity and death; likewise, in the south-western quarter, it causes the intoxication of enemies. In the west, it bestows cattle, and that which is situated in the north-western quarter is said to grant wealth. Furthermore, in the north, it grants prosperity.

O Parameśvarī, for the practitioner, there is no doubt that [the mantra] residing in the northeast causes confusion among enemies; however, when it resides in the center, it certainly destroys all the undertakings of one's foes. Of this very [mantra]...

If the recitation were not performed at midnight, a curse from the deity would arise that is extremely difficult to overcome; therefore, one should recite this and worship it at midnight. Thus ends the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*.
In the *Hitā*, the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Cart-Mechanism," Lord Śiva said:
"In the great *Pañcarātra-tantra*, the Vaiṣṇava tradition has been declared; by propitiating this Goddess Śrī, one becomes the protector of the three worlds."
Those [energies] situated in the wheel of the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyākeśvara) are said to consist of Śiva and Vidyā;
they exist indeed in the wheel of the Moon. Therefore, Śivā is composed of Śiva.
In the great tantra *Siddharatna*, the tradition of the Gaṇapas is declared to be sevenfold.
Adorned by tens of millions of great tantras, the Goddess who is identical with them is Śivā; or,
she who illuminates the solar knowledge through the great tantras of the Sun-god is the Goddess who consists of that very essence, declared to be the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).

By constantly serving that Goddess through the four sacred abodes (caturāyatana), the deities of the four lineages have been described in connection with the Lion-Throne; O Supreme Sovereign, there is no doubt that this leads to their prosperity. Of her—
"By mere remembrance, great calamities flee away. [Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the Exposition of the Fourfold Tradition, in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
The Lord said:
Alternatively, O Mahādevi, we shall explain the description of the Nityās in their proper sequence.
O Pārvatī, there are many varieties of the Kāmeśvarī mantra;
among them, the Kāmeśvarī Vidyā, which is difficult to find on earth, is now being told. III.
Having first uttered "Pureśī," then "Tārā" at the end, followed by the word "Hṛt";
then having spoken the word "Kāmeśvari," [and] "O bestower of the fruits of will and knowledge" (*icchājñānaphalaprade*);
then having spoken "subjugation of all beings" (*sarvasattvavaśam*), [and] the word "O maker of the entire world" (*kari sarvajagat*)... kṣo.
They say: "BHAṆĀNTA KARIHUṂHUṂ CĀṆAŚCA TRIPUREŚVARĪM.
Having written the thirty-six-syllable Vidyā in reverse order, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating it twice through the first three portions, beginning with Kāmeśvarī.
[The procedure for] meditation on the Ṛṣi and others, the Yantra, worship, and so forth;
thus ends the daily ritual of the venerable Kāmeśvarī Nityā. The Lord said:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall explain the Vidyā of the venerable Bhagamālinī, [beginning with] Vāgbhava...

At the end of the word *vaṃbhaga* is *vāgbhava*; likewise, *bhagameva* and *vāgbhava*. At the end of *bhagini* is *vāgbhava*, and at the end of *bhagoda* is *vāgbhava*. *Bhagamālā* is *vāgbhava*, and that which begins with *vāgbhava* brings about fortune (*bhagāvaha*). *Bhaga* is in the secret place (*guhya*).
Vāgbhava, Bhaga, Yoni, and Vāgbhava; at the end of Bhaga is Pātinī, then Vāgbhava, Bhaga, Sarva, and the word Vāgbhava—
having written this, then Bhagavaśaṅkari, Vāgbhava, and Bhagarūpetā.
One should write "O sister" (*bhagini*) and then "Vāgbhava"; "O one with moist vulva" (*bhagaklinne*) and then "Vāgbhava";

and at the end, one should write "Bhaga. Then [one writes] "O you who possess all vulvas" (*rūpe sarvabhagāni*), and then "Bring them here" (*ime hyānaya*) and "Vāgbhava. At the beginning of "Vāgbhava," [one writes] "O Goddess" (*bhagavati*).

One should utter "gavānte" (at the end of *gavām*) and likewise write "vāgbhava" (the seed-syllable of speech) at the end of "bhaga"; one should write "vāgbhava" after "bhageṣu", and having written "vāgbhava" after "rete",
[one writes] "bhagaklinne" or "vāgbhava", and then "bhagaklinne" and "aṃ".
The Blessed One should speak that [mantra] as "Bhagaṃ drāvaya," and having written it, [it is] "Bhagoṃ dhe bhage" and so forth.
"O Bhageśvarī, agitate all beings with *vicce bhagam*.
One should write the Vāgbhava (*aiṃ*), the *bhagaklam*, the Vāgbhava, and *gajeṃ*. One should write the Vāgbhava, the *bhagablūṃ*, the Vāgbhava, and *bhagabheṃ*."
One should write Vāgbhava, Bhaga, Blūṃ, Vāgbhava, and Bhaga; one should write Vāgbhava, Bhaga, Vāgbhava, Bhaga, and Oṃ; one should write Vāgbhava, Bhaga, Blūṃ, Vāgbhava, and Bhaga. Bha...
Having smeared all parts with cow dung, one should draw the vulva (bhaga) as before;
having drawn the five vulvas of the god of love (Manmatha), the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) should be placed upon the earth; then one should worship the Goddess again.
O Lord of the Gods, this third [form] is eternal, bestowing both enjoyment and liberation; it is said to bring the three worlds under one's control.
Between the *bhaga*s and at the end of the *bhaga*s, one should write the syllable *hara* along with the *mātmaka*. At the end of the *bhaga*s...

Then, having uttered this vidyā— “te pañcamaṃ kāmaṃ tataḥ vaibhagamālinīṃ ṅe tā”— which brings the three worlds under control and is adorned with one hundred and twenty-four [syllables], it is indeed the fifth.
This Mālinī is the source of all debts (or desires), eternally bestowing all perfections.
Subhaga is its seer; Gāyatrī is said to be its metre;
and O Beloved, *ha-ra-la-ma* is its seed-syllable, while *hrīm* is its power (*śakti*).

O Supreme Goddess, the preceptor should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllable of the Woman (*strīvījaka*), *klūṃ*, as the *kīlaka*, differentiated by the six long vowels. Likewise, he should perform the placement of Kāma and the placement of the arrows (*vāṇanyāsa*) as before.
She stands in the midst of a Kadamba grove, possessing the splendor of the rising sun,
adorned with various ornaments, capable of attracting the three worlds,
and holding a noose, a goad, a book, a bow, and a pen for scratching on palm leaves.

Having thus meditated upon the Mother of the Universe, who bestows both boons and fearlessness, a person should, while conquering their appetite for food, recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Then,
the wise practitioner should perform a fire sacrifice with one-tenth of that number of Bandhūka flowers, smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), within a triangular [fire-pit].

One should draw the maṇḍala thus: first a hexagon, then a sixteen-petaled lotus, then an eight-petaled lotus, and finally the orb of the earth; having worshipped the Goddess in the center, one should then worship the limbs and the surrounding retinue. This is the Vidyā.
One should worship the triad of powers within the three triangles, beginning from the front corner and then worshipping them again within those [triangles]: Śubhagā,
Bhagā, and likewise Bhagasarpiṇī, and Vāṇā.
The wise practitioner should worship there as before; he should worship the group of six beginning with Bhagamālā in the six corners,
as well as Vaśaṅkarī, Rūpā, Nityā, and Klinnā-svarūpiṇī.
And likewise the Blessed One, the Supreme Goddess who grants boons— namely Svaretā,
Klinnā, and also Klinnadravā—
as well as the Amoghā Vidyā and the deity Klinnadevatā.
One should join these sixteen Goddesses with the word "bhaga";
one should worship the Mothers, the Goddesses of the directions, upon the eight petals; and Indra and the others on the circle of the earth, and then one should worship the Goddess again.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Bhagamālinī. The Lord said:

Having first uttered Bhu-vaneśī, then *Nityaklinne Madadrave*, and finally the wife of Vahni (Svāhā)—this is the Vidyā consisting of the letters of Rudra, which is most excellent. Brahmā... [said: "It is so."

The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Samudita, the meter (chandas) is said to be Virāṭ, the deity (devatā) is stated to be Nityaklinnā, and the supreme woman is Drāviṇī. The first seed-syllable (bīja) is Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā), and the power (śakti) is considered the pin (kīlaka).
O Beloved,
the supreme teacher should sequentially assign the six limbs by means of two, two, and two [syllables] respectively;
[he should meditate on her] as having red limbs, wearing red garments, with the moon as her crest-jewel, and three eyes.

One should constantly meditate upon Nityā, who is adorned with red ornaments, whose eyes are smeared with the intoxication of wine, who holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup that likewise removes great fear, and who is resplendent upon a lotus seat.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar) in a tenth part of that number; thus the wise practitioner becomes one who has completed the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
Alternatively, one may perform the homa with Madhūka flowers or with lotuses grown in water.
One should draw a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and then a square representing the earth. First, having worshipped the Goddess, one should then worship the limbs and the attendants.
Within the triangle, one should worship the Goddess Nityā, Klinnā, and Madadravā.
One should worship [the goddesses] at the base of the petals and in the middle of the petals of the Mother;
one should worship Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā, Madadravā, Drāviṇī, and Kṣobhiṇī.
This is the procedure for the Nityāklinnā Nityā. The Lord said:
"O Maheshani, I shall now describe the supreme goddess Bherunda;
having uttered the syllable *Bharau*, it should be well-encircled by two *Tvaṃkushas* (the syllables *Tvaṃ* and *Kūṃ*), and deprived of its final letter."

The ten-syllable mantra, consisting of the letter *ca* at the four gates adorned with the letter *ra*, enriched by the moon of grace (*anugraha*), and containing the seed-syllable (*tāra*) and *svāhā* within its belly, becomes a great destroyer of poisons for the Lord of Gods. Its seer is Mahā... [the rest of the text follows].

Viṣṇu is said to be the Gāyatrī metre; this supreme Śakti is the deity. The third is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), while the Śakti is the Vahni-jāyā (the wife of fire, i.e., the Svāhā). The kīlaka is indeed the Śṛṇi (the ploughshare). [This is applied] in the division of the six long vowels.
Performing the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable *dena*, [one should meditate on the goddess] who resembles ten million moons,
flowing with streams of nectar-liquid; she is blue-throated, three-eyed,
adorned with various ornaments, and radiant like a sapphire.

Having thus meditated upon her, who is adorned by the splendor of the peacock-vehicle [Kārttikeya], who holds a noose, a goad, a skull-cup, a small dagger, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is embellished by the golden Garuda-emblem on her crown; having meditated thus—
One who has conquered the senses should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; O Goddess of the Gods, one should then perform oblations with white lotuses for one-tenth of that number.
Thereafter, one should draw a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square on the ground.
With the seed-syllable *dhīpraṇava* (oṃ dhīḥ), one should place two *śṛṅga* (prongs) on the two sides of the triangle;
within the triangles, one should assign the triad beginning with the fifth [vowel];
and the remainder should be inscribed at the tips of the corners of the triangle.

O Dear One, the practitioner of mantras should inscribe the *mālā-mantra* sequentially upon the eight petals; having divided it into eight syllables, he should write Bheruṇḍā— who consists of sixty-four syllables and is the destroyer of great poisons— and Bhuvaneśī.
Having uttered "Muñca āryatā tribhuvane," one should bow to that Vidyā;
O Siddhā, O Invincible One, O World-Worshipped One, in the midst of wandering,
wandering, and great delusion, one should write the two "Hūṃ" syllables consisting of the nature of the letter *dhī*, followed by "Vicce" and the pair [of syllables].
Then Lekaulekurumāla, followed by Bheruṇḍa, Śikhicālin, and Khyavāhinī; then Nīlakaṇṭha, Caru, Dreca,
Vetāla, Soma, Mātṛkā, and Bhuvaneśī.

Its form consists of sixty-two syllables; its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Brahmā, its seed-syllable (bīja) is the Lord of Beings (Bhuvaneśvarī), and its deity is to be known as Bheruṇḍā, the bestower of the goals of human life. [This is accomplished] by means of the seed-syllable itself through the differentiation of the six long vowels.

One should draw the six-limbed meditation (ṣaḍaṅgaka-dhyāna) and the pair of previous goddesses' worship; then, one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet in their proper sequence upon the ground. Having invoked the Great Goddess (Maheśānī) there, one should worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras).
The worship of the limbs is as before; thereafter, listen: one should worship Triśikhā, Nīlakaṇṭhī, and Aindrī in the three corners in sequence.
On the two sides of the triangle, one should worship Vaitālī and Somamātṛkā.
Then, one should worship Tribhuvaneśānī, Siddhā, Ajitā, Lokepūjyā, Mahāmohā, Kulā, Kaulā, and likewise Kusvapnalā on the eight petals, beginning with the front [petal]. Then, Mā...
"O beautiful one, Indra and the others are to be worshipped on the eight petals; thereafter, one should worship the Goddess again on the earth. Thus ends the ritual for the Nityā Bheruṇḍā.
The Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the [ritual for] the Nityā."
Having written "cavahnivāsinīm" and "parām," and then "vahnayantevāsinyai namas," this eight-syllable mantra, O Maheśānī, bestows the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
Vasiṣṭha is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is its meter (chanda).
It is said by the learned that the syllable *aiṃ* is the deity, the goddess, and the fire-abiding one;
the seed-syllable and the power (*śakti*) are at the beginning and the end, while the pin (*kīlaka*) is in the middle.
One should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅga*) by repeating the three words of the goddess twice.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the three parts of the body in three places, the preceptor should meditate [on the goddess] who has the luster of molten gold, is adorned with various ornaments, and holds a noose,
a goad, a svastika, a spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while visualizing [the goddess] wearing a crown of three jewels and dispelling the darkness of the three worlds; one should then perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number.
One should ascend [the mantra] with clarified butter as the vehicle; then the mantra becomes perfected.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus and write the vidyā on each petal, one syllable at a time, and thereafter draw the circle of the earth (bhū-vimba).
O Pārvatī, having worshipped the central seat and the directions within it,
one should then worship the [energies] yellow, white, reddish, black, smoky, intense, spark-emitting, radiant, and flaming, and thereafter worship the lion-throne.
One should invoke Vīma and worship him with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).
Having first worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*), one should worship [the deities] upon the eight petals:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, and Aśva.
O beloved, one should worship Rabhasa, Vaiśvānara, Kaumāratejas, Deveśi, and Viśvamukha in sequence; then, on the eight petals,
one should worship Mukha, Vārāhī, and the others.
Having worshipped [the deities] on the eight petals, the teacher [should worship] Indra and the others;
then, upon the ground of the mandala, he should again worship the Goddess, who is adorned by the ten digits of the great seat of Fire (Vahni-mahāpīṭha). Thus [it is said].
The Ritual Procedure for the Ever-Abiding Nityā. The Lord’s Speech: Or else, O Mahādeva, having drawn the supreme Mahāvidyeśvarī Nityaklinnā, one should draw the seed-syllable at her mouth.
At the end of *hṛllekhā* is *phaṭ*, followed by the Moon-seed (*caṃdra-bīja*) with the visarga;
this fourteen-syllable Vidyā has Brahmā declared as its Seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī as its stated metre (*chandas*), and the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*) as its Deity. The first...

The *hṛllekhā* should become the *kīlaka* for the power of the twenty-three syllables. The preceptor should assign the limbs (*aṅgas*) by means of four, two, two, two, and two [syllables] respectively. [With the word] *japā*.
Resembling a flower, radiant with red garments, adorned with jewels, eternal, and decorated with various ornaments;
[she holds] a noose, a goad, and a skull-bowl filled with the wine of the gods.
Having meditated upon her who bestows [these], the wise one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
he should offer oblations with ghee, sesame seeds, and rice grains in one-tenth of that number.
The mandala is thus: a triangle, a lotus of four petals, a lotus of eight petals, and an enclosure of earth.

Having drawn the Goddess in the center, one should worship her; first, having worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*), one should worship [the goddesses] in the triangles: Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī. After that, there is the worship of the Vedas and weapons, and the Veda-mātṛs.
One should worship Tāca, Hṛllekhā, Yoginī, and Candraśekharā in the four corners of the Veda-diagram (the square) according to the sequence beginning with the east:
Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā, and [Ma].
One should worship Dadruvā, Drāviṇī, Cakṣobhiṇī, Vasvarā, and Mātara;
likewise, the Lokapālas should be worshipped on the earth at the junctions of time.
Thus ends the procedure for Mahāvidyeśvarī. The Lord said:

Now I shall describe the Dūtī, capable of attracting the three worlds. Having uttered the mantra of Bhuvaneśī, one should write "Śivadūtyai namaḥ. O Dear One, this Śivadūtī consists of seven syllables and is the mistress of the three worlds.
The seer is Rudra, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śivā;
the beginning and end are the seed (bīja) and power (śakti), while the middle is called the pin (kīlaka).
One should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) by repeating the mantra three times according to its three divisions of knowledge.

One should constantly meditate upon her who resembles Durvāsā, who has three eyes, who is seated upon a great lion-throne, and who holds a conch, a bow, arrows, a trident, a noose, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times.
One should perform oblations with sesame seeds soaked in honey and clarified butter, numbering one-tenth [of the total].

One should draw an eight-petalled lotus and outside it, a circle representing the earth. Having worshipped the Goddess there, one should honor her with the full range of ritual offerings (*upacāras*).
Having worshipped the fire at the entrance of the forest, one should worship on the eight petals:
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, Prabhā, Śraddhā, Medhā, and Dhṛti—the eight; and on the circle of the earth, the lords of the directions (Dikpālas). Again...

"Having worshipped the Goddess, the lord of men shall become happy. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Nityā Śivadūtī. The Lord said: Now I shall describe the Great Goddess Tvaritā, the bestower of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). Tā...
One should write the armor (*kavaca*) as *raṃ parāṃ ca kha cha khe kṣaḥ*,
and having uttered the heart-mantra consisting of *strīṃ hūṃ*, one should write the weapon (*astra*) as *kṣe parāṃ*.
This Tvaritā, whose syllables are those of Rudra, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The seer is Īśa, the meter is Virāṭ, and the presiding deity is Pārvatī; the seed-syllable is *ka*, and it is proclaimed that the power (*śakti*) is *ca*.
The pair *caccha* is the heart, *tu* is the head, and the pair *che-kṣa* is the tuft (*śikhā*).

Having assigned *kṣa* to the two arms, *trī* to the armor, *strī* to the two *hūṃ*s, *haṃ* to the two eyes, and *kṣe* to the two feet, it is proclaimed as the *Kṣephustra*. [One should meditate on her] with dark limbs,
adorned by lotus-like hands and feet that are red and beautiful, [mounted upon] a bull.
Adorned with anklets and crest-jewels, golden parrots as her ornaments,
and a girdle of gold,
she is a slender couple with a pair of full, rounded breasts, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands.
Adorned with bracelets and armlets of polished conch-shells, with arm-rings of red gunja berries,
and ornaments of the lord of serpents and bells;
with ear-ornaments shimmering like snakes and eyes as red as those of one intoxicated, she possessed dark, curly locks.

One should meditate upon the goddess Kairātī, who destroys all fear; she holds a skull-bowl marked with the ash, vermilion, and flowers, is adorned with the abode of the rolling eyes [of her consort], and is seated with majesty upon a shimmering lion-throne. Ravi.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with madhūka flowers amounting to one-tenth of that number for the Goddess of the Gods; thus, the rite of purification (puraścaraṇa) is accomplished. One should draw an eight-petaled lotus and encircle it with the outer square diagram.
One should write the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) eight times in each of the eight corners;
in the center, one should write Bhuvaneśvarī, and surround her with the *mātṛkā* letters on the outside.
This is declared to be the wheel named "The All-Protecting" (*sarvarakṣākara*). Therein...
One should worship the external Maheśānī with ritual offerings;
having first worshipped the limbs, one should worship [the goddesses] upon the eight petals: Huṃkārī, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedanī, and likewise Kṣepaṇī.

O Lord of Gods, one should worship the woman Huṃkāriṇī, the bringer of welfare, with the seed-syllable Śrī; thereafter, the world-protector Agni, who wields a bow, O beloved, is to be worshipped as Phaṭkāriṇī.
On either side of the door stood Vijayā and Jayā, adorned with ornaments and holding in their hands cane-staves made of gold and jewels; meanwhile,
Kṛṣṇa shone with his curly hair and a moving crown.

The servant (Kiṅkara) is to be worshipped first; outside of that, one should worship in sequence Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and then one should again worship the Goddess. One should worship her, the great protectress, with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings.
Thus ends the procedure for the Nityātvāritā. The Lord said:
"Now I shall speak, O Maheśāni, of the Vidyā Śrīkulasuṇdarī;
now I shall speak of the supreme Nityā, who bestows the goals of human existence."

Having uttered Tripureśī and likewise Bhairavī known as Nityā, followed by three *huṃ* syllables—this is the Vāṇa-vidyā consisting of five syllables. O beloved, this is the Tripureśī yantra; [now follows] the worship of the Ṛṣi and other [limbs]. Pañcā...
This [seed-syllable] *kṣarī-vāṇa* is eternally the supreme;
this is the rule for the eternal non-dual [mantra]. The Lord said:
Now, furthermore, we shall explain the Vidyā of the Great Goddess, the Blue-Flagged One (*nīlapatākinī*), beginning with the *tāra*.
First, the word *hṛtpada* (the heart-place), then the word *Kāmeśvarī*,
then the word *Kāmāṅkuśā* is spoken, then *Kāmapatākikā*; at the end of the path of *Bhaga*, [the word] *Patākā*, and near *Bhaga*.

Having written the three heart-mantras, one should then write "astrāya te. At the end of "parama," one should likewise write the secret triple *huṃ* syllable. In "madane" [one writes] "madanānta," and then one should write "trailokya" in the body. *Drā*.
One should likewise draw her armor (*kavaca*) and weapons, as well as her beloved consort.
The supreme goddess Nīlapatākinī consists of six syllables; she is Kāmeśvarī, and her *yantra* is now described. She is red in color.
Clad in red garments, adorned with various jewels,
and possessing a shimmering blue banner of sapphire, she sits upon a lotus; her ears are graced by golden necklaces, and she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Having meditated upon Parameśānī, who is capable of attracting the three worlds, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds in the tenth part of that number. O lady of excellent hips, one should worship this Kāmeśī Vidyā. Thus [ends the section on] Nī.
The Ritual for the Eternity of the Banner of Speech. The Lord said: Now I shall explain the supreme knowledge that always bestows victory;
it is adorned with the sounds of Śiva, Candra, Sūrya, Ātman, Agni, and Rudra.
One should write this [mantra] for victory, pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.
I am its seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī its meter (*chandas*), and the Self (*svayam*) its deity.
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is in the middle of the heart-syllables, while the power (*śakti*) and the pillar (*kīlaka*) are one's own seed-syllable.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed with the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels;
[the deity is] one-faced and ten-armed, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
her face terrible with fangs, and adorned with a garland of human heads.
Reduced to mere bone and skin, resembling a heap of glowing embers,
clad in a tiger skin, exceedingly majestic, adorned with a new silken garment,
she bestows victory upon her devotees in battle by her mere remembrance.
One should worship her who holds a trident, shield, jar, sword,
goad, bell, two thunderbolts, noose, fire, and the gesture of fearlessness, the ever-victorious bestower of success;
one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number.
Then, by offering lotuses smeared with the three sweets, this [mantra] becomes perfected.
