Having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus,
and an enclosure of the earth, one should write the seed-syllable in the center and the seed-syllable within the triangles.

One should write the six syllables in the six corners and the vowels on the petals according to their respective pairs; then, one should write the great seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha and surround it with the Mātṛkā letters.
Having invoked the Great Goddess here, one should worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras).
Then, one should worship the enclosure of the six limbs within the triangle;
thereafter, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in the six corners.

One should worship the six Yoginīs on the eight petals and the Mothers in due order; then one should worship the World-Guardians in the square and again worship the Goddess. Thus ends the ritual for Vijayā Nityā. The Lord said:

One should establish the great *Nityā*, who is indeed all-auspicious (*Sarvamaṅgalā*), enriched by the *Jīva*, *Vāruṇa*, and *Tārā* [syllables], and who at the end of all things is the locus of auspiciousness.

Writing this nine-syllabled *Hṛdaya* of *Sarvamaṅgalā* upon the heart, [one attains the goal]. [The Seer is... *(Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a portion of a ritual manual or commentary on a mantra. The translation reflects the syntactic structure of the Sanskrit fragments as they appear.)*
The goddess Candramaheshani is said to have the Gayatri meter;
"Yam" is the seed-syllable (bīja), while the power (śakti) and the heart (hṛdaya) are likewise the seed-syllable.
By repeating the three parts of the Vidyā twice, the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is formed. [She is seated upon] a white lotus...
Eternal, beautiful, with a luster equal to the moon and the kunda flower, exceedingly serene, bestowing boons, adorned with various jewels, wearing infinite strings of pearls,
flowing with the liquid of nectar, and granting boons and fearlessness.
One should remember her as the increaser of good fortune; having thus meditated, one who has conquered the god of love should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform oblations with ten-thousandths of that number using white lotuses soaked in ghee. Eight...

Having invoked the Mistress of the Gods (Sureśvarī) there upon the vessel, which is the reflection of the earth, and having worshipped her with the ritual offerings (upacāras), one should perform the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, on the eight petals, she should be worshipped in the sequence beginning with the East (pūrva). Rā...
One should worship Kākramudvatī, Nandā, Śuddhā, Saṃjīvinī, Kṣamā, Adhyāyinī,
Candrikā, Hlādinī, and Puratoyā; thereafter, Brāhmī and the others, along with Bhūmi, Viveka, and Kukīśvara, should be worshipped.
Having worshipped her again and offered many gifts, [one honors] the one who dwells in the lunar orb;
thus ends the ritual procedure for Sarvamaṅgalā Nityā. The Lord said:
"I shall now proclaim Jvālāmālā, the supreme bestower of the goals of human life. Om."
Having uttered the seed-syllable *kāra* and "namo bhagavati," one should draw this Jvālāmālinī, who consumes all beings,
within the wheel of the *hāri* syllables; and she blazes with the mantra "jātavedasi."
One should draw two blazing pairs, each consisting of a pair of *huṃ* syllables, twice; likewise, one should inscribe the *vahni*, *vidyā*, *kavaca*, and *astra*.
These forty syllables shall constitute the wheel of one's own letters in their proper sequence. *Ṛ*.

O beloved, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Ṛṣi Śiṣṭu Kaśyapa, the *Chandas* Gāyatrī, the deity Tviṣimān, the seed-syllable *Repha* (Ra), the power (*śakti*), the *Kīlaka*, and the armor (*kavaca*).
One should then assign the limbs (*aṅgas*) using the twelve, twelve, five, eight, and four [syllables] respectively.

O Īśvarī, one should draw a forty-four-petaled lotus, and outside that, an eight-petaled lotus and the square of the earth; one should write the Great Vidyā in the pericarp and write [the other mantras] on the petals in sequence.

One should write the letters of the Durgā-mantra, the praises of the Goddess, and the vowels (*svarāḥ*) in pairs, O Supreme Mistress; one should encircle them with the letters of fire (*vahni-varṇa*). Having written [the mantra] with the *jātavedas* [mantra], one should again write the words "Om mama rā".
One should write *tīyatoni dāhātivedaḥ sanaḥ*;
at the end of the year, having written *atisaṃlikhya durgāṇi*, one should write *viśvānāve asiṃdhūṃ ca*; and one should write *dvāritātyagniḥ*.

O lady of excellent hips, I am this Durgā, whose form is that of the fire-god Jātavedas. One should worship the garland of flames seated within my diagram (yantra). First, having worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) with the Śaktis in the cardinal directions and the center, [one worships] Jayā.
Having worshipped these goddesses— Cavijayā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, and others, as well as Durmukhī, Vyāghramukhī, Siṃhamukhī, and Durgā— one should invoke the Goddess and worship her.
Having first worshipped the limbs [of the mantra], one should then worship the Goddess Jāgatītāpinī,
who is born from the womb of the Vedas and has the form of fire;
likewise, one should worship Setukhaṇḍāyātuhaṃtrī and Naramukhī.
Gīśvarī, Madavahā, Somarūpā, Manojayā,
Marudvegā, Carā, Triścatī, Brakopā, Yaśovatī, Toyātmikā, Nityā, Dayāvatī, and Hāriṇī.
Niraskṛtī, Avedamātā, Madanapriyā, Mārādhyā, Ānandinī, Aparā, Ripumardinī, Varā, Mukhī,
Daṇḍinī, Durgā, Gāyatrī, and likewise Nirav...
Dyāviśālākṣī, Śvāsodvāhā, Arcanandinī,
Vedanāvahnigarbhā, Siṃhavāhā, Dhuryā, Durvahā, Riraṃsā, and Tāpahāriṇī.
Having abandoned the desire for the kingdom and having worshipped the city and other [shrines], one should worship the Mothers on the eight spokes; on the ground, one should worship Ekakuñcīśvarā.
Then, having again worshipped the Goddess adorned with golden ornaments—
Possessing the splendor of a rising streak of lightning, adorned with a golden garment, seated majestically upon a great lion-throne, and formidable with garlands of flames,
she holds a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, a trident, and likewise a ḍamaru drum.
One should meditate upon and worship her as holding a drinking vessel and granting boons; she is the Great Vidyā Jvālāmālinī, the destroyer of enemies—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the ritual for the Nityā Jvālāmālinī. The Lord said:

Alternatively, one should write the mantra adorned with the bindu of grace (kānugraha), which belongs to the Great Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, who is wondrous; by the mere remembrance of whom great calamities flee away. Ṛ.
For this mantra of the mouth of Brahmā, Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas), Citrā the deity, the syllable *ka* the seed (*bīja*),
and *ta-tā-rā* the younger brother [the son] who is the power (*śakti*) that bestows the goals of human existence.
The preceptor should assign the limbs [of the mantra] according to the distinction of the six long vowels;
where there is worship of Mātṛkā and likewise of the Goddess, the wise one,
having worshipped the Mothers and the World-Protectors, should recite the mantra of the Goddess.
One should sacrifice one-tenth of a hundred thousand oblations with ghee, sesame seeds, and barley;
this [mantra] is yellow for paralyzing, resembles the *bandhūka* flower for subjugation,
has a dark-bodied form for killing, and resembles smoke for eradication.
Her limbs are ever radiant with wisdom; she is always clothed in diverse garments and eternally adorned with various ornaments.
She is ever resplendent with manifold saffron paste, enriched by the beauty of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and in some places she wears various types of raiment.
"O Dear One, the Nityās have been described in sequence as bestowers of all prosperity.
[Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nityās," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. The Lord said:
This reality, which consists of all things, is called Tripurā.
This very goddess, endowed with the quality of sattva, is called the waking state (jāgrat).
She, whose nature is power (śakti), creates the three worlds. Arising...
The constant awareness of the waking state, the alertness, and the withdrawal of the mind—
these four constituent parts (kalās) are established in the waking condition;
when united with this very [state], it is declared to be the form of Śiva.
Forgetfulness at the time of death, fainting, sleep, and being enveloped by darkness—these are to be known as the portions within deep sleep; that deep sleep is the very form of Śiva.
From that state arises the Goddess who is dual in nature, whose form is *rajas*, and whose essence is fearlessness.
The conjunction of *sattva* and *tamas* is designated as *rajas*.
At the end of deep sleep and at the beginning of waking, the state of dreaming consists of *rajas*.
Longing, delusion, anxiety, and the mind’s recollection of sense objects [arise from it].

The four *kalās* are established within the state of dream; that Goddess who transcends the *guṇas* is designated as the Fourth (*turyā*). She is characterized by mere radiance, manifesting from deep sleep up to the end of the waking state.
The fourth state (turyā), which has reached the condition of having no remaining states,

is free from existence and non-existence, transcends the qualities (guṇas), and is described as such; it is dispassion, the desire for liberation, and a mind purified by tranquility and other virtues.
These sixteen digits (kalās) of the fourth state (turyā) have the excellent reality as their exit;
through the ripening of that very fourth state, it becomes the seventeenth digit.
Just as the sweet nectar [emerges] from the ripening of fruits such as the *katuraṃbha*, so too does this occur.
O Dear One, when the seventeenth kalā of the Great Goddess (Maheśānī) is being uttered, those mantras are merely the designators of the mantra;
one should contemplate the reality that is devoid of utterance by means of the mind alone.

Through contemplation and through the state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya), one perceives that very Brahman alone as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) in the form of the fourth state (turya), O fair-faced one; and this group of sixteen digits (kalās) is established within the syllables of the Śrī-vidyā.
Great mantras emerge like sparks from a great fire;
in the same way, O Dear One, the letters of the Mātṛkā emerge from the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable].
Therefore, that very seed-syllable of his is called Vāgbhava.
By that very speech, the Goddess Kāmeśī, who is the form of the seed-syllable, then deluded the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile;
she, vibrating as the Mātṛkā of the Bindu, consists of both male and female.
O Lord of Gods, by means of great delusion they pin down the three worlds;
therefore, O Goddess, being proud of their good fortune, they protect the entire world by that very pinning— thus she is called Śakti.
Thus, the Goddess who bestows the great empire of the digits of the three peaks,
who consists of Lakṣmī, the Mistress of the World adorned by the host of Mahākośeśvarīs, is awake in the three worlds.

Then that supreme Goddess Kāmeśvarī, endowed with the treasury of Śiva, fulfills all desires; she, who is established upon the great lion-throne, who pervades the universe and possesses universal form, eternally fulfills all desires.
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Akathādi, she whose form consists of a hundred thousand syllables is the goddess Kalpalatā; she is the flower of speech, the command, and the art of imagination,
the eternal bestower of good fortune, adorned with the luster of jewels.
Shining forth through the creation that favors living beings, she is the Mother of the Universe;
honored by the four Vedas through her four abodes, the Goddess then became the sovereign, the temple of bliss for all worlds. Thus...
O beloved one, Tripurā-Śivā abides having placed all this before her— she who bestows the eternal sovereignty of the world;
O Mistress of Gods, she is the absolute Brahman-form dwelling in the midst of the phenomenal world.

Thus, the Great Goddess herself becomes the seventeenth digit (*kalā*), whose nature consists of sixteen syllables, yet who is essentially the group of sixteen Nityās. This concludes the exposition of the Nityās. Pārvatī said: "Tripurā..."

O Sadāśiva, how can Śivā—the Supreme Sovereign, composed of all mantras, whose nature is consciousness—be described or how can she be worshipped? Īśvara said: Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon a radiant lotus at the crown of the head.
There, one should meditate upon one's own Guru, who has the luster of camphor, appearing in his own form— gracious, radiant, adorned, and graced with tranquility;
having eternally saluted him who holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, one should worship him with this [mantra].
Having drawn the square consisting of eight parts, one should write *ha-sa-ṣa-ma-la-va-a-ti-lā* joined with fire (*ra*) three times;
having adorned it thrice with vowels, it is decorated with the face-covering, the left side, the ear, and the eyes. Vī...
O auspicious lady, in this *jatraya*, one should write the word "Śrīparāntepāvake," which consists of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, as the station for worshipping all;
and in the city at the crown of the head, one should write "Nātha Sarvaguru Svayam."

After "Guru Śrī Gurunātha," one should write "Ha Sa Kṣa Ma La Va Pā," followed by the letter "Re" with a long vowel (Ā), protected by the ear (the letter Śa), and consisting of the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā; having thus formed the *piṇḍa*, one should first write the fourth [vowel] and then write that [same] again.
The third [syllable] should be written as before, and the second also, O Pārvatī;
thereafter, at the end of the venerable Śambhu-guru, one should again write the first [syllable]. At the end of the four initial *kūṭas*, one should write the third of the initial [syllables].

O Goddess, O Beloved, he who remembers this mantra— adorned with forty well-counted syllables and presided over by the Lord of Devas— and contemplates his own Guru from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra* as being subtler than a spider's thread, like the rising sun...

One should long remember the mantra consisting of *klīṃ* for the pacification of inauspiciousness; one should write the name of the beloved at the end of all [the syllables] of the god of love (*Kāmadeva*). This mantra, beginning with "O Heart of the Beloved" (*priyādi-hṛdaya*) and ending with "water" (*toya*), is for the purification of the teeth; it consists of four hundred thousand [recitations] of the seed-syllable (*anu*).

One should wash the face for the sake of attaining success; thereafter, one should perform the rite of bathing and sprinkle the head and the body. Having thoroughly sprinkled [the self] while endowed with the secret mudrās, the practitioner, who destroys sins, [should worship] with the mantras of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
One should sip water with the *Tvirā* [mantra] and perform the threefold libation (*tarpaṇa*) in three ways,
beginning with the gods, sages, and ancestors. Then, the practitioner of mantras, adorned with all ornaments, should wear red garments and apply red unguents to his body.

Remaining in his own home, the wise one should perform the triple consecration with the Vidyā that embodies the essence of reality; having likewise taken the triple water from the Cula-kī river with the Vidyā, he should contemplate it there as flowing.
O Dear One, the sin residing within the nāḍī is located in the left side of the belly;
it is a man with the luster of lampblack, whose head is the murder of a Brahmin,
whose two hips are the theft of gold, and whose heart is the drinking of liquor.

O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate many major sins (mahāpātakas) as the hair on the body, while all the collections of minor sins (upapātakas) and various other groups of sins should be contemplated as being upon all the limbs.
O Goddess, the wise one should mentally visualize [the deity] holding a sword and shield; having meditated upon a diamond-stone (vajraśilā) upon the ground, O beautiful one, he should strike there.
Then, recollecting the threefold solar mantra, he should offer the arghya water.
O Goddess, one should first utter the *Hṛllekhā* heart-mantra, then the head-mantra *Haṃsa*,
and thereafter the great *Vidyā* of four syllables, the presiding deity of all the Saura [mantras].
She wears a crown consisting of a mass of radiant jewels and bears the shimmering crescent moon.

Then, meditating upon Gāyatrī— the auspicious one who possesses the luster of gold heated by the sun, whose form is like the solar disc, and who holds the noose, the goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons— one should thereafter recite her mantra, which consists of three syllables that are the very nature of the seed-syllables.
O Goddess, one should write "vāgbhaveśvari vidmahe" at the end of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable];
having uttered the second *kūṭa*, [one says] "kāminīśvari dhīmahi";
then, having uttered the third *kūṭa*, [one says] "tataḥ śaktipracodayāt. Ya.
One should perform as many recitations as possible, and thereafter recite the Śrīvidyā. Then,
one should go to the sacrificial hall, which is adorned with lac,
beautiful with various paintings, and smeared with cow dung on the floor.

Fragrant with the scent of beautiful flowers above and incensed by the smoke of incense, delightful with rows of garlands of lamps and radiant with scattered blossoms— having arrived there, the wise man, silent, knowing, and ever pure, should perform sacrifice.
The pavilion for the worship of Tripura should be fully adorned with all ornaments.
O lady of beautiful eyes, the worship of the pavilion should be performed with the mantra ending in "Namaḥ" and preceded by "Oṃ," beginning with Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and Dhātṛ.
Having worshipped Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and likewise Śaṅkhanidhi in sequence,
and then Padmanidhi, one should worship Puruṣa at the conclusion;
one should also worship Dvāraśrī, Gaṇeśa, and Sarasvatī.
Having worshipped even the threshold, one should worship within the circle of the doorway;
then, one should first join the *hṛllekhā* mantra and the seed-syllable of Śrī. At the end of the name, the word "Śrī" should be uttered, followed by "I worship the sandals" (*pādukāṃ pūjayāmi ca*).
Having worshipped all the Mothers by means of this sequential method,
one seated upon a red seat should perform the extraction of the *cakra*.
One should draw a wide *śakti* once above another *śakti*.

One should enclose it within a fire-pouch according to the sequence for breaking the joints; having extended the lines toward the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, one should perform the recitation so that,
O Goddess, a ten-cornered figure is produced exactly as prescribed.
The wise one, having drawn the lines of the four central corners by dividing each respective junction, likewise produces a seven-sided figure;
it is like a single equilateral triangle of power that grants bliss to the two eyes.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus outside with a beautiful, auspicious, and straight-lined arrangement;
likewise, one should delineate an excellent sixteen-petaled lotus within.
O Supreme Goddess, one should then draw a circular mandala on the ground,
adorned with four beautiful gates; one should place flowers there upon stones from the Gaṇḍakī river, or on gold, silver, or copper.
A wise person should draw the seat of the goddess on birch bark using a stylus made of gold mixed with lac and vermilion;
on a cloth or a metal plate, one should draw it using vermilion powder mixed with lac and vermilion.
Alternatively, O Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing all aims, one should draw a single line on the ground with saffron or with sindūra powder.
O Maheśānī, this cakra should be adorned with a *bindu* in its center. Then...
O Maheśānī, O beloved Mistress of the Gods, this central wheel consists of a triangle, an eight-spoked wheel, a ten-spoked wheel, another ten-spoked wheel, and a nine-spoked wheel; O Sureśvarī,
everything from the center up to the eight corners of the lotus is the middle [wheel].

O Pārvatī, O beloved, this auspicious diagram, consisting of the nature of the *bhaga*, should be marked with nine *yoni*s; it is composed of forty *bhagas* and three *bhagas* respectively, O dear one, and consists of eight petals, sixteen petals, and a square, in sequence.
Just as the eight—
In the performance of those respective rites, the wise one,
facing east and sitting properly, should bow to his own Guru and then correctly recollect the previously mentioned mantra along with the Guru’s name.
The mantra-practitioner, having terrified the gods, earth-dwellers, and spirits with slaps on the heels and hands and upward whirling movements,
should perform the purification and other rites;
he should then inscribe the end of Tripurā using the first and second syllables.
O Maheśānī, the weapon of Tripurā consists of the first two [vowels], Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā;
her mantra is Tripureśī, and not otherwise.
One should worship [the deities] from the middle finger to the little finger during the ritual for the purification of the hands.

O Supreme Goddess, one should offer that seat to Sundarī; having uttered the seed-syllable of Vāk (Vāgbhava), one should cast it there for Tripureśvarī. Then follows the worship of Hṛllekhā, named Sundarī, and of Tripureśī.
Then one should offer the *krāsana* (the seat of grace) presided over by Puravāsinī.
This triad of seeds beginning with the seed of Śiva has been proclaimed;
this is the Vidyā of Tripura, and the worship of Tripureśī is likewise [threefold].
One should worship this Śrī, beginning with *Purūśīha*, followed by a pair of seed-syllables (*bīja*), and ending with *Śivādyā*,
as the seat for all mantras. Having omitted the final syllable of *Sundarī* and joined it with the syllable consisting of *Vala* (the letter *Va*).

O Maheśvarī, we meditate upon the mantra of Tripureśī, who is born of Śiva and resides upon the Sādhya and Siddha seats of Goddess Mālinī. O Maheśvarī, one should perform self-protection with the mantra of Tripureśī for the sake of attaining prosperity.
The mantra of Dābhairavī, endowed with the *utsarga*, is the knowledge for the invocation of the form;
it is the perfected and supreme Goddess, the bestower of prosperity, O Parameśvarī, [the worship of] Bhairavī. Thus [ends the section from] the Śrī-Dakṣiṇa...
In the *Nāmūrti-saṃhitā*, the twenty-fifth chapter, concerning the procedure for the purification of the hands and so forth, the Lord said: "Śiva, Candra, Manmatha, Ura, Śakti, and Vindumālinī."
Indeed, she consists of the letters *kṣa*, *mā*, *viṃ*, *dvarddha*, *mā*, *trā*, *śva*, *na*, *va*, and *rṇā*;
she is the auspicious Goddess whose nature is emptiness, established in the form of space, and as the abode of all, she sustains the universe within her own conscious self.
This [goddess], melting away from the root up to the abode of Brahmā by means of the Moon,
flooding everything, and generating the Mother of the Universe (Viśvamātṛkā),
is therefore composed of light, arising from Manmatha in the form of the mind.
Causing all to cross over, she is called the Source of the Universe (Viśvayoni); through the function of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), she becomes Mātṛkā within the universe.
Renowned as the Inner Illusion (Antarmāyā), by her this world is sustained.
The Supreme Sustainer of the World, whose form is forgiveness, may she protect [us]. The Supreme Śakti is of the nature of the Bindu;
Maheśvarī is of the nature of Nāda; beyond Nāda is the state that cannot be conceptualized, for it lies outside the scope of thought.
Thus, O Brahman...

The mantra of Tripurā is born from the letters *ha*, *ma*, and *ya*; indeed, great mantras do not exist with any other letters. All mantras are likewise pure, sakala (with parts), and those designated as both.

O Sovereign Goddess of all Āgamas, listen; one should worship the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] within the mature Śuddhavidyā, which is honored by all traditions, which is Kāmā, Kāśī, Śakti, and the Fourth State (Turya-bhūmi). By means of this, all the Vidyās are inscribed.
Kāma followed by Danu is called Madanāgraja;
having omitted the younger brother Śiva, this mantra with Sāgra is "Vidyā" when it resides in the heart.
Or, Kāma together with his elder brother [Śiva], but without Kāmānuja [Dakṣa].

One should meditate on this Vidyā, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation: the first *mada* (ma), the power of the Lord of Love (kāmānīśakti, hrīṃ), the first *kā* (ka) without the younger brother (the anusvāra), and the *vāgbhava* (aiṃ) preceded by *hasa* (ha sa) without the younger brother (the anusvāra). Thus:
*mahaḥ kā ha sa aiṃ*. This is the Vidyā propitiated by Candra.
Accompanied by *hasa* and the others, it is sung as the power (*śakti*) known as *Ahasyitī*; presided over by Kuvera, this Vidyā bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Having abandoned "I" (*ahaṃ*), the great mantra begins with *vāgbhava*, *kāma*, and *hasa*.
Having omitted the fourth and eleventh, one should write this [mantra] in the enclosure of the power (śakti-kuṭa);
having omitted the three following Kāma, as well as Sahasrādya and Aja— this is the Lopāmudrā-pāśa, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
This Vidyā, which grants the accomplishment of all aims when its power is joined with the Kūṭa,
bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation once the Kāmarāja has been propitiated;
of this very Vidyā, the two powers are known as Bindumatī and Dvaya.
Having abandoned laughter and the rest, she is declared to have as her deity one propitiated by Agastya;
she is the abode of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa according to the tradition.
Having abandoned the first pair [of letters], she is the beginning of speech; having abandoned the first [pair], she is the beginning of desire, Śiva, and so forth.
One should cast the garland of drops of power (śakti-bindu) there, having abandoned desire;
this is the Agastya-vidyā of Śakti, the deity propitiated by Nandin.
Having abandoned the three [breaths] of the younger brothers, one should today [perform] the mental churning of speech with the letter *ha*.
One should draw the three peaks of Mount Agastya, worshipped by the Sun, situated between Sahā and Dyamanta; furthermore,
one should draw the third syllable of the Śānti mantra in the middle of that peak.
O Supreme Goddess, this six-peak [mantra] begins with *saha* and is to be worshipped by Viṣṇu;
it is the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] beginning with *agasti*, and this very same [mantra] begins with *sa* and so forth.
It consists of five parts of the Viṣṇu-vidyā, and its presiding deity is the one propitiated by Skanda.
Having written the two-fold ignorance (avidyā) in the manner described,
one should abandon the fourth and fifth [syllables] which reside in the heart of Śiva;
then there is the fourfold Vāgbhava and the fivefold Kāmarāja.
One should write the three syllables of the *Kṛtikūṭa* and the *Kāmarāja*;
in the place of *Māyā*, one should sequentially write a pair of *Harī* syllables.
Worshipped by Durvāsas, this [mantra] bestows the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*).

These twelve mantras are pure and bestow the accomplishment of all goals. There may also be other pure variations; they shall be told out of compassion for you. Indeed, there is no variation of this mantra-lore even in all the Āgamas.
Śiva, Candra, Ka, Śakti, and Tu; Hṛt, Laṃ, Khā, Vāgbhava—this becomes [the first].
Jīva, Īśa, Mādana, Eka, Aravinda, Bindu, Sṛk, Pṛthivī, and Parā—this is Kāma.
The third [syllable] is Tārtīya, and the second is worshipped by Candra. Ku.
One should draw the *Kūṭa* of *Vera-Śakti* and the *Kūṭa* of *Kāma*. Then one should write the *Vāgbhava*, the *Kāmarāja*, and the *Śakti-bīja*.
[These are] Śiva, Kāmeśa, Śakti, and the one worshipped by the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada). Vi.
O Parameśvarī, for one who desires the beginning [of the practice], the god of love (Manmatha) is the final [deity] of Viṣṇu;
he is worshipped by Nandīśa in the power of the pair beginning with the end of desire.
However, O Supreme Goddess, there is no distinction whatsoever in the solar Vidyā of Viṣṇu.
I shall now describe another Vidyā, resplendent with three peaks: the letter *jī* (ja), the subtle *śa*, and the supreme *vā* (va); *ka* is the fifth for Viṣṇu;
and for Śakti, one should know the last of the *kāmas* (ma)—this second Vidyā is worshipped by Viṣṇu.
One should write this triad of kūṭas: *hasa-śakti-kabhūmāya*.
Likewise, when the power of speech (*vācikā śakti*) is to be worshipped, she becomes the other [form] worshipped by Skanda.
She should be known as the mantra of Agastya, the supreme speech ending in the consonant *ha*.
At the end of Mātrayāntā are Bhūjīva and Trikuṭā, worshipped by Śiva;
these varieties, O fair-limbed lady, are pure and bestow supernatural powers (siddhi).
I shall now describe two pure varieties that grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should also write the mantra *jīveśakāmabhūmāyā* with the suffixes *vācika* and *āme*.
This very same [mantra] is the Vidyā worshipped by Śakti; it is the six-syllabled *kūṭa* consisting of the syllables *ka*, *śakti*, *viṃdu*, *mālī*, *īśaktī*.
Or [it may be]: *ka-śakti-vindu-mālī-īśaktī-kūṭa*. Or the six-syllabled [mantra].
O Supreme Goddess, this Unmanī-vidyā, which is endowed with Cika, Meha, Kā, Ākāśa, Kṣmā, Kāsa, Agni, Śakti, Kāsa, Kalā, Ākāśa, Vahni, and Mat, bestows liberation alone.
These, when purified, should always be recited; they grant success, of this there is no doubt.
Now, O Maheśāni, I shall describe the mantras known as Sakala.
In the Vidyā of Kāmarāja, one should utter the middle "life-breath" (jīva) without the vowel *u*.
The mantra *aṃ te jīva śiva syāt* is worshipped by Vidyā and Varuṇa;
having added three *bindus* to this very mantra, one should cast them therein—
this is the Kāma-vidyā, highly honored by Dharmarāja.
The Vidyā beginning with *ka-sa-ka-kṣ-mā-di-hṛllekhā-ha-sa-la-smara-takṣā-māḥ*,
followed by *hṛllekhā-manmatha-ī-śaktā-usakalāgni-mahī-parā* and worshipped with fire (*vahninā*), destroys the great multitude of obstacles.
One should write the pair of Agastis (ga-ka), followed by Vahni (ra) and the final letter (ha);
this Vidyā, worshipped by the King of Serpents, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
[The mantra] consists of Ka-Śakti (a), the pair of Vahnis (ra-ra), Bhū (la), Vahni (ra), and Bhuvaneśvarī (hrīṃ).
Adorned with *hakāra*, fire (*ra*), *halā* (the letter *la*), *māyā* (the letter *ī*), *sara* (the letter *u*), earth (*la*), fire (*ra*), and *maṇḍita* (the letter *ta*), this goddess—

who is to be worshipped as *māyā* (the letter *ī*) and *vāyu* (the letter *ya*)— is the destroyer of the flood of great sins. She is *ka* (the letter *a*), *śakti* (the letter *e*), the lunar power (*i*), fire (*ra*), earth (*la*), *māyā* (the letter *ī*), *ka* (the letter *a*), *hāla* (the letter *ra*), and *rā* (the letter *ā*).

She who is worshipped by Yama, Indra, Agni, Māyā, Soma, and Pūjita; she who is desire, the wish-fulfiller, patience, illusion, auspiciousness, the source of desires, the root of the world, and the peak-syllable of the power of Kāmeśvarī; she who is the sovereign of all worlds.
This Vidyā, presided over by Īśāna, fulfills all desires;
she is the consort of Kāmarāja at the end of the pair, the life-force of the earth, and another form of Madanā; this Vidyā, propitiated by Rati, accomplishes all goals and purposes.
One should write it ending with the presiding Vidyā and ending in reverse order;
this six-syllabled Supreme Goddess is presided over by Nārāyaṇa. Kāma at the beginning, then Vāgbhava, Kāma, Eka, Ha, Kṣmā, and Parā.
This Vidyā, worshipped by Brahmā, is either Śakti or Vāg-Āgastyakūṭa;
it is Agastya, Vāgbhava, and the non-dual Vidyā of Brahmā.
This Great Vidyā, honored by all living beings, fulfills all desires.

O Supreme Goddess, by means of those twelve divisions, the Supreme Sovereign, together with her powers, should be known as pure, impure, and the Great Non-dual (Mahābheda). Having written down the pure Vidyās, one should then write those that are their opposites.
O Dear One, just as many pure and impure divisions as there may be, so many indeed arise in succession; likewise,
O Goddess, all these divisions arise from the division of the pairs of powers (śakti).
O Lord of Asuras,

you must also know through the mouth of the Guru that she who is known as Āturyā, whose nature is Brahman and who is the dense depth of all supreme knowledge, is the Sovereign Goddess; otherwise, one shall incur bondage.
We shall establish the supreme fourfold knowledge of Maheśāna; this has been told as one way,
and now another method is being described,
by the mere remembrance of which the merit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices is attained.
Having first joined the pair of seeds being recited, one should remember that which is called the second *bheda* beginning with *parā*, *svara*, and *indu*.
This indeed is to be served at the beginning of the Vedas; it is called the third *bheda*, which is Brahmā himself.

O Maheśānī, by the single utterance [of this], the wise man [attains his goal]. Now, however, the fourth method is being described, which is difficult to find on earth; by the mere remembrance of which great calamities flee away of their own accord.

He is himself Viṣṇu, he is himself Rudra; of this there is no doubt. How much more so, O Goddess of the gods, is he the all-pervading Kāmeśvara himself? [The merit of] thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices and crores of Vājapeya sacrifices [is attained by him].
O beloved, the merit of thousands of human sacrifices is obtained from a single utterance [of the Name];

likewise, the pilgrimage to holy sites beginning with Kāśī and the circumambulation of the earth are attained merely by pronouncing the Name; and thousands of baths in the Gaṅgā are gained simply by the utterance of the Name.
How much more so, O Goddess, for one who possesses the mantra; there is no doubt regarding the Brahman. A wise person should write the pair of the second [syllable] in reverse order.
Then, having placed the young girl (Bālā) facing inward, he should write that immediately thereafter.
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the third [conjunction] in union;
this Śrīvidyā has been declared by me, and it is impossible to describe even with hundreds of millions of tongues or hundreds of millions of mouths, O Goddess.
O Goddess, how can I describe the story of Pañcāśyenā?
Śrīvidyā, the queen of all vidyās, cannot be fully praised;
she is endowed with sixteen syllables, yet she herself is the fifteenth digit.
By the grace of the glorious Guru, who bestows supernatural powers and perfections, one becomes a knower of the mantra of Brahman, which is eternal and free from disease; it is not otherwise.
[This applies even to those burdened by] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and the theft of gold.

O Supreme Goddess, the remembrance of Śrī destroys in an instant all those things marked as minor offenses (upapātaka); all auspicious mantras become [ineffective] before You. The nineteen-syllable mantra of both Anārāyaṇa and Hari begins with "Śi..."
The *Vividhāmaheśānīsiddhi* consists of seventeen syllables;
all the *Dvaṃdvavidyās* consist of nineteen syllables;
and the *Nārāyaṇī* and *Vaiṣṇavī* consist of twenty-five syllables. [Thus] it is known.
Otherwise, one may incur a curse through the mouth of the Guru;
for the sixty-four crores of Yoginīs along with the circles of Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍala) will surely destroy the practitioner who lacks the instruction of the Guru.
[Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Śrīvidyā Mantra," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. The Lord said:
Having become mentally absorbed in Śrīvidyā, on the left side...
O Maheśvarī, O beloved, one should fill a square mandala with water;

likewise, one should worship one's own tri-yantra with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). Then, having placed a conch filled with water along with its handle there, [one should proceed].

Having properly worshipped whom, one should worship the maṇḍala before him; there, the wise one should worship a square and install the *yaṃtra*. One should worship the maṇḍala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon in due order.
The pure practitioner should worship the goddess Masta in her distributed forms within the triangles;

having repeated the ritual twice, one should worship her with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the hexagons. One should worship the Fire-god with the first seed-syllable (*ādya-bīja*) in the form of the yantra. Hemā...

O beloved, a vessel made of bell-metal or specifically one produced from a coconut shell is a great vessel that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. A vessel produced from a coconut shell bestows all sovereignty and happiness, as well as liberation.
An excellent vessel, specially consecrated with incense and the like, perfumed with incense, and which always brings about all prosperity,
should be established upon a tripod; then one should draw the previously mentioned yantra in that very same manner.
O beautiful one, having uttered the Kāmakūṭa mantra, one should worship;
having offered libations, one should especially worship that vessel made of *maya*. One should pour water equal to one part of the three parts of the special [substance] into it as well.

One should draw the previously mentioned yantra and perform worship; then, one should worship the Vidyā within the triangle, and subsequently, the three *kūṭas* in their proper order according to the Vidyā.

O Goddess, one should worship within the subject matter of the Śrīvidyā by means of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) method; O Beloved, this is the sequence for all [mantras] of the Goddess, and one should not practice with indolence here.
One should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Goddess's root mantra in their proper order.
Having uttered the peak-syllable *Kt*, that water takes the form of the moon;

having worshipped it, one should sequentially perform [the rite] consisting of the *Mātṛkās*. Therein, O beautiful one, one should meditate upon the Great Vidyā of the five sheaths, beginning with *Tārtī*.

O Goddess of the Gods, one should mutter the seed-syllable of the venerable Guru (*yaṃ*), the *Haṃsa-vidyā* mantra, and the *Śrīvidyā* seven times on each day of the week; then, having touched the *arghya* water, one should thereafter worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. [Then] the *cidā*...

One should meditate upon the abode consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) situated at the gateway of the eyes; with that [light], one should then sprinkle all other materials for worship. O Dear One, by that means, even the self becomes entirely of that same form. [The thumb...]
O Sundarī, this *tattvamudrā*, which destroys great sins, is declared [to be formed] by the ring fingers through the left path;
this *jñānamudrā* is said [to be formed] by the thumb and forefinger.
In the worship with *nāyā* flowers, as well as in the worship of libation (*tarpaṇa*),

the practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual of elemental purification (*bhūtaśuddhi*) for the sake of purifying the body; by means of the *vāyu* seed-syllable, the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) joined with sin [are purified].
Having dried it with the fire-seed (RAṂ), one should burn it along with the sin; then,
having made the body immortal once again, one should revive it with the water-seed (VAṂ),
O Goddess of Gods, and stabilize it with the earth-seed (LAṂ).

Then, having performed the ritual purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), one should properly perform the donning of armor for the body; one should then place the deities of the four seats (*caturāsanadevatā*) upon the feet, the calves, the knees, and the *mūlādhāra*.
The knower of mantras should place [the mudrā] on the heart with three fingers, excluding the little finger and the thumb; he should place it on the head with the middle and ring fingers;
he should place it on the crest-lock with the thumb; and he should place it as armor with all ten fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the placement of the eyes within the heart,
one should then place the weapon (*astra*) with the index and middle fingers, O Beloved; the wise practitioner, having recited it twice, should perform the rite that provides self-protection.
One should install the formless [state] as all-pervasive for the sake of attaining siddhi.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the supreme installation of Śrīvidyā:
one should contemplate the radiant, complete Vidyā within the Brahma-randhra.
One should meditate on the sixteen-syllable mantra that drips nectar and bestows great good fortune;
then, one should brandish the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā at the region of the left shoulder and cast it down at the base of the foot to seize the tongues of enemies.
Having thus meditated on oneself as the creator of the three worlds, one should place the *tilaka* mark;
one should place it completely upon the face as a circlet (*veṣṭana*). Again, one should likewise place it completely above the forehead. Saṃpū...

One should install [the mantra] by means of the *ṛṇayāca* and *adeha* [methods], which are non-pervasive; then, having cast the *yoni-mudrā* at the end of the pervasive [mantra] into the mouth and reciting it,
one whose body is prepared for installation agitates the three worlds instantly.
Having formed a fist, the practitioner of mantra should likewise extend the index finger like a staff;
this is called Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī, and it punishes enemies in an instant. By placing the thumb within the fist, it becomes the Seizer of the Enemy’s Tongue (Ripu-jihvā-graha).
Having joined the two hands, one should worship with the index and ring fingers;
likewise, on the left, one should join them in the shape of a womb by rubbing them together.
By joining the thumbs on top, this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*.
O Dear One, by means of this mudrā, one shall bring the three worlds under control; having rotated the ring finger all around the crown of the head, O Goddess,
one should cast it into the Brahma-randhra and then place it at the base of the thumb.

O Dear One, one should apply the *amika* on the forehead and remember the sixteen-syllable mantra; one should meditate upon the three worlds as crimson—this is known as the "Enchantment" (*saṃmohana*) placement (*nyāsa*).
[One should place it] on the two feet, the two calves, the two knees, the two hips, the navel, and the back.
O Pārvatī, [one should worship] on both sides of the navel, as well as on the two breasts, the two shoulders, the two ears, the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head),
and the mouth; thereafter, in the region of the ears, on the two ear-rings in sequence.
This great Hāra-nyāsa is said to consist of sixteen seed-syllables (bījas).
Thereafter, one should perform the Golaka-nyāsa, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
Afterwards, one should install the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, which takes the form of Gaṇeśa and the planets.

[One should meditate upon] the Mother of the Universe, who embodies the lunar mansions, the yoginīs, the zodiac signs, the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and the phonemes; she is marked by the vidyās of all the traditions,
[located] in the regions of the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, throat, heart, and navel.
One should install the Ādhāra-vyūhaka up to the secret Yoginīs; thereafter, one should perform the Sṛṣṭi-nyāsa, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
[One should place them] in the Brahma-randhra, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, and the two lips.

One should sequentially place sixteen syllables at the joints,
the tips of the fingers, the head, the forehead, the heart, the mouth, the tongue, the heart, and the joints;
one should place the sixteen syllables in the mouth and in the locations of the vowels in due order.
One should then place the five seed-syllables on the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the mūlādhāra; then the three seed-syllables on the brahmarandhra, the mouth, and the bladder.
After that, one should place the three seed-syllables on the mūlādhāra, the heart, and the brahmarandhra.
One should place the five seed-syllables on the hands, feet, arrows, and heart;
one should perform the pervasive placement of the *golaka* for the sake of great good fortune.
O Goddess, the wise one should place the complete Śrīvidyā in the heart.
The subtle practitioner should mentally place flowers in the "well of health" (anāmayāvī);
having thus arranged his body, he should sequentially perform the mudrās.
Make three separate sections from the previously mentioned yonimudrā.
With the thumbs, the little fingers, and the middle fingers respectively,
this is the mudrā named Trikhaṇḍā for the rite of invoking Tripurā; thereafter,
one should block [the breath] with the ring fingers and the little fingers along with the middle fingers.
When the two index fingers are joined at the webbed space of the thumbs like a staff, this great mudrā is proclaimed as Kṣobhiṇī (the third);
it is called Drāviṇī when [the same] is done with this very mudrā.

O Supreme Goddess, one should join the two middle fingers together in the form of a hook; this is proclaimed as the third mudrā, the Trailokyākarṣiṇī (the Attractor of the Three Worlds). The two hands should be joined in the shape of a hollowed bowl (*puṭa*).

Having formed the two index fingers in the shape of a hook according to the clearly defined sequence, and having placed the other [two] middle fingers below them in that same order, one should join the two little and ring fingers together and worship all [the deities].

O Supreme Goddess, the fourth mudrā, which brings all under control, consists of the two thumbs placed at the tips [of the fingers] facing each other; having joined the two hands with palms facing one another, the two little fingers are placed inside the middle fingers, and the two index fingers are joined on the outside.
Form the *nāmeśarā* [mudrā] at the region of the nail of the middle finger;
then, like a staff, [place it] upon the thumb. This is proclaimed as the fifth mudrā, named *unmādinī*. Such is this very mudrā.
Forming the gesture of the great goad (*mahāṅkuśā*) with the index, middle, and ring fingers, this is the *mahāṅkuśā* mudrā;
its mantra is proclaimed as the great seed-syllable known as *Aṅkuśa*. Vāmoda...
Having placed the right arm upon the left arm,
O Goddess, one should then sequentially join the hands;
the pair of the little and ring fingers should then rest upon the back of the middle fingers.
O Great Goddess, one should place the index fingers between [the thumb and middle finger] on both sides;
having made the two thumbs straight, one should recite this [mantra] for the earthen element.
This is the Khecarī Mahāmudrā, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
This is proclaimed as the great seed-mantra (*mahābīja*) for victory, which is her *mantra*.
This is proclaimed as the *samayamudrā* of them all.
O Goddess, [the gesture] with clearly visible hands, followed by the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the *akuṭa* [mudrā].

Then, one should simultaneously join the pair of ring fingers and thumbs; next, one should place the two middle fingers in a state of being entwined below, and the two ring fingers should be curved and placed at the very bottom of all.
This seed-mudrā is called Maya; its mantra is "Ha Sau. This ninth [mudrā] is proclaimed as the previously mentioned Yoni-mudrā.
Shining forth within the assembly of Śaktis, it is common to them all.
The Vāgbhava-mantra is the mother of this entire universe.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Mudrās of the Mother," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.

The Lord said: O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, one should install the *cakra* upon a site produced from white sandalwood, red sandalwood, and *śrīparṇī*, and not elsewhere. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*sanyasta*),...
One should meditate upon the body as the sphere of the Brahmāṇḍa, which reveals the nature of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; it is a square,
a bow, a triangle, its cavity, and the face, [all] being formless.
This Meru-maṇḍala is known as Laṃva;
above it is the pervasive Cakra, which unfolds from the sixfold syllables.
Because it indicates the object of speech while remaining dissolved, it is remembered by yogis as Aparā.
*Parā* is the supreme glory; *Sāmbhavī* is in the knowledge of the *Paśyantī*; the *Madhyamā* is among all living beings; and the *Vaikharī* is within the sources of knowledge.
Thus, this thousand-petaled lotus is endowed with the words of speech.
Above that is the supreme wheel, the abode of the supreme nectar; it is auspicious, having four corners,
eight petals, sixty-four petals, a hundred petals, a thousand spokes,
ten thousand spokes, a hundred thousand petals, and ten million petals.
I meditate upon the Lord of the Wheel (Cakranāyaka) in the center of the pericarp-seat within that [lotus], which is richly adorned with radiant splendor in the expanse of the sky;
he is the progenitor of the six great paths, throbbing and facing in all directions. Ṣa...

Now, hear concerning the path of letters (*varṇādhvan*) within the yoga of the present moment: it resides in the forms of the *ḍadha* syllables, in the petals of the wheel of words, in the worlds, and in the junctions of the three;
it is situated in the seat of the *mātṛkā*, where all mantras unfold. Twenty-six...

The wheel, filled with the hundredfold [reality], is fashioned according to its root; it is elevated upon five lion-thrones, the seat of the wheel which is the path of the Kalās. It is filled with nine wheels, and likewise joined with another, the supreme [wheel], making sixteen.
O lotus-eyed one, the Śrīcakra expands pervading the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), which is said to be of the nature of the letters;
thus one should contemplate the Śrīcakra as moving through the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
In the pericarp is the supreme Vāstu, and from that, the imperishable Consciousness;
from that, the Supreme Self, and there, the lunar radiance;
from that, the stainless essential nature, and from that, the manifestation of Sattva and the other qualities.

The seat of the treasury of consciousness (caitanyākośapīṭha) arises from one's own self as the fivefold teaching; the seat of the beloved of manifestation (sphuraṇāvallabhāpīṭha) arises from the *svadhā* [mantra]; the seat of the lunar [nature] (vaiṃdavapīṭha) arises from the *svarūpa*; and the jewel-seat (ratnapīṭha) is proclaimed to be the universe arising from the *tattva*.
O Dear One, in the supreme abode of Śrīvidyā, beginning from the eastern petal of the cakra,
I worship the Pādukā who is seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly of Mahākośeśvarīs,
the mother of all auspiciousness.
Having uttered this, the wise one should worship the Pādukā of the Supreme Light.
In this very manner, one should worship the Pañcapañcikā;
this reality, which consists of all things, is merged within the Supreme Reality.
This reality, which is the soul of all, is the beautiful lady of all auspiciousness;
through the union of the three *bindus*, she exists as the threefold Tripurā.
One should conceive of the *bindu* as her face, and below that, the two breasts.
One should contemplate her, together with the half of the supreme limit (parārdha), as facing downwards.

Thus she is the form of Kāmakalā, manifesting directly as the imperishable (akṣara); she is the Mother of the Universe (Viśvamātṛkā) alone, consisting of the three points (bindu) and the half-measure (ardhamātrā).
Therefore, O Goddess, she is called the power Tripurā;
for other [goddesses], the eternal triad of bindus belonging to Tripura does not exist at all.
By her will, creation comes into being, and therein it goes to its dissolution.
She, the Great Goddess Maheśānī, should contemplate herself thus:
"Seated upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas) known as O, Jā, Pū, and Kāmarūpa, [I am] upon a lotus whose crown is adorned with a serpent possessing as many hoods as the number of lunar days."
There, on the seat of the eight lunar mansions (Aṣṭāvakra), she resides within the lotus of the respective eternal Kalās;
seated upon the seat of Kāmeśvarī, she is her consort,
the sovereign of the three worlds through her command, ruling over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
She is beautiful with her limbs composed of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*,
having the nature of a lotus fiber extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*,
possessing a luster like the rising sun, and resembling the *japā* flower.
Her body shone like freshly smelted gold, radiant as a pomegranate flower;
it was adorned with a braided tress (*dharmilla*) filled with intensely fragrant blossoms,
and her hair, dark as a swarm of bees, gleamed with fine locks.
Resplendent with a forehead-mark of shimmering pearls and rubies, beautiful with a necklace of flashing gems, radiant with a crown and tiny bells,
her moon-like face glowing with red lac and adorned with a mark of vermillion.
And the king [beheld] the daughter of Śambhu, who was adorned with a tilaka-mark shimmering like a digit of the moon;
who was beautiful with the playful movement of her eyebrows and the flickering glances of her eyes kissing her ears;
and who was resplendent with golden earrings shining like strings of diamonds and pearls.
With the luster of her ear-ornaments, she made the surface of her cheeks appear like clusters of blossoms;
with her nose-pearl, radiant as Indra and shining from her moon-like face,
she surpassed the splendor of the essence of the knowledge of Brahman through the sweetness of her smile.
I bow to the auspicious Goddess, whose lotus-hands are as delicate as the petals of a red lotus,
who spreads a canopy of moonlight from the nails of her lotus-hands across the expanse of the sky,
and who is languid with the weight of her well-rounded, firm, and lofty breasts.
To those whose chests were elevated by the weight of great necklaces of fresh pearls,
[she appeared] with a slender waist, a deep navel, and a beautiful, thin middle;
she was adorned with a girdle fashioned from priceless gems and tiny jeweled bells.
Her hips were beautiful like the orb of the sun, adorned with a line of hair;
she pervaded the entire circle of the three worlds with the radiant luster of her shimmering red garments;
and she was resplendent, shining with a divine bodice variegated with brilliant jewels.
She who shines with slender waists and thighs that are tremulous and graceful,
whose divine form is encircled by anklets vibrating with the luster of the nine gems, and whose lotus feet are touched by the crowns shimmering upon the heads of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor;
she wore a silken garment as red as a noose fashioned from young sprouts;
and she held a goad marked by the crescent of a second moon, capable of drawing [the world] toward her.
She who bears the bow of the qualities that have become bees for the lotuses of the sixfold sciences,
who carries the five arrows shining like a mine of lotuses,
and whose body is as magnificent and deep red as saffron, resembling a great deer.
[He saw] the Goddess, rich in the splendor of all ornaments, adorned with every decoration;
the supreme Goddess who consists of all the gods, who consists of all mantras,
who consists of all sacred fords, and who is the supreme embodiment of all scriptures.
He who thus meditates upon the Great Goddess— who consists of all sacred fords, whose nature is the support of all, the progenitor of all prosperity, the beautiful one who bestows all auspiciousness—
residing in the midst of the Kadamba forest.

Then, having emerged through the opening of the channel-petals while carrying [the breath], she should contemplate: "Where shall I place the beautiful lady of the Kula upon the lap of my Lord Śiva? O Dear One, [she should do so] with the Vidyā that takes the form of invocation and with that mudrā.
The wise one should display the mudrās and perform the threefold libation (tarpaṇa),
having propitiated [the deity] with all the auspicious and manifest services ending with incense, lamps, and food offerings; then he should again display the mudrās.

Having again satisfied [the deities], one should worship the Goddess of the Gods and the Tithinityā; at this time, O Goddess, one should worship her who consists of that particular lunar day (tithi). He who worships them one by one, beginning from the first day (pratipad) up to the full moon (paurṇamāsī), [attains success].
The practitioner of mantra shall obtain good fortune and attain great sovereignty.
One should worship in sequence from the first day until the end of the fortnight, increasing and decreasing by one [day] at a time.
Having visualized the Great Mantra consisting of fifteen vowels, [one should proceed].
One should abandon everything at the end in the middle [of the mandala] through the division of five by five;
in the center, O Goddess, one should worship the Great Nityā who consists of me (Mayī). One should worship the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā in their proper sequence.
In the midst of the victorious, stainless city, one should worship the mandala of the Guru.
The Gurus beginning with Parā, the Siddhas, O Goddess, and those who are both supreme and inferior— the Aparās and Mānavas—
are to be known by the number of the Vedas multiplied by eight (thirty-two).
O Parameśvarī, those ending with the word Ānandanātha are proclaimed as males; those ending with Āvā are to be known as females. O Sundarī, listen as the gurus of Kāmarāja are described.
Beyond that is the Guru Paraśiva, known as Aprakāśa;
Parāśakti, Kaulīśa, the goddess Śuklā, and likewise Aṃbikā; Kuleśvara, and likewise the goddess Kāmeśvarī, and the Guru Aṃbikā.
Then Abhoga, likewise Klinna, Samaya, Sahaja,
Gaganaviśvavimala, Madana, Bhuvana, and Guru—
these are proclaimed as the Goddesses of the Self's Play (Līlā) in their respective order.
The lineage of Lopāmudrā and Agastya shall be equal to the supreme [lineage].
Then follows Paramādyaśiva, followed by Kāmeśvarī and Ambikā; and then, in due order, all the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha).
Listen as I describe the group of four known as the radiance of the Goddess Prajñā:
Dīvya, Citra, Kaivalyadevya, and Mahodaya;
Cidviśvaśakti, Caraka, Kamala, and Manohara; and Parasvā.

The pair of Ātman and Guru are to be praised by the wise; they are the common gurus of all sciences in their respective order. Furthermore, there is the Supreme Light (Paramakāśa), as well as Parādi and Vimṛśa. Tṛ... [text fragment]
Third is Parameśānī; then Kāmeśvarī and the others, ending with Mokṣa, Amṛta-saṃjña, Puruṣa, and Ghora; or else, Sadguru, Siddha, and Īśa, in successive order.

Udbhava, Para, Sarvajña, Svastha, Siddha, Govinda, Śaṅkara, and Mānava— the teacher of the human race— these constitute the triad of one's own gurus at the beginning, the middle, and the end of the lineage.
Indeed, when there are twelve gurus, one should then contract the pair at the end of the nine, eight, and [remaining] syllables; three gurus should be joined there, otherwise the lineage is lost. Jā.
O King, such a person is not worthy of the row [of disciples] even if he has received the mantra;
otherwise, one must never cause a contraction of the lineage (*guru-saṃkoca*).
Those who are devoid of the traditional succession (*paramparā*) and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge [are excluded].
O Goddess, what do the rays (marīcayaḥ) do for those who violate their commitment?
O Supreme Goddess, he who performs the sequence without a Guru suffers a great loss; of this there is no doubt. O Āli...

The gurus are to be worshipped with the triad for the sake of attaining success; O Goddess, one should worship the guru with the Guru-mantra. Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for meditation in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
The Twenty-Eighth Chapter. Īśvara said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme sequence of the Śrīvidyā, beginning with the worship of the limbs in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
The best of mantra-knowers should worship according to the sequence of their respective mudrās.

O Dear One, the creation-chakra (sṛṣṭicakra) consists here of the earth-circle, the sixteen-spoked [circle], and the eight-petaled [lotus] in succession; the method of worship therein is now described.
One should worship the ten-cornered [lotus] and the second ten-cornered [lotus], as well as the wheel of maintenance (sthiticakra) and its worship, according to their distinctions; likewise,
the eight-cornered and the three-cornered [lotuses] constitute the fire-wheel (vaidava) and the wheel of withdrawal (saṃhṛti).

The third [group] consists of all the *pūjyās*, which is called "the complete" (*sakala*); the fourth is the *vidyās*, which are indeed all-inclusive (*sakalāḥ*). A wise person should worship them in sequence.
In this very manner, one should worship the multitude of *vidyās*.

The wise person should worship everything— the Śrī-kośa, the one situated upon the lion-throne, that which consists of the Kalpalatā, that which consists of jewels, O Goddess, and that which consists of the four abodes— as well as the fourfold lineage, all of which is profound. Trailo...
O beautiful one, the fifty letters in the form of the wheel that deludes the world should be joined there with the Siddhis;
O beloved, they have the luster of molten gold and hold nooses and goads.
One should worship those with lotuses in their hands, who bestow great treasures, jewels, fine gold, and hidden hoards upon practitioners;
they are the embodiments of the supernatural powers (siddhis) of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), and mastery (īśitva).
The eighth [siddhi] is the enjoyment of the power of mastery (*vaśitva*) and the fulfillment of desires at will;
one should worship the manifest attainments (*prāptisiddhi*) and the success of all desires in the southern parts of the doors as well as in the corners, in due order.
They should be worshipped by the teachers starting from the western direction in an upward sequence:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Indrāṇī as the third;
Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī, and Vārāhikā shall be the sixth.
One should meditate on Cāmuṇḍā and Lakṣmī on the other side; she holds a noose and a goad, bearing all [the weapons] in due order:
the Vidyā, the trident, the thunderbolt, the spear, the discus, and likewise the mace.

O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of attaining siddhi, one should sequentially meditate upon the lotus of the *dhairyāntaramālikā*, endowed with all ornaments: first *Sarvadyākṣobhiṇī*, then *Drāviṇī*, and likewise *Ākarṣiṇī*. *Dhai*... [text truncated]

O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of attaining siddhi, one should sequentially visualize the lotus of the breath-mechanism (prāṇayantra) as endowed with all ornaments; likewise, one should meditate upon Akṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, and Ākarṣiṇī, who are at the forefront of all [the powers].
The mudrās known as Vaśyā, Unmādā, Aṅkuśā, and likewise Khecarī,
Vījayoni, and Trikhaṇḍā, [are positioned] from the eastern and western parts;
they resemble rubies and are adorned with vermilion tilakas.
Clad in red garments and adorned with red garlands,
all [the goddesses] are marked with their respective mudrās; holding nooses and goads in their hands,
they should be worshipped with diligent application of mudrās for the sake of attaining one's desired perfection.
In the western direction and so forth, in the manifest four-cornered wheel that fulfills all desires and is expanded by the vowels of the *kalās*,
one should worship the secret [deities] in sequence, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order.
The eternal Kāmākarṣiṇī, likewise Budhyākarṣiṇī,
Ahaṃkārākarṣiṇī, Śabdākarṣiṇī, and similarly Sparśākarṣiṇī and Rūpākarṣiṇī.
O Goddess, [I shall describe] the attractor of tastes and likewise the attractor of scents; similarly, O Beloved, the attractor of the mind and the attractor of fortitude;
as well as the attractor of names and the attractor of seed-syllables.
O beloved goddess, these are the eternal Kalās: Amṛtākarṣaṇī, Smṛtyākarṣaṇikā, Śarīrākarṣaṇī, and Ātmākarṣaṇikā; they reside eternally in the center of the lunar maṇḍala.
One should constantly remember those [energies] joined with their respective vowels, showering nectar as they flow,
bestowing the gift of saffron jars filled with the nectar of the noose, goad, and ambrosia,
and possessing the consonant groups beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'la' within the wheel that agitates all.

One should remember [the goddesses] who are more secret than the Goddess herself, worthy of worship, fond of *vadhūka* flowers, holding nooses, goads, and shimmering, playful blue lotuses in their hands,
in the four directions starting from the east and in the corners starting from the southeast in due order.
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgādimadanā, Anaṅgamadanāturā, Anaṅgarekhā, Anaṅgavegā, and Anaṅgapūrvikā. Aṅku...
In the wheel of the Great Bestower of Good Fortune (Mahāsaubhāgyadā), which shines with the letter Ka, resides Śācatathānaṅgamālinī Parameśvarī;
there dwell all the Yoginīs known as the Saṃpradāya, adorned with every ornament.
All of them, resembling cochineal insects, possessing proud and intoxicated youthfulness,
and being most beautiful, hold a noose, a goad, a mirror, and a vessel of nectar; they are positioned starting from the west in reverse order.
O Goddess, one should worship the Śaktis according to the tradition for the sake of accomplishment:
the Śakti Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī,
the Śakti Sarvākarṣaṇikā, and Sarvāhlādakarī, O beloved.
The power that deludes all, the power that causes the paralysis of all,
the power named "the paralyzer of all," the power that brings all under control,
the power that delights in all objects, and the power that causes the intoxication of all.
The power that accomplishes all aims, whose form is every prosperity,
the power consisting of all mantras, which brings about the destruction of all dualities— [she resides] within the wheel that accomplishes all aims, beautified by the letters of the alphabet.
Resembling a cluster of blossoms, adorned with shimmering jewels,
possessing profound and great beauty, with full, rounded, and firm breasts,
she placed upon a jeweled pedestal the ornaments desired by the practitioner.
One should visualize the Kula-yoginīs with smiling faces, bestowing divine objects made of various jewels and holding nooses and goads;
one should worship those who grant all accomplishments in reverse order, beginning from the west.
The goddess who bestows all accomplishments, the giver of all prosperity, she who makes everything dear, the performer of all auspiciousness,
the goddess who grants all desires, and the liberator from all suffering.
The goddess who pacifies all death, who wards off all obstacles, who is beautiful in every limb, who bestows all prosperity,
and who is the maker of all protection within the wheel adorned with the letters of the rosary.
One should recite the *nigarbha-yoginīs* in reverse order, beginning from the west;
they possess a radiance like a thousand rising suns, are adorned with ornaments of pearls,
and their hands shine with the noose (*pāśa*), the ṭaṅka weapon, and the pearl garland of gnosis (*jñāna*).
A wise man should worship these [goddesses], who bestow fruits according to one's desires; they are the goddesses who are all-knowing, all-powerful, and bestowers of the fruit of all sovereignty,
consisting of all knowledge, and destroyers of all diseases.

O Supreme Goddess of the tenth day, you are the nature of all supports, the remover of all sins, the goddess consisting of all bliss, the embodiment of all protection, and the bestower of all desired fruits. O Sovereign of all!
In the deep *cakra* expanded by the eight groups of consonants,
one should worship the secret Yoginīs in reverse order, starting from the west; they possess the luster of pomegranate flowers and reside beneath the perimeter of the Śrīpīṭha.

Clad in red garments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents, one should worship them properly with red flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*); they grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Deeply adorned with various ornaments, they wield the five arrows and the bow.

One should write the eight groups of letters arranged in their respective classes, bestowing boons upon the obstacles; these great syllables of the eight groups should be marked with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
At the end of the *a*-group, one should write the letter *ra*, followed by *va*, *kṣa*, *ma*, the left ear (*u*), and the *bindu*.
O beautiful one, one should write the Goddess Vāgdevatā, who is to be worshipped and named Aśinī; at the end of the *ca*-group, one should write the supreme Kāmeśvarī joined with the *kula*.
Then, [one writes] the letter at the end of the *ca*-group, enriched by the earth (*la*), the left eye (*i*), and equal to the moon (*a*).
Then, after the worship of Nenamohinī at the end of the ṭa-group,
one should worship Vimalā— who consists of the letters of the ta-group,
followed by fire, time, the fire of destruction, the left eye, and the digit of the moon— at the end of the ta-group.
O Goddess, one should worship Aruṇā at the end of liberation (pavarga); it is described hereafter. [The mantra is:
Vyoman (Ā), Jīva (U), Mahī (Ū), Nīra (E), Vāyu (Ai), adorned with Argheśa (M).
By this, the practitioner of recitation (japinī) is to be worshipped; it is described hereafter at the end of liberation. Pha.

One should worship Sarveśvarī with the mantra ending in the letter *ra*, the vowel *u*, the wind (*ya*), and the ear (*śa*). The wise one should worship the eighth goddess, Kaulinī, with this mantra: the end of the group of vowels (*au*), followed by *kṣa*, fire (*ra*), and the *bindu*. Thus, the wise one should worship the goddess Kaulinī.

O Great Goddess, at the conclusion of the eight-fold rite (*aṣṭakānta*), one should worship these two deities of speech within the wheel that bestows all accomplishments, using the great syllables of the *Tvak* mantra.
This [wheel] is enriched with the beauty of three lines and expanded by all the phonemes (*arṇa*).
One should worship the Yoginīs of the *Rāpararahasya* in sequence, according to the Western tradition, through the division of pairs and pairs;
O Dear One, Kāmeśa and Kāmeśvarī, as well as the arrows, are common to all.
O Dear One, one should worship the pair of bows of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī in sequence: the fourth [vowel] and the second [vowel], marked respectively by the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
then the *anaṃta* (the letter *m*) enriched with the *bindu*, and the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśa*) which is *hṛllekhā*.
O Supreme Goddess, the wise one should worship Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī in sequence; likewise, the Aṅkuśa (the goad) should be worshipped equally for both.
In the four directions, [one should worship those] who are richly adorned and possess bodies elevated by youth.
Having the form of red streaks of lightning, adorned with loose flowers, richly embellished with various jewels, and holding their respective weapons in their hands in due order;
auspicious, they are endowed with the mantras of the *jaṃbha*, *moha*, *vaśa*, and *stambha* [powers]. Aṃ...
Outside the gateway, one should worship the eight weapons;
in the three corners, one should fully worship the three goddesses endowed with the three *kūṭas*:
Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśī, and the third, Bhagamālinī.
Kāmeśvarī is white in color, anointed with white unguents,
adorned with ornaments of shimmering pearls and various jewels;
she holds, in sequence, a book, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Placed before her is the worshipful Rudra-śakti,
proclaimed as Vajreśvarī; she is smeared with saffron, adorned with glittering jewels,
wears garments the color of the rising sun, and has dark, curly eyes.
O Maheśvarī, Vajreśvarī is adorned with a sugar-cane bow, flowers, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she holds Viṣṇu on her right side and is the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu.
To the north is Bhagamālā, who possesses the luster of freshly smelted gold.

The Sovereign of the World, adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless jewels, the Great Goddess who is the Power of Brahmā, holds in her lotus-like hands the noose, the goad, the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), and the excellent arrow; she is the destroyer of the threefold afflictions.

Mahātripurasundarī, who consists of all bliss, whose form is Nāda, who transcends the sphere of sound, and who is preceded by the delight of the Yoginīs known as the Supreme and the Non-supreme Secrets— she who resides in Trikūṭa is to be worshipped.
One should worship the Goddess, who consists of consciousness and is the embodiment of Brahman, with the Śrīvidyā;
one should again offer libations and worship Her with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.
O Dear One, one should worship the Goddess with many mental and manifest offerings, as well as with mudrās.
The practitioner should visualize her, possessing the luster of the *bandhūka* flower,
beautiful with various ornaments, and the subduer of the three worlds;
he should remember all her hands bearing their respective mudrās, facing toward Śrīvidyā.

One should worship the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī) in sequence with the *praticakra* mudrās; then, O Dear One, in the center of the wheel, one should perform the primary worship of Tripurā, who has the luster of crystal and is adorned with pearls and jewels.

One should meditate upon the eternal Tripureśī, who destroys great sins, who possesses the form of Sundarī, whose complexion is like saffron, and who holds a book, a rosary, a water-pot, and an excellent lotus.
Adorned with all ornaments, holding a book and a rosary,
and displaying the Varada and Abhaya mudrās, her face radiant with majesty—
a goddess like unto her, the dweller of Tripura, should be meditated upon.
O Maheśānī, Tripurāśrī has eyes with reddened corners, reeling from great intoxication; she possesses full, round, and firm breasts,
shines with the luster of a thousand rising suns, and is adorned with divine ornaments.
Holding a book, a rosary, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she who bestows all bliss is further called Amalinī.
The goddess, possessing the luster of an indragopa insect, holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who removes fear, bestows perfect joy upon practitioners, is perfected, destroys poison,
grants prosperity, and is Bhairavī, the bestower of great accomplishments.
Having understood that this wheel consists of the presiding deities of each individual wheel together with their respective accomplishments (siddhis) in due order, one should worship the wheel;
thereafter, there should be a salutation [with the thought], "I worship the Pādukā."

In the *svāhā*-oblation and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should remember [the mantra] as "I offer libation" (*tarpayāmi*). Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate all the rays within the *Śrīcakra* in the form of the goddesses, each resembling her own respective mantra.
"It must be kept secret by you, O auspicious Pārvatī, like your own private parts.
[Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Worship of Śrīvidyā," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.]
The illustrious Lord said: Having offered as an oblation (naivedya) that which is endowed with the six flavors, purified by cow products, and accompanied by camphor,
one should offer betel-leaf to the Supreme Power (Paraśakti) and perform the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma).

O Beloved, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform recitation (*japa*) and praise (*stuti*) to the Goddess of Good Fortune (*saubhāgyadevatā*) as much as one is able, O Supreme Goddess, using even the first two verses; likewise [with] gold...
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus on a vessel made of silver, bronze, or other materials;
in its center, one should place *gandha*, sacrificial rice (*caru*), or a mudrā.
Furthermore, upon the eight petals, one should place lamps filled with clarified butter (*ājya*).
One should rotate [the wheel] three times with the *ratnavidyā* mantras while meditating on it at the crown of the head;

or, for the pacification of all obstacles, one should remember it at the end with the root mantra. O Goddess, who consists of the nine [wheels] and is joined by all the wheels and their presiding deities! ĀḤ.
O Goddess, accept this *rārtika* for my success;
the practitioner, kneeling on the ground with his left knee, should fashion the mandala to the left,
characterized by an entrance, using both hands with the breath flowing through the nostrils.
One should worship the four-cornered celestial wheel (vyomacakra) with this mantra:
the Tāra (Oṃ), Bhuvaneśānī (Hrīṃ), the pervasive [syllable] (Āṃ), the maṇḍala [syllable] (Hūṃ), the letter Ṅa, and the heart-mantra (Namaḥ); this mantra consists of twelve syllables.
Having placed there a vessel mixed with wine, shared [with others], and honored with flowers, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) right there with the *kalārṇa* mantra.
One should write: "Tāraṃ parā sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvaṃ ca bhūli."
To them, one should offer the *bali* by reciting "huṃ" followed by the fire-born consort (svāhā) three times;
one should perform the previously mentioned *bali* offering for the pacification of obstacles.
This fourfold *bali* offering is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Then, having satiated the Kumārī, the knower of mantras honored the rays of light of Tripura with offerings of food and drink;
he [honored] the supreme consciousness, the Mistress of the wheel of powers of the Khecarī, belonging to the Supreme Goddess.
Out of compassion for the Guru, one should unite [the offerings] within the profound knowledge of the Self;
then, for the sake of accomplishment, one should cast the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) into the northeast corner for the followers of Śiva and Śeṣa.
O Goddess, the knower of the Guru-mantras should then offer the vessel of honor (*arghapātra*) to the Guru by his name.

And with the mantra, according to the instruction, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) to oneself; O Lord of Gods, being pure and wearing the mudrās, one should again perform the act of supporting (ādhāraṇa),
which has the characteristics of a lamp.
One should consume that which stands in the middle of the *rātrika* with the root mantra itself; O Pārvatī, you should lift up the vessel with Kāpālinī,
and the second [vessel] with Dakṣa through union.
Through union with these three, one should satisfy the Dwellers within oneself;
the first is to be known as the form of Brahmā, the second by the knowers of all mantras as the form of Viṣṇu, and the third by the best of mantra-knowers as the form of Īśa (Śiva).
O Supreme Goddess, having slightly raised [the vessel] with the five mudrās,
