having drawn forth the mantras residing therein, and having sprinkled it with the remaining water, O Supreme Sovereign, one should strike the directions and become happy; thus [the rite] is completed.

O beloved, that which is indescribable and unknowable, declared by me as the single Imperishable (akṣara) through the method of the "net-syllable" (jālākṣara), like the lamp of the moon— this must not be hidden from you, O auspicious one, for it is like the embryo of a mother's paramour.
[Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Sacrifice of the Bali Offering," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā.
Pārvatī said: "The Lord has been properly indicated by the mention of the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites."
Indeed, it has been spread out for the sake of the welfare of practitioners through ritual action and procedure.
Then the Lord, the illustrious Īśvara, said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of the Śrīvidyā mantra; [using] śamī wood and dūrvā sprouts..."

With the leaves of the *aśvattha* and those originating from the *arka*, one who is composed should worship the Goddess’s Śrīcakra for the duration of one month; such a teacher destroys the sins accumulated over a thousand births within that month. One should worship [the deity] set with jewels.
O beloved, one who always wears that [image] made of gold campaka flowers will certainly become a bearer of the supreme command at all times; he shall destroy all sins,
even those accumulated over ten million lifetimes, throughout the earth encircled by the oceans.
He who worships the Lord with silver *caṃpaka* flowers attains happiness and prospers eternally; he shall become wise and victorious everywhere. [One should worship] the Liṅga facing westward...
O Maheśvarī, having stayed in a place that is empty of sound, or in a self-arisen cave, or at a mountain peak, one should recite the mantra using a rosary made of coral,
pearls, rudrākṣa, or lotus seeds.
Alternatively, a wise person should perform the recitation using a rosary made of crystal, ruby, emerald, or other beautiful gems. When only one hundred thousand recitations have been completed,
those who cause obstacles for those moving upon the earth will [be overcome], and when even their [obstacles] are removed...

Then, being pure, the wise one should regularly perform those three visualizations even with the slightest degree of agitation; or else, the wise one should recite them mentally, or through speech, or in a whisper. Mental utterance is [the best].

The fruit of ten million recitations is bestowed by even whispered recitation; O beloved, by the command of the venerable Guru, a verbal mantra becomes a hundredfold more effective than that; and at one-tenth of that [number], it is [the fruit of] mental recitation.

One should not offer oblations with flowers born of the *brahmavṛkṣa*; rather, one should perform the homa with safflower blossoms saturated with the three sweets. This vidyā becomes perfected; it is the destroyer of ignorance and the source of the virtuous.
O beloved, [the fire-pit] may be in the shape of a *kuṇḍa*, a lotus (*bhaga*), circular, or semi-circular; or, O beloved, it may be a nine-triangle wheel, or square.
For the lord of speech (*vākpati*), the triangular pit brings about attraction, as does the lotus-shaped one. Circular...

O Goddess, in the *laṃ* [figure] there is the bestowal of prosperity; in the *rāśi* (zodiac sign) [figure], fear arises. In the great nine-triangle (*navatrikoṇa*) [figure], one becomes a possessor of the *khecarī-siddhi*. In the square (*caturasra*), all that is auspicious always arises; it is pacifying (*śāntika*).
One shall accomplish nourishment, fortune, health, happiness, and so forth;
indeed, one shall achieve the ten siddhis at the lotus-marked [center], of this there is no doubt.
And with jasmine and *mālatī* flowers smeared with the three sweets, one becomes the Lord of Speech.

O Goddess, by offering *karavīra* and *japā* flowers with ghee, one gains mastery over the women of the three worlds; furthermore, having mixed camphor, saffron, *nada*, and musk, one becomes possessed of desire and good fortune. [Likewise] with *caṃpaka* flowers...
By constantly offering oblations for seven days with lovely, copper-colored *pāṭala* fruits, the practitioner attains prosperity. O Goddess,
one should offer oblations of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and bdellium.
Indeed, by offering the beautiful women of the entire city smeared with honey and ghee, they certainly become submissive;
and by offering curd, milk, honey, clarified butter, and parched grain at a crossroads, one attains the power of moving through the air (khecaratva) and becomes free from death at any time.
Alternatively, one should recite the vidyā with a focused mind for one hundred thousand times;
then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part of that number according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure,
thereby accomplishing [the subjugation] of all those dwelling in the world of men, the heavens, and the nether regions (pātāla).
By means of black mustard seeds and salt, one may agitate this world;
by offering eight hundred oblations of curd, one shall destroy untimely death;
and by taking two parts each of ghee and milk, there shall be ten thousand and eight hundred [results].
O King of Kings, one should bring [the deity] under control by offering guggulu resin with clarified butter;
health is attained by performing one hundred and eight oblations with ghee and dūrvā grass. [One may also achieve this] with red karavīra flowers smeared with honey and ghee, together with guggulu.
One should bring twenty lords of the earth under one's control;
with *karavīra* flowers smeared with honey, one shall bring [the object] under control along with their retinue.
For seven nights, one should sacrifice with clarified butter and *śaśinā* (camphor) as before. Pā.
Through worship with *ṭala*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *śatapatra*, *jāti*, *mālatī*,
fresh *mallī*, *mallikā*, *padma*, and *kiṃśuka*—
whether mixed together or used individually— one becomes wealthy.
One attains all good fortune and is called a master of speech through wisdom;
indeed, by means of *mucukunda* flowers, bilva leaves, fruits, *amita-nīraja*, *jagara*, and *rājapa* flowers, the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are surely attained.
With dates, *kharjūra* fruits, grapes, and the excellent fruits of the mango tree,
the practitioner shall accomplish whatever task is intended in the mind through *homa*. One should satisfy Śrīvidyā by means of worship and *homa*.
Having scattered the *caru* offering everywhere through the worship of virgins (*kumārī*) and other rites,

and having satisfied the Guru with the previously mentioned offerings of oblations (*bali*), one should worship the circle (*cakra*) and the married women (*suvāsinī*); then that virtuous person should bestow abundant wealth upon them.
One should offer *magra* flowers and *homekusuma* flowers in many oblations;
with all the kernels from within a coconut, O beloved of Manas,
one should likewise offer the *varada* fruit along with the *magra*.
One should offer oblations with pomegranate fruits from which the seeds have been removed;
likewise, one should offer grapes, ensuring they are entirely seedless. One should offer plantain fruit that is pleasing to the mind, provided it has not been cut into small pieces.

One should offer a complete *laṃ* syllable that is light; O Goddess, one should offer musk and saffron the size of a *guñjā* seed, and one should offer a hundred handfuls of sesame seeds. Likewise, a wise person should offer parched grain (*lājā*) in the measure of a single handful.
The grain should be the size of a single mouthful, and likewise the cooked food;
the camphor should be half the size of a betel nut, and the sandalwood should be shaped like a betel nut;
likewise, one should offer agallochum and clarified butter with things that cause satisfaction of the mind.
One should always offer curd and milk according to the fourfold division of qualities; O wise one, this is dear to the mind of the Mother of all oblations.
Now I shall describe the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which destroys great obstacles.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is twenty-four finger-breadths wide, beautiful in every respect,
square, and pleasing to all eyes; then, it should be encircled by a girdle (mekhalā).

O Supreme Goddess, leaving one finger-breadth on all sides, three very beautiful lines should be drawn; they should extend upward by a number of finger-breadths equal to the sun (twelve), the Vasus (eight), and the Vedas (four), and all three should have a width of four finger-breadths. O Kumbha... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
To the west of the *ḍa* [letter], one should fashion a vulva (*yoni*) possessing the proper characteristics:
eight fingers in length, eight fingers in width, with a middle [portion] of six fingers, O Goddess, and two fingers in height; it should be beautiful to behold.
O beautiful one, the measurement for a square *kuṇḍa* has been described to you;
whatever applies to this one applies likewise to the others.
A wise man should construct all the *kuṇḍas* according to that measurement.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow-dung and water, one should draw three lines each from east to west and from south to north;
having sprinkled them with the *praṇava*, one should arrange the sacrificial seat (*viṣṭara*) in the center.
One should draw a triangle there with its apex pointing downward and write [the seed-syllable] within that enclosure;
outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus and then a circle of the earth.
One should worship that seat (pīṭha) by distinguishing it layer upon layer, beginning with Maṇḍūkā.

Then [he worships] Kama, Rudra, and Kalagni at the beginning and end; then the Adhara-shakti, Kurma, Ananta, Varaha, and Prithivi; and likewise the kanda, the stalk, the lotus, the pericarp, and the petals.
One should worship these very [deities] without flowers in those respective places:
Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya at the cardinal directions of the pedestal (pīṭha), and their opposites in the corners; one should worship them upon the pedestal.
Then, having worshipped again with the *tāra* (the syllable Om), one should worship the sacrificial seat (*yāgaviṣṭaraka*). In the center,

having meditated upon the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātṛ*), who is in her fertile season (*ṛtumati*), who is the head of the Vedas, and who is presided over by the Puruṣa, as being situated within the union of their sexual organs;
Having circled around the fire-pit, the wise practitioner should discard a small ember; with the Astra-mantra, he should utterly destroy all malevolent spirits, and thereafter,
having transferred the Fire of Knowledge (Jñānāgni), he should kindle the sacrificial fire.
One should contract that [fire], which is flashing forth in all directions according to the analogy of one lamp from another, back along its own path through the womb-path;
then, one should kindle the pure fire within the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
First with the *vyāhṛtis*, and afterwards with the fire-mantra (*agnimantra*) in due order; then one should pray with the mantra:

"O Cit-piṅgala, [use] the pair *hana*, burn, burn, [and] grant in two ways; O Omniscient One, command, svāhā! (cit piṅgala hana dvaṃdvaṃ daha dvaṃdvaṃ yaca dvidhā sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā). Then, one should bow.
I bow to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings (Jātavedas), the consumer of oblations, who is golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions;
having thus performed the ritual worship, one should assign the tongues and limbs [of the deity].
The syllables of the seven tongues of flame are proclaimed as *śa-ṣa-ṣa-ṇa-va-la-ra-ya*, endowed with the sixth vowel (*au*) and marked by the *bindu* and *nāda*.
The first is ruby-colored, the second golden, and the third is auspiciously red.

O Supreme Goddess, one should sequentially join and place [the syllables] with the seed-syllables: Lohitā, Acatā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, Karālikā, and Kālī, in order upon the penis, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes. O Sovereign, one should assign them according to their sequence.
The Rāścis, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Pannagas,
Piśācas, and Rākṣasas— these seven classes are to be remembered;
likewise, Sahasrārcis, Svasti, Pūrṇa, and Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa.

One should assign the six limbs with [the mantras] "Dhūmavyāpin," "Saptajihva," and "Dhanurdhara," ending with the word "Hṛd" in the dative case; thereafter, one should assign the eight forms (mūrtis):
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, and so forth.

One's own belly is the fourth; then one should place Vaiśvānara as the fifth, and Kaumāratejas as the sixth. One should install the faces of the Viśvedevas upon the head, the shoulders, the sides, the hips, the navel, and the regions of the waist and flanks.
These [mantras] are the forms of the fire of all that is to be known (*ajñeya*), following the sequence of the limbs (*aṅga*).
Having thus deposited [the mantras] upon his body and sprinkled it all around with water,
he should then strew *darbha* grass in the directions and leave the remainder for Vaiśvānara.
O Jātavedas, bring the man here from every direction; O red-eyed one, at the conclusion of all things, accomplish the rites as well—Svāhā!
This [mantra] is the *Tāravaktra* with the *Citpiṅgala* ending in *Ane*.
Then, having worshipped the nine fires, one should worship the tongues [of fire]; then one should worship the limbs in the center and in the six corners;
then the deities of the directions—the lords of the Vasu-petals, the Earth, the Vedas, and the quarters—should be worshipped again.
Having worshipped Agni Vaiśvānara, who is triangular and of reddish luster, clad in white garments,
adorned with red jewels, seated upon a lotus, and holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons (*vara*), a lotus, the *svastika*, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhīti*).
The wise one should meditate upon [the deity] adorned with various golden garlands;
then, having sprinkled the vessels with arghya water for purification, he should turn them face upward and place them there. He should then pour [the water] into the praṇītā vessel.
One should pour water from the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels into the vessel [for the *arghya*],
and likewise place all other sacrificial materials (*homadravya*) into the various vessels;
one should also place a flower into the *śruk* vessel, the *śruva* ladle, and the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
O beloved, one should prepare a vessel provided with the aforementioned [ingredients] and fumigate it on all sides;
in all the pits for the wicked, one should surround them with garlands of lamps arranged in three rows around the sacrificial pit, and then offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis.
Having worshipped Brahmā in the south, one should indeed offer oblations with the Vaiśvānara mantra;
for the sake of attaining perfection, one should contemplate the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*.
Having worshipped the Śrīcakra according to this procedure, one should contemplate it therein.
Then, having invoked Mahātripurasundarī together with all the goddesses who are the mistresses of the wheels (*cakreśīs*), one should subsequently offer oblations with ten *ājya* libations,
following the sequence beginning with the dismissal (*visarjana*).

One should offer oblations of clarified butter to the Yoginīs, beginning with Prakaṭā, who are the mistresses of the wheels of the head, one offering for each in due order; thereafter, one should offer oblations to the supreme goddess of one's own chosen deity using the aforementioned substances.
An oblation in a ruby-colored [fire] bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhi*); in a Rudra-colored or golden [fire], it leads to the attainment of the fruits of all desires;
in a red [fire], there shall be pacification (*śānti*), and in sequence, immobilization (*stambhana*).
Exorcism is performed with Dhūminī, as are inciting hatred and causing death;
thus, O Goddess, the supreme characteristics of the fire-oblation have been told to you.
There is no other way, O lady of excellent complexion, for the pacification of the multitude of worldly obstacles.
Taking recourse in the location of the lamp, one should perform recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should draw a tortoise (*kūrma*) consisting of eight squares and designate a central space.
One should write the vowels in pairs, following the sequence starting from the east.
One should write these seven groups of letters in order starting from the east; the eighth group of letters should be joined at the end. This is the Kūrma-cakra (Tortoise Diagram).
Wherever the letter of the location [of the deity] falls, there the Goddess’s success resides; of this there is no doubt. 90.
The syllable *Stha* is to be known at the mouth; on its two sides are the two *Karas*.
There, the center is the fruit of emptiness, while the pair of squares is the giver of death.
This is the belly of the tortoise; the feet follow in sequence from the west. *Ro*.
If it should fall between the *gaha* and *nikara* [sections] of the tail, it bestows poverty and causes suffering; therefore, one should resort to the mouth.
In that very place, O beloved, there is accomplishment through the command of the venerable Guru, and nowhere else.
One may designate a region, a site, a city, or even a village;
or even a lamp should be prepared—how much more so should one perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) and sacrifice?
Thus ends the section on recitation and fire-oblation in the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*.
The Thirty-Second Chapter, titled "The Characteristics.
The venerable Lord said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice (*sādhana*) of the King of Wheels (*cakrarāja*), for one whose mantra-knowledge (*vidyā*) has been thus perfected.

Listen to the procedure: having drawn a wheel with vermilion powder, one should meditate upon the effigy of the target there; then, by writing their name with a pen made of *kāñcana* (gold), it shall instantly become blazing and thus delude them.
Then, O beloved, it is further explained: freed from fear and having cast aside shame, the practitioner (mantrin), situated in the midst of that [state],
should contemplate himself and the sādhya as having a ruddy radiance.
Bhāgyasundara, surrounded by mudrās, should worship with red offerings; for him whose name is correctly recited ten thousand times, she indeed becomes a servant,
appearing as a woman of unseen form and bearing the marks of the wheel.
Having drawn [the diagram] with meditation and having assumed the *yonimudrā*,
there shall be a swift attraction of a daughter of the gods, a princess, or even a daughter of the Vaiśya caste,
using equal parts of *gorocanā* and saffron.
One should offer sandalwood paste from Mount Gandhamādana, a tilaka performed one hundred and eight times,
flowers that enchant all, fruit, water, food, perfume, clothing, ornaments, and betel nut— all previously consecrated with mantras— to whomever [the mantra] has been entrusted.
O Goddess, even a female servant becomes like a queen by gazing upon her;
one should worship [the deity] with red karavīra flowers smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) for exactly one month, while meditating on the name of the person to be won over.
O Maheśānī, performing [the ritual] thus until the end, one should worship her who possesses a ruddy luster;
within a wheel fashioned from vermilion, one may in an instant delude even a king and swiftly attract even Rambhā,
who is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
One should indeed draw a wheel with a red liquid in a "house of thought" (a diagram); by means of a wife, a messenger, or anyone at all, it destroys fever in an instant.
With the juices of arka and nimba, one should draw [the wheel] using an arka twig as a stylus.
One should draw the wheel in a place where the two [parties] meet;
having placed it in cow urine, it will effect enmity within eight days.
One should fumigate with sandalwood at night, or otherwise wear it upon one's clothing. Then, eight...
By repeating [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one may delude the three worlds. Then,
having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should draw [the design] with yellow pigment (rocanā) and contemplate a beautiful image of the deity’s form, richly adorned with ornaments.
One should inscribe the Great Vidyā of one's birth-name, joined to the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the generative organ,
interspersed with the *saṃ* and *ku* syllables, and placed within the joints of all the limbs, together with the *Kāmakūṭa*.
Having become intent upon the goal, one whose body is the installation (*nyāsa*) of Śrīvidyā should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times while performing the Kṣobhiṇī seed-syllable and mudrā;
one should then unite that [Vidyā] within the abode of desire (*kāmagṛha*), which consists of the digits of the moon and the sun.
Overwhelmed by passion and excessively distressed, tormented by the arrows of desire,
she named Trailokyasundarī was instantly and utterly infatuated;
or else, the knower of mantras, having encircled her with the *mātrikā-cakra*, [should act].
One should properly worship the wheel and maintain the complete Vidyā;
then there is no doubt that one becomes invulnerable to all wicked beings, such as tigers and the like.
[One should worship] with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron.
One should write one's own name in sequence and write the *mātṛkā* as before;
by that, there is no doubt that the practitioner attains freedom from old age and death.
O Goddess, having joined [the letters] individually with the *Kāmakūṭa*, [one should write] the letter *Sa*.
One should surround the Mātṛkā letters outside up to the end of the three triangles of the *dhāraṇī*; this, placed within gold, should be worn on the crest-lock or anywhere at all.
Even the kings who are world-protectors and honored by the three worlds become subdued.
By this procedure, all fevers such as those arising from the combination of humors (sannipāta) and so forth are brought under control; having properly prepared the excrement,
one should cast it at a crossroads in the middle of the land, in the directions starting with the east, in due order.
The kings shall always be his servants due to his good fortune;
he shall contemplate the earth, which is composed of radiant splendor, along with all things moving and unmoving, within the periphery of the disc for six months. Then, that man [attains his goal].
By this, one certainly becomes beautiful and charming in the world;
having seen it, one attracts people, destroys poisons, and likewise removes fevers. Furthermore, by its gaze at night, one takes away poisons and effects possession.
One should worship that which is drawn with vermilion with a one-pointed mind;
it performs attraction even from afar, from hundreds of yojanas.
One should worship [the deities] in sequence in the cardinal directions and corners without interruption.
When this world is thus brought under control—and not otherwise—one should draw the wheel upon birch bark using yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and saffron (kuṅkuma).
One should inscribe one's own name within it, or [the name of] a country or a city. Maṃ...

The practitioner of mantras should cause a wheel to be placed upon the ground at a dangerous or uneven spot, or he should hold it; by that means, he agitates the city in an instant. [The substances used are:
the juice of the *unmatta* plant, lac, the milky sap of the *arka* plant, saffron, and yellow orpiment.
Having mixed together musk and lac, one should write [the name] with it; O Goddess,
whatever fear there may be for that person— whether from thieves,
disease, planets, enemies, lions, or any other source— [is destroyed].
Whether it be *hija* or *vājija*, it deludes everyone in an instant.
A wise man should draw [the diagram] with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*),
placing the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the middle, situated within both triangles at the bottom.
Therefore, one should wear that wheel; after seven days, one will become a servant (kiṅkara).
One should draw the mantra on the rim of the wheel with yellow substances, and below it, having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should cast it toward the eastern direction.
Therefore, even Brahmā and even a Jīva would fall into muteness;
by this procedure, one should draw that [diagram] with indigo juice.
Facing south, the mantra-practitioner shall burn his enemies in the fire.
One should scrape [the surface] with buffalo dung, horse dung, and cow urine;
having placed it in fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), it shall produce enmity in an instant.
One should write the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the center and enclose it within the syllable *kāma*.

Having drawn [the figure] in the sky with substances such as *rocanā* (yellow pigment) so that it is visible to the eye, one should swiftly cause the enemy to be driven away; this is declared to be "forcible expulsion" (*haṭhoccāṭa*). [This is done] with *rocanā* mixed with milk and extracted from the juice of great indigo (*mahānīlī*).
One should draw a wheel with lac-dye and bring the four castes under one's control;
by this rite, one should establish it in water, and by that water, through bathing, drinking, or eating, one attains great good fortune—of this there is no doubt. Pī.

One should worship that wheel in the east; it subdues all disputants. The wheel smeared with vermilion in the north brings the world under one's control. Then, the wheel drawn with red ochre and worshipped in the west [achieves the same].
O beloved, if a man places this— which brings subjugation even to deities, let alone women—
into milk that has been forcibly smeared with *rocanā*, it effects paralysis, enmity, disease, and expulsion.

Situated in the midst of fire from which [the seed-syllable] has been burnt, it shall destroy all enemies; if it is placed in the midst of cow urine, it shall cause the eradication of the enemy; O Supreme Goddess, by that very same [method], it shall bring about enmity. Siṃ.
One should draw the wheel at a distance, in a secluded place or at a crossroads, beginning from the outermost edge toward the center, and write the Mātṛkā [alphabet] there.
According to the sequence of the Kula practice, one should worship the Krama during the night.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that one becomes a sky-walker (khecara) from Dhaka;
on the night of the fourteenth day, standing firm, one should worship Rudra upon the Rudrabhūmi ground.
By the count of six months, through that [practice], one becomes none other than Rudra himself.

The practitioner of mantra attains everything that generates supernatural powers— collyrium, the power of invisibility, the magic pill, sandals, incantations, the sword, good fortune, vetālas, yakṣiṇīs, servants, and so forth; it is not otherwise.
On every fourteenth and eighth lunar day, being composed in mind,
one should worship the Śrīcakra for twenty-one nights upon the surface of a *preta-śilā*; in that way, the practitioner becomes worthy of worship even by the gods.

O Maheśvarī, by means of the noose, goad, bow, and arrows— these human weapons— one becomes Kāma; he becomes the captor of the women of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla), and he himself performs a great attraction.
In the same way, O Dear One, by means of the weapons of Kāmeśvarī, the self of the Goddess attracts men throughout the three worlds, and kings become her servants;
this meditation on the Kāmakalā has been described according to the distinctions of its seed-syllables.
O Goddess, through the worship of Vāgbhava, the knowledge of Sarasvatī arises;
one should worship her, who is adorned with white ornaments and garments, with white flowers. O Goddess, by this rite, the worship of Vāgbhava is accomplished.
Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the incapacity of the arts of love (*kāmakalā*):
Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and Mahākāma— these five previously mentioned desires follow one after another in sequence.

One should delude this world with this essence of desire: the seven Great Kāmeśvarīs, who reside in the temple of the god Madana situated between desire and passion, who dwell in his chamber, and who are the fish-bannered one (Kāmadeva) contained within their fold. Mū...
O Great Goddess, subtler than the thread of a spider's web in the creation and destruction of the world beginning with *la*, the power Kuṇḍalinī exists within the *kūṭa* of powers;
she is the goddess Tripurā of the three peaks, the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
Since sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great power always bestow accomplishment upon the virtuous by taking refuge in this wheel—
thus ends the application of the Vidyā in the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā*.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Accomplishment of the Seed-Syllable" (Bījasādhana).
The Blessed Lord said: Now I shall describe the rite of initiation (dīkṣā), which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds, according to the previously mentioned method for the nine-fold [mantra].
The practitioner should join the marked interior with the intellect;

thus the weapon-mantra (astra) is produced. O Dear One, [the mandala] consists of an eight-petaled lotus, then a twelve-spoked wheel, then a sixteen-spoked one, then a twenty-spoked one, and finally two circles.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus on the ground;

then, in its center, one should worship the supreme Tripurā. Having first worshipped the limbs (*aṅgas*), one should worship the three cities within the triangle, and the Mothers upon the eight petals.
She who intoxicates, she who is without birth, she who is eternal, stainless, untainted, moistening, and afflicted by passion; she who flows with the liquid of intoxication,
she who is beautiful, she who follows the path of the Blessed One, and likewise Kāmeśvarī.
The mistress of lovers who kindles desire, Lalitā,
unshakeable through the Lalitākrama of her own free will;
the auspicious Śaṅkarī of terrifying nature, Kamalā, the mistress of the lotus, with a blue neck.
Vāviśālākṣī, Bheruṇḍā, and Parameśvarī are to be worshipped in the [first] kalās; then, in the twenty yonis, Māyāvatī, Mahākṣī,
and Sarvavaśaṅkarī, along with Samayā.

Samayī, Īśānī, Nityānandā, Mahodayā, Sarvasaubhāgyadā, Ānandā, Candrikā, Candraśekharā, and Sarveśvarī—these are to be worshipped on the eight-petaled lotus of the seat (pīṭha). Bhū... [end of fragment]
One should worship Tripureśī within the house, marked by the *dīkṣā-yoni*;
in front of her, one should worship the *kalaśa* together with its base using grains,
and fill it with special perfumes, flowers, gold, and jewels.
Having properly worshipped the Cakrarāja nearby, the preceptors should assign a beautiful name joined with the first syllable; then,
they should unite the disciple with those very gurus.
Having first prostrated correctly, one should write down all the venerable teachers on the ground; then, having worshipped the Vidyā properly with flowers and other offerings,
O Dear One, one should show the Vidyā— having been recited a hundred times— to the disciple.
If there should be great affection for the disciple who has given his life,
then one should mutter the supreme sixteen-syllable Parā-vidyā into the right ear with a single utterance; O Dear One, one should not give it to anyone else.

One should bestow the knowledge of Śambhu known as Khecarī upon a king who has granted his kingdom, or even upon a son who has given up his life; for such an instruction, which is beyond description, arises from the vision of Brahman.
One should sprinkle oneself three times with sprouts placed in the water-pot; then one becomes consecrated, and at that time, that leader of initiates,
endowed with the reality of the mouthfuls of water (gaṇḍūṣa-tattva), is worthy for the worship of Śiva.
Otherwise, O Pārvatī, there is no accomplishment whatsoever for one who possesses conceptual thought;
for such a person, there is no success anywhere, as Śrīvidyā turns her face away.
All of this is given to the Guru, who can even wash away ignorance.
Therefore, O beloved, this initiation has been declared which brings about the perfection of mantras. Having been initiated, O Maheśānī, one should perform the ritual application;
one should perform the rite of the special *argha* offering and afterwards bring forth the messenger (*dūtī*).
One should accept a beautiful-faced woman adorned with the rules of the samaya-conduct,
born from one of the eight fields and families, youthful, with lovely eyes,
filled with joy and delight, whether she be of ordinary form or have a deformed face.
One should avoid a woman who is deformed, aged, secluded, or angry.
Having recited the *Bhagamālā* mantra, one should worship her vulva;
there, one should worship the *Śrīvidyā* as proclaimed in the sequence of the nine wheels (*navacakra*).
O Goddess, one should worship Śrīvidyā, the sixteen-syllabled mantra, in the form of Kāmeśvarī, resplendent with the weapons of Kāma, upon the *liṅga*.
I shall now describe Kāmeśvara there in his various forms, O beautiful lady.

One should worship her who dwells in the supreme seat (Parā-pīṭha) shining above the seats beginning with the Vedas; who is the Goddess Kalā within the heart of the three peaks (Tri-kūṭa); while muttering the mantra "Śivāya Ca";
and indeed, one should worship Svādhiṣṭhāna with its own syllable by means of the Lord of the Nine Wheels (Nava-cakreśvara).
O Beloved, he who is capable of assuming any form at will is the master of the science of love; O Goddess, the sound *sīt* is the sacred syllable *oṃ*, and speech is called *japa*.
A kiss is eternal bliss, and the pressing of the breasts is the worship of Śiva.
Nail-scratches, tooth-marks, and the like, as well as worship with flower garlands and so forth,
beating, and the offering of oblations— know these to be the rites for the "heroic flower" (vīrapuṣpa).
Having taken the semen (vīrya), one should place it specifically within the *argha* water.
With that nectar, one should satisfy the Śrī Devī according to the Kula path.
Because of excessive disclosure, the feces, urine, and likewise the menstrual blood of women, as well as the semen and other primary Kula substances, are not [to be disclosed] except by good fortune.

If Bhairava arises [within him], he attains siddhi; of this there is no doubt. The knower of mantras who is free from conceptual construction is directly Brahman; of this there is no doubt. Having understood the rites for specific desires and occasional rites, one should propitiate Śrīvidyā.
O Supreme Goddess, here the authority belongs only to one who has been initiated; he who,
having seen what is written in the book and having understood it for himself,
performs [the rite], is freed from the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth.
"He is defiled by this; of this there is no doubt—he shall dwell in hell.
[Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Dīkṣādūtī-yajana," in the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā. Śrī.
Īśvara said: Furthermore, O Mahēśānī, I shall describe the great Pavitrāropaṇa rite; when this is performed, everything is considered accomplished, whereas otherwise it is said to be as if empty.
He who does not perform the pavitra rite once the year has passed—
Having unified the three [months], its fruit is forcibly brought about by those of evil mind.
O Dear One, Āṣāḍha is the best month, Śrāvaṇa is middling, and Bhādrapada is inferior; this applies to both the bright and dark fortnights. It is praised...

It should be during the bright fortnight, or if that is not obtained, during the other [the dark fortnight]; one should perform worship on the fourteenth, eighth, and full-moon days, as well as the new-moon day. The cord should be made of fine silk or likewise of cotton, and it should be threefold.
Having tripled [the threads] and washed them with pure water, one should then dry them while facing west with the mantras of the right [hand]; thereafter,
one should have beautiful purifiers (*pavitra*) fashioned with mantras.

One hundred and eight knots are best, fifty-four are middling, O beloved, and twenty-seven are the lowest; or else, O beloved, one may make ten knots according to one's capacity with the mantras recited facing north.

O Daughter of the Mountain, O Supreme Goddess, on the day before the day of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitra), she should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) using various substances such as vermilion, turmeric, and saffron; or else, O Sovereign Lady, she may perform the preliminary consecration on that very same day.

After the daily worship together with those who have taken the pledges (samaya), one should request the thread-vessel from the left using the mantras for the upper lion-throne; then, having performed protection and veiling with the *su* and *va* mantras, [one proceeds].
A tooth-stick, as well as fragrant substances, ashes, sandalwood, clay, white mustard seeds, and the dhātrī fruit— these eight,
beginning from the east in successive order, are the pure thread and the vessel.
One should cast [offerings] upon the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*).
Kumāra, Soma, Svāhā, Īśa, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhīdhvaja,
Sūrya, Sadāśiva, and Sarva are the deities for the nine days.
In the Sūtras, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa on the three threads; likewise, Kriyā, Pauruṣī, Vīragāyatrī, Aparājitā,
Jayā, Vijayā, the Goddess Muktidā, and Sadāśivā.

One should worship all the deities residing at the knots—the Manonmanī, Navamī, Daśamī, and Sarvatomukhī—with the ritual offerings (upacāras). Having invoked them with the root mantra (mūlamantra), one should worship the Kalās within the sacred threads (pavitra).
O Goddess of gods, O Beloved, one should then meditate upon the Śrīvidyā, who consists of the sixteen Nityās.
The procedure for the consecration (adhivāsa) has been declared; thereafter, the propitiation (ārādhana) shall take place.
Following the daily worship (nityārcanā), this occasional rite (naimittika) shall occur:
[the offering of] sacred threads (pavitra) along with food to all the maidens.
Thereafter, one should worship one's own guru with garments, ornaments, cows, and wealth according to one's capacity;
having prostrated, one should contemplate him in the form of the Goddess.
Free from stinginess regarding one's wealth, one should then place the sacred thread (*pavitra*) upon him.

Where the Guru is worshipped, there the ritual act becomes fruitful. In the absence of all others, one should worship another who has arisen from the same lineage as the Guru. Wherever one worships one's own Guru, there these ritual acts become successful.
O Parameśvarī, if it is not worshipped, these [offerings] become fruitless.
After offering the *pūrṇāhuti* into the fire, one should offer the *pavitraka*. One should worship that which is the goal and the accomplishment of the Śrīcakra and present it to Her.
"Indeed, for one who does not perform this, even their worship is fruitless.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the *pavitra*. Śrī Īśvara said:
"O Maheśānī, O beloved, I shall now describe this *anāropaṇa* (the non-installation)."
O beloved, the sādhakas should perform [the rite] even with a goat whose horns have fallen off;
the three months beginning with Caitra, both the bright and dark fortnights,
and among these, each preceding period of time is the most excellent of all.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or the full moon day,

one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) during the first part of the night, or even immediately; having first addressed *Damana* and the others with the four *Kalpalatā* mantras and so forth.
Bathed by the tears from the eyes of Rati, born from the eyes of Kāma;
salutations to you who delude the sages, gandharvas, and siddhas;
for the sake of Śiva’s work, you are not new by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed Rati and Kāma, the wise practitioner should worship them there; he should personally uproot the *damana* plant along with its roots and sprouts,
or else have it brought by another, or obtained from the crown of the Goddess’s head.
O Goddess, one should establish [the vessel] in the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala;
having established this vessel filled with water, one should then worship it with the Praṇava,
the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī, and "namas" as well.

Now the mantra of Kāma for the Great Goddess is being told: *Oṃ*, the seed-syllable of desire (*Klīm*), and *Kāmāya namaḥ*. One should worship Madana, who has entered the bud, there with these two mantras.
One should place small boxes upon the petals of the central lotus, starting from the east,
using eight distinct mantras accompanied by eight substances in their respective order:
Kāma, Bhasmaśarīra, Anaṅga, and Manmatha.

Vasanta, his companion Saṃjña, Smara, Kṣudhanurdhara, Puṣpabāṇa, and Tārā and the others, ending with Aṅga and Hṛd, are proclaimed [as the limbs]. O beloved, [the substances] are camphor, a pair of yellow pigments (rocanā), and musk. Then... 12. O beloved... a.

O Pārvatī, having properly worshipped Damana with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth— namely, guggulu, saffron, dhātrī fruit, sandalwood, and a collection of fragrant flowers— these being the eight substances; |||

With a serene mind, one should recite the Anaṅga-Gāyatrī according to one's capacity: "Kāmadevāya vidmahe, Puṣpabāṇāya dhīmahi, tanno Anaṅgaḥ pracodayāt. (We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon him whose arrows are flowers; may that Anaṅga inspire us.)
"Salutations to the one whose arrows are flowers, who brings joy to the world;
to Manmatha, the eye of the universe, and the beloved of Rati’s affection.
O Goddess, after this mantra, one should then offer salutations. Now...
Holding Madana in his hand, he should make a request to the Goddess:
"O Śivā, you have been invoked by me this very day;
O Goddess, by your command, the Pūrṇaparvata [rite] must be performed according to what is available."
One should satisfy Tripurā with the mantra known as Jñāpanā;
then, O Lord of Gods, having worshipped the Mother of the World— who bestows the fruits of all desired objects— with sixteen syllables, using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
O Goddess, O Sovereign Mistress of Desire, fulfill the desires residing in my heart; with this, O Goddess, one should pray, and thereafter, O Sovereign Lady, one should perform the *damanaka* ritual,
covering it with armor and likewise with the *astra* mantra.
Then one should perform the vigil; however, if there is no immediate vigil, then having risen at dawn,
one should perform the daily worship (*nityapūjana*), and thereafter perform the occasional worship (*naimittika*).
One should worship with devotion; having performed the worship together with that very [mantra],
along with beautiful flowers mixed with the central [flower],
and having duly prepared an excellent food offering (naivedya) containing camphor, one should offer it to her.
One should offer betel and then pray:
"O Mother of the Vedas, embodiment of all mantras and the essence of all vidyās, by your command, may this desire of mine be fulfilled. Then, [one should honor] one's own guru...

Having worshipped him with flowers, ornaments, garments, and other offerings, and having given the *adamana* fruit to him, one should bow down and propitiate him; thereafter, one should joyfully engage in water-sports together with one's companions.
One should perform the gift of food endowed with the six flavors;
for the wise person who thus performs this sequence of the installation of the restraint,
his annual worship becomes presided over by Śrīvidyā.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Installation of the *Damanaka* and the Procedure for Occasional Worship," in the *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Saṃhitā*.
This *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* is complete. May there be auspiciousness! In the year 1950 of the Kali era, in the month of Caitra, in the middle of Jambūdvīpa.
